He provides analysis, breakdowns, profiles, and reports on important news and transactions from and about the Ravens. His professional resume as a sports reporter includes covering local events, teams, and athletes in his hometown of Anchorage, Alaska for Anchorage Daily News. His coverage on the Ravens and other NFL teams has been featured on Heavy.com/sports, Maryland Sports Blog and most recently Baltimore Beatdown from 2021 until 2025.

title: 3 Winners and 8 Losers From Ravens' Deflating Loss To Bengals
full_text:
The Baltimore Ravens lost back-to-back games for the first time this season in Week 7 on Sunday by allowing a second straight divisional rival to come from behind as the Cincinnati Bengals beat them 35-13 at home .
With franchise quarterback Lamar Jackson out with an ankle injury for the third week in a row, they came into this game as slight underdogs to come out on top but looked like they were well on their way to defying the odds and pulling off the upset after dominating the first half.
Unfortunately,  they went from pitching a shutout to getting shut out in the second half and blowing another double-digit lead for the second week in a row in even more epic fashion. With the loss, they fell to 4-3 and are bottom of the division, where they rightfully belong given how they've played the past two weeks.
Here are several Ravens players and coaches who stepped up and showed out, and others who made some costly mistakes from coaching and execution standpoints.
The two-time Pro Bowler was the only player who balled out in this game and couldn't be stopped no matter what the opposition did to try to slow him down. Flowers eclipsed 100 receiving yards in the first half of a game for the third time this season and for the first time without Jackson playing either half. He finished with a team-leading eight catches on 11 targets for 137 receiving yards and his third touchdown of the season.
ZAY FLOWERS TOUCHDOWN!!!!! 48-YARD TOUCHDOWN TO @ZayFlowers !!! Tune in on CBS! pic.twitter.com/RDspeiOR3T
In a game where Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow was nearly sacked what felt like a half dozen times, the second-year pro was the only defender who managed to actually get him on the ground. Green's third sack of the season and the Ravens' lone sack of the game came at the perfect time, as it secured their first-half shutout since it came in the final 31 seconds and kept the clock running with Cincinnati out of timeouts.
No one picks up Mike Green up the middle leading to a Ravens sack and a 13-0 halftime lead. pic.twitter.com/u3qtCq5E0k
The second-year pro didn't have to attempt a field goal over 40 yards, but the fact that he made all three of his kicks, which included an extra point, bodes well for him after a costly miss inside 50 yards last week. It remains to be seen if Loop has truly gotten past his second-half kicking issue, as the Ravens bypassed their only field goal opportunity in the second half to try to capitalize in the red zone on fourth and short.
There were so many culprits from this unit who were culpable for the Ravens' downfall in this game that they deserved to be lumped together. After only allowing Burrow to complete half of his dozen passing attempts in the first half for a measly 43 passing yards and no touchdowns, they got carved up and torched for 249 and four touchdowns in the second.  Burrow went 16-of-18 over the final two quarters because the Ravens' defensive backs were being taken advantage of and making mistakes every which way.
They failed to plaster in coverage on extended plays, did not properly pass off routes in zone and just straight lost and were outmatched in one-on-one situations at the intermediate level and deep down the field. Tee Higgins went off for 148 receiving yards on six catches, while Ja'Marr Chase made several impressive key grabs, and both scored touchdowns.
The Ravens were able to build their double-digit lead by predominantly having backup quarterback Tyler Huntley throw the ball all over the yard, in large part because their running game couldn't get going, and that didn't get any better after halftime. They weren't able to get any traction on the ground and were especially poor when it came to short-yardage situations, even before stud first-round rookie left with a knee injury. Their inability to win at the point of attack in the trenches has been the main reason the offense as a whole has struggled in Jackson's absence and why they've gotten held to under 100 yards rushing as a team in back-to-back games for the first time since Weeks 2 and 3 of last season.
In his first game against his former team, the four-time Pro  Bowler went from breathing down Burrow's neck for most of the first half despite facing constant double teams to not being much of a factor in the second, along with the rest of the Ravens' pass rush. He finished with a team-leading two quarterback hits, one of which was nearly a sack, but his revenge game was ultimately spoiled by an epic second-half collapse from the unit as a whole.
After a torrid start to the season, the future first-ballot Hall of Famer has been held to fewer than 100 rushing yards and out of the end zone in back-to-back games for the first time since Weeks 13 and 15 of the 2024 season. While he claimed that he had a "terrible" individual performance, that was simply him falling on the sword for his blocking, or rather lack thereof, since he was contacted in the backfield far too often for negative plays and runs that barely got back to or past the line of scrimmage.
For the second week in a row, the first-year play-caller went from looking like the next coming of Sean McVay in the first half to having no answers or adjustments in the second. With his young tight ends struggling to make and sustain blocks out of condensed formations, he didn't run the ball enough out of spread formations, and his biggest mistake was not using his mobile backup quarterback's legs enough.
Huntley isn't Lamar Jackson in terms of his ability to cut and move laterally; nobody is, but he is a strong North-South runner. Doyle didn't dial up a single quarterback power or draw for him and waited until it was too little, too late to call his first and only quarterback sneak, which didn't come until the fourth quarter when the Bengals were up by 22 points and had all the momentum, and it failed miserably.
As has been the case in all three of their losses and even in some of their wins, the Ravens struggled to bring ball carriers and pass catchers down in open space and short of the line to gain, and especially in high-leverage moments after halftime. They went from flying around and playing fast and physical downhill with great results in the first two quarters to missing multiple opportunities to make key stops and force negative plays for sacks and tackles for loss.
According to PFF, the Ravens missed 11 tackles (7 on pass plays). Here's 4 from the 4th quarter. pic.twitter.com/fkc5MK6DUA
Chances of winning division
While the Ravens still possess a winning record heading into next week's massive road conference matchup with the Buffalo Bills, they're now the only team in the AFC North without a win against a divisional opponent. If the rest of their rivals keep stacking wins, they won't be able to make up any ground until December, since they close out the regular season with four straight division games, concluding with a road primetime game against the Bengals on New Year's Eve and a home finale against the Pittsburgh Steelers 10 days later
Having Huntley under center in this game instead of Jackson nerfed any chance the Ravens had of winning a shootout with Burrow and the Bengals, but it didn't come to that until after halftime. However, as bad as being without a two-time league MVP is, that should have no bearing on how woefully poor the defense played for the final two quarters.
A collection of star-studded talent that was being hailed as a potential top-10, if not top-five, unit got absolutely dog-walked up and down the field on their way to making history in the worst way by becoming the first team in the franchise's 31-year history to get outscored by 35 or more points in a half. The fact that they haven't scored a single second-half point in six of the eight quarters they've played without Jackson is an embarrassing travesty that falls on the shoulders of the players and coaches collectively.
Josh is a writer for Baltimore Ravens On SI focusing primarily on original content and…

title: Everything Ravens Coach Jesse Minter Said About Lamar Jackson And What It Means for Sunday
full_text:
Ravens rookie head coach Jesse Minter, now going on a week into quarterback Lamar Jackson’s absence from an ankle injury, was more guarded than ever speaking about the lingering isse after Wednesday’s practice.
Minter spent three weeks calling it a “day-to-day” situation with Jackson even though the two-time MVP said last week it was a high-ankle sprain that was “very, very painful.” Minter would not even specify whether Jackson did any more or less work than he was able to do last week and he repeatedly referred the injury report.
When the injury report was released, Jackson was listed as a full participant. He suffered the injury at the end of the first half in Week 4 against the Titans, he did not return to practice until last week in a limited capacity, and Baltimore has continued to blow double-digit leads at an astounding rate without him, now 4-3 heading into a crucial game at Buffalo they are frankly unlikely to win without Jackson.
“He was able to get some work in, but I think that will come out about 4 (pm), I believe,” Minter said about his injured QB. When pressed on the matter about the extent of Jackson’s work Wednesday, he said: “Um, yeah, I think the more you are able to do, and respond from and feel from raises your optimism but, again, we’ll kind of see how it goes through the week.”
When Jackson was brought again, Minter offered: “I think the injury report will kind of say how the practice went.”
Minter is wise to take a more cryptic route given how things transpired last Friday when Jackson spoke to the media for the first time since suffering the injury and spoke to a timeline quite different to what the front office was giving Minter as his public marching orders on the situation (just another ugly public embarrasment for the Ravens ignominious PR chief). The CBS broadcast added to what could only be rightfully perceived as a disconnect from how the team was couching the injury, and how the player himself was speaking about it.
Our instincts and reporting have been far better than the media at large since the moment Jackson suffered the injury, and at this point, a short turnaround against Jacksonville at home in prime time, we’d be surprised if Jackson played Sunday unless he practices fully all week.
Kyle Hamilton (knee), by far the best performer on a struggling defense so far, was among those who did not practice Wednesday (rookie guard Vega Ioane did not either and is expected to miss time with a knee injury). Minter said he “felt pretty good” that some of the players who were unable to work on the field Wednesday could still be back for Week 8. Middle linebacker Roquan Smith (knee) also missed practice.
The Ravens have lost 17 times since 2019 when leading by 10-or-more points and have done it twice in a row against AFC teams and three times this season. General manager Eric DeCosta, who loves to gush about his relationship with Jackson but can’t ever get his contract extension like a competent GM, got to handpick Minter and his novice staff, should have been fired when Harbaugh was, and his job security is a major subplot to the upcoming trade deadline for his latest middling roster.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: What Ravens Week 7 Debacle Changed About Their NFL Trade Deadline Plans
full_text:
The Ravens’ long-suspect defense was getting exposed by bad NFL quarterbacks in the second half of games all season so the fact they got shredded by Joe Burrow Sunday wasn’t much of a surprise. However, the blasé response from a roster loaded with defenders in the top 10 in compensation at their position was alarming.
Longtime NFL coach Marvin Lewis explained to us the poor coverage technique and communication breakdowns that have crippled this Ravens secondary as it has most of them since 2019. Overwhelmed rookie head coach Jesse Minter was asked about the effort of his defense after yielding 35 unanswered points in the second half to the Bengals and remarked about their tackling issues. He’s openly pondering who, among his highly-compensated defensive roster and a secondary almost entire filled with first-round picks, will emerge as a real leader - 'Who's the guy that's going to grab everybody together, get them together on the sideline?’ he opined at his Monday press conference.
Yeah, this is critical mass, already, nearing the midpoint of the first season without a proven head coach in Baltimore for a loooong time.
The only person in power in Owings Mills who is being more runover and exposed than Minter is the perpetual underachiever who hired him – general manager Eric DeCosta. The guy who amassed even more money and power when longtime head coach John Harbaugh and his experienced staff were fired in January, despite needing to be fired at the same time.
The guy who likes to strut the sidelines like a coach with his sunglasses on at night looking for the cameras during prime time games – oh, he’s sweating now with his head in his hands in the locker room after games. The guy who always blames coaches for his roster failures is alone on the hotseat now; DeCosta knows his defensive backs are a joke and now he needs to do something about it. Already $370M committed in payroll, and with injured MVP quarterback Lamar Jackson able to dictate any more he wants with any team he prefers this offseason , DeCosta must try to salvage his defense, and Sunday brought it all to a head.
Believe it or not, DeCosta needs a defensive back, desperately (preferably a slot corner), and he needs to ship one out.
It’s not just about on-field direction, it’s about sending a message now going on seven years of getting DeCosta-ed game after game: three losses with a double-digit lead in the second half this season – two in a row! - and 17 since 2019, when DeCosta took over for legend Ozzie Newsome (and like every other Newsome protegee, we see just how little of Newsome’s unique genius transfers to others).  Sure, it would be great if DeCosta backed up his silly narrative about wanting both Maxx Crosby and "closer" Trey Hendrickson back in March with a trade to the Raiders without backing out and exposing himself this time. But that was just a grift to try to sell tickets .
Despite years of shunning most every other personnel group on his roster to stock up on DBs, they have a crisis there. The Ravens are getting killed in the slot, their corners and safeties have poor ball skills and never impact the football. And more than anything else, they better change their choking culture with over-entitled and underachieving players on bloated contracts – ever-rewarded for being one of DeCosta’s favorites – and shake up the dynamics of a failing locker room.
They won’t get anything for Humphrey with that $15M salary ($19.3M in total take-home pay this season) at the deadline and it doesn’t matter. He’s worn people out on multiple coaching staffs and in that locker room for years, he’s had one truly good and healthy season in the past four, and if they haven’t moved him to the slot yet, maybe that’s telling us all something. Because the slot coverage has been as bad as any in the NFL.
TJ Tampa could get a run on the outside with Nate Wiggins (you better get a real GM in here before DeCosta does another asinine contract with one of his over-drafted first round picks who lacks anything close to a playmaking gene). Maybe that helps.
But if you keep sending the message to this overhyped and over-coddled secondary (man do DeCosta and complete baseball failure Mike Elias have a lot in common) that everyone keeps their job no matter what, and the performance on the field and in the locker room and on the sidelines doesn’t matter, then keep your mouth shut and eat it when you keep getting DeCosta-ed every week.
Because that’s what’s going to keep happening.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: Ravens GM Claimed He Wanted Crosby And Hendrickson In March. He Should Prove it Now
full_text:
Believe it or not, Ravens general manager Eric DeCosta has built another failure defense.
Of course, it happens every year – outside of one time with Mike Macdonald in charge – with a feeble roster devoid of playmakers on that side of the ball but filled with bloated contracts he loves to dole out to his favorites . Turns out even genius rookie head coach Jesse Minter – looking overrun and clueless in the second half of games with the most novice staff in the NFL (like DeCosta wanted) – can’t keep this team from constantly blowing double-digit, second-half leads and losing.
Now they’ve DeCosta-ed two weeks in a row to division foes, and three times already this season and they’ve DeCosta-ed a record 17 times since 2019. Baltimore has allowed more points than any NFL team in the second half (114) with an unfathomable -70 scoring differential. And, as always, DeCosta’s handpicked players offer zero pass rush when it really counts - $30M alleged "closer" Trey Hendrickson has four pressures, a 10% pressure rate and no sacks in the fourth quarter – and the team does not have a second-half interception despite being thrown on constantly.
DeCosta, every bit as smug and condescending and egomaniacal as Orioles baseball failure Mike Elias, thinks he’s a rare roster builder. But his first-round pick corners and safeties (Kyle Hamilton is a linebacker) and top-10 paid corners have combined for as many picks this season as my dog Meatball. Minter, lauded as a defensive scheme savant, is getting undressed every week – usually by bad quarterbacks – in his zone looks in dime coverage; he’s scared to blitz and he can’t muster pass rush late in games bringing just four.
The Ravens are 20th in opposing passer rating; 27th in opposer passer rating targeting the slot. They-re getting destroyed by anything close to a No. 1 receiver and Minter is already opining about aimless locker room leadership. Man, we are only seven games in with DeCosta’s handpicked coach and fraud alerts are going off all over Owings Mills. Did I mention the top two coaches the Ravens fired, to keep DeCosta in charge, John Harbaugh and Todd Monken, are top NFL Coach of the Year candidates?
So, um, what’s this overhyped GM going to do about it? The one who, if the billionaire he works for wasn’t checked out and half-asleep, would have been fired when he fired Harbaugh in January? Maybe DeCosta should just do what he was running his mouth about in March. Seems logical enough. Being a man of his word and all, and such a hotshot dealmaker.
Hey Eric, just go back to that big plan you had this winter. The one you couldn’t shut up about when you bailed out of the Maxx Crosby trade. Surely that wasn’t just a grift to help your boss sell tickets was it? That wouldn’t be you.
You don’t want to be the King Of No Rings forever, do you? Man up, champ.
In case you missed it – this is what was being peddled over at Baltimoreravens.com on March 11 with the breathless headline: Ravens Wanted To Get Crosby And Hendrickson:
“General Manager Eric DeCosta confirmed reports Wednesday that Baltimore actively worked on deals with Crosby and Hendrickson at the same time. “That was definitely a possibility for us. Not to say that it would've happened, but definitely something that we had contemplated and discussed with Trey."
So since then, DeCosta failed to get Lamar Jackson signed – again, as usual – and he could be in his final year here if that’s what the two-time MVP decides he wants . DeCosta built maybe his worst offensive line yet – that truly saying something by his lowly standards – and he’s helped cultivate another controversy about Jackson’s health by having his puppet coach call a high-ankle sprain that’s cost Jackson three games a “day-to-day” situation going on a month.
Boy, this perpetually-underachieving exec, who built a career and reputation off of Ozzie Newsome’s work (DeCosta is the epitome of Newsome’s fruitless scouting family tree ), really has dug himself a big hole this time. But good thing he already told his fanbase what to expect back in March, with that master plan for two dominant edge defenders (well, Hendrickson doesn’t defend much of anything in the run game, but you get the idea).
Because nobody needs Crosby more than this huckster right now. And nobody flapped his jaws about him more in the offseason.
There isn’t a more desperate and panicked exec than DeCosta anywhere in the NFL right now.
The Seahawks (with the kind of elite GM) DeCosta pretends to be) landing All Pro guard Quenton Nelson for far less than DeCosta just gave up for concussed lineman Cam Jurgens, a delusional bounty for a struggling lineman is a bad look (Ravens had their worst run blocking of the season in Jurgens's first game with them, bummer). And multiple GMs I’ve touched base with believe the Raiders would still deal Crosby for two ones. So there’s hope!
Now, the problem is, the league knows DeCosta’s word doesn’t mean much, and they know he played the medical card as an excuse to pull out of the Crosby trade because the entire industry believed he had overpaid (just like he ended up doing for Jurgens, funny how that works). And because Hendrickson had a soft market (since he’s older and become injury prone and is a liability on early downs).
But Eric, your prayers have been answered! Crosby returned for Week 1, miraculously, and guess what? He’s still kicking ass.
Get this, he’s playing like 95% of the reps for the Raiders and can still dominate games. And we all know he’s a significantly better football player than Hendrickson, I mean that’s why you went after him before Hendrickson and then (oh man this is rich) concurrently. And Hendrickson turns out to be the guy who can’t finish a game or stay off the injury report. Yeah, who could have seen that coming.
And worst of all, the guy actually leading your pathetic roster in sacks – Tavius Robinson – is out for year. You already started mortgaging the 2028 draft for Jurgens, Jackson has you by the throat in that negotiation, and with a record $370M payroll, what’s another $15M for Crosby? You think Jurgens was worth $17M? Crosby at $29M next year is a steal.
It's only money, and Steve has plenty; but your word is worth everything, isn't it?
Salary cap issues? Take that base salary down to vet minimum, give Crosby the money up front, maybe tack on money on the back end to get him to come back here. Least you could do for the odious way you handled him in March. Who cares about draft picks now when you’re wasting what could be Lamar’s last year in Baltimore. And let’s be real, most of yours don’t really pan out, anyway.
You weren’t taking your fans for fools back in March, were you? You wouldn’t have your vast in-house media laundering false promises and BS, would you? No way. Not you. So go execute that big plan you and Bisciotti were hatching six months ago.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: Three Players the Ravens Need To Move On From Before the NFL Trade Deadline
full_text:
The Baltimore Ravens have reached a crossroads way before the mid-season point, losing two straight in truly ridiculous fashion -- shutting out their opponents in the first half and then getting shutout and overtaken in the second.
Thus, the Ravens currently sit with a 4-3 record in last place in the AFC North -- a division they were heavy favorites to win -- and with a road game in Buffalo on the horizon, things could start to unravel quickly for Baltimore.
With the NFL trade deadline less than two weeks away, the Ravens must consider unloading a few players in order to either acquire some immediate help in return, or start loading up on draft capital for next year. Either way, several names on Baltimore’s roster just don’t make any sense for the team anymore, regardless of what eventually becomes of the 2026 campaign.
Here are three players that the Ravens should consider trading away before the deadline:
As hard as it is to say goodbye to the top pass-catcher in franchise history, it’s time.
Andrews hasn't just become a non-factor in the Ravens’ offense , but also a liability with dropped passes. Sure, there is no clear successor at the tight end position, and Baltimore wasted a huge opportunity by letting Isaiah Likely walk in free agency, but Andrews is just not cutting it anymore (averaging $13M/season makes it tough).
Rookie Matthrew Hibner was, at one point, playing on more than half of the Ravens snaps, and fellow-rookie Josh Cuevas has seen his usage go up steadily as the season has progressed. Veteran Nick Vannett took some snaps away from Hibner once he was promoted from the practice squad in early October, but that was expected. Blocking specialist Durham Smythe, on the other hand, will miss the rest of the season due to an Achilles’ injury.
The depth chart might not be in a great place, but Andrews is not making very much of a difference anyway. He hasn’t reached 50 receiving yards in any game (he's done it once since the start of last season), and has a single receiving touchdown for the season. He’s also recording personal lows of 7.8 yards per catch and 5.5 yards per route run.
Baltimore really needs to spread out Andrews’ targets among the remaining three tight ends and rookie wideout Ja’Kobi Lane, and see who will step up as the passing game’s safety net of the future.
At an average of just 20 rushing yards per game and 12 receiving yards per game -- as a pass-catching alternative to Derrick Henry in the backfield -- Hill is just not working out. At his current pace, he would finish the season with under 350 rushing yards and just over 200 receiving yards, and he hasn’t scored once either way. He hasn’t logged a broken tackle for the year, either.
The Ravens haven’t been great at maximizing Hill, either. He’s averaging 3.0 yards before contact per rush -- compared to Henry’s 1.9 -- and 6.7 yards per rushing attempt, but Baltimore isn’t giving him enough carries to make a difference or at least find a rhythm.
The market for soon-to-be 29-year-old running backs with limited production and no previous experience as the top guy will be miniscule, but Hill does contribute on special teams and is considered a reliable blocker. It’s just that he’s not taking enough of the load off Henry’s shoulders .
Adam Randall is still on IR with no word on when he might be coming back, and the Ravens have Jonathan Ward on the practice squad, so looking for a street agent option could work. The pool of available guys with experience as primary runners is attractive for a team looking at a one-year rental, including Raheem Moster, Alexander Mattison, Kareem Hunt, Antonio Gibson, Miles Sanders and Joe Mixon, and each one of them should have an accessible price tag.
Walker’s case is truly strange. A 25-year-old fourth rounder from 2024 who has the same number of touchdown catches than starts in his pro career (five), but just 11 receptions over 20 games played.
His 0.75 yards per route run this year seem almost impossible to believe, yet here we are.
It seems Baltimore’s passers just don’t trust Walker, because his usage on the field isn’t dramatically low. He’s played in almost 40 percent of the Ravens’ offensive snaps this year, yet has managed just nine targets and four catches. All this despite top wideout Zay Flowers missing one game and top rookie Ja’Kobi Lane missing four this year , so there have been some chances.
If the Ravens aren’t going to try and develop Walker, they should trade him to a team that will. Rookie fourth-rounder Elijah Sarratt has played in just one game and sorely needs some of the reps that Walker has been handed with no returns. The compensation for Walker will be very low, but his production after two and a half years has been even lower.
Rafael brings over two decades of experience writing about all things football.

title: Ravens Film Room: Why The Secondary's Failures Are Likely To Keep Getting Exposed
full_text:
There was every reason to suspect that Joe Burrow was going to carve up a suspect Ravens pass defense, which was struggling in critical areas even against lowly quarterbacks. And sure enough Burrow threw four touchdown passes with a perfect passer rating in the second half, as the Bengals mustered 35 unanswered points.
Is there any reason to think it will be any different against former MVP Josh Allen on Sunday? Or a quality Jaguars passing attack on a short week after that? Was there anything in the film against the Bengals – or in obvious passing situations late in games or when attacked in the slot or when managing third-and-long situations – that would portend a turnaround anytime soon?
This secondary has not been good for quite some time, and it is not good under rookie head coach Jesse Minter, no matter how much money failing general manager Eric DeCosta spends on certain players and no matter how high he picked them in the draft. It’s screaming out for a shakeup, but Baltimore already has a $370M payroll, they overpaid for lineman Cam Jurgens in trade and would have to find someone to take a big salary (like this defensive player’s for instance ) off their hands to make a meaningful addition.
These DBs do not get their hands on the football, they are not scheme disciplined they look like man corners who are lost in many of Minter’s zone concepts in the most important times. At this point it’s fair to expect this to be who they are, once again, unless the pass rush ramps up in a remarkable way.
A year ago, $19M corner Marlon Humphrey and recent first-round pick Nate Wiggins were one of the three most exploited corner duos in the NFL; it’s not nearly that bad this year, but they also haven’t faced many quality QBs, and Wiggins, who had been stout against the Bengals in the past, struggled mightily on Sunday (six completions on eight targets for 80 yards and a TD) and needs to slough that off, because Humphrey isn’t ascending in any way shape or form.
“He's played better football,” longtime NFL coach and defensive coordinator Marvin Lewis told me on “The Daily Flock” of Wiggins after watching Sunday’s film. “And he just has to get back, in my opinion, to doing that. Some of the things that have happened in  a lot of their games, they've been having some communication errors in the back end.
“And I think that's you see that across the NFL quite a bit. That's why you see the offenses motioning into all these bunches and stacks and formations to make guys communicate on the perimeter. And if one guy doesn't see it the same or communicate it, then you leave a guy wide open. And that happened a little bit … Yeah there's some things probably, technically, I would clean up um guys coach people differently in today's NFL.”
Many of these issues are lingering and deeply embedded and Minter tweaking the scheme hasn’t changed nearly enough. The Ravens are 20th in the NFL in opposing passer rating (95.5). but when you filter out the linebackers – who account for all three interceptions on this team (none in the second half of a game) you see how acute the coverage problems are.
Minter, who badly needs someone with head coaching experience like Lewis to join him on staff , is averse to blitzing and is now down a starting edge defender for the season (sack-leader Tavius Robinson). If $30M pass-rusher Trey Hendrickson doesn’t start operating like the “closer” he was hyped up to be , this defense is cooked.
Wiggins has never had strong ball skills, they refuse to move Humphrey to the slot (perhaps that will come if TJ Tampa gets activated from IR this week), and free safety Malaki Starks (another recent first-round pick) has yet to look anything like a ballhawk despite this defense being set up for him to, in theory, be just that.
Ravens corners and free safeties in coverage this season:
Opposing QBs : 91/ 135 (67.4%), 1139 yards (8.4/att.), 7 TD – 0 INT, 110.7 rating
7 Pass Break Ups, 12.5/comp, 17 comp 20+,  55 1st Downs
Minter said: “You could look at a bunch of different plays where it's something different - where it's certain coverage one play, certain coverage another play, certain guy one play, certain guy another play, playing a coverage one way versus the same route, or playing a coverage two different ways versus the same route even though we're in the same coverage … To me, it just starts with us putting them in a better position. [It] always starts with the coaching, in my opinion, and I'll leave it at that.”
Minter is playing in dime nearly a third of the time, which is nearly twice as much as anyone else in the AFC, and it’s not working. He’s going to end up shifting to more nickel (five defensive backs), and better hunt better match-ups in the slot. Blitzing and playing man better become more a part of this mix, too.
We’ve been writing this for weeks,  but if Humphrey can’t help this team in the slot, then where can he? Should be his strength. This had been a failure from scheme and execution.
Burrow didn’t lean into the slot as much as we thought he might, but did go 5/6 for 51 yards and TD when targeting those pass catchers. On the season the Ravens are among the NFL’s worst, allowing a 121.9 rating on slot targets (27th), and 75% completions (48/64), with four TDs.
Minter needs to switch it up in there.
He probably needs linebacker Teddye Buchanan, working back from season-ending ACL surgery, to help more in coverage against bigger bodies and try to free up Kyle Hamilton to hunt the ball more. If Minter ends up having to move Hamilton more to a free safety role, it’s a bit of a white flag about how this defense was supposed to function, and time to wonder if 2026 is going to end up far closer to 2025 than anyone has the stomach for.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: It's Time To Start Worrying About Derrick Henry. History Says Ravens Better Limit His Workload
full_text:
The Ravens’ default in Derrick Henry’s first two seasons in Baltimore, when times got tough, were simply to ride the workhorse back to stabilize the offense and keep the defense off the field.
And perhaps, once Lamar Jackson returns from an ankle injury that rookie head coach Jesse Minter insisted on calling “day-to-day, ” the combination of those two in the backfield will reignite a staggering run game. But there is also serious reason for concern that this 2027 offensive line will be general manager Eric DeCosta’s biggest failure of them all, and that a desperate trade for Cam Jurgens won’t be a panacea, and that Father Time is creeping in on Henry unlike at any time prior in his career.
What has been bread-and-butter – gutting teams with outside zone, winning in short-yardage, and the expected surge from a renewed emphasis on under-center runs – is now more like a moldy croissant – Henry is starting to look like a 32-year-old running back (historically when careers expire at that position as 55 years of data pointed to ). And at a time when the Ravens let All-Pro fullback Pat Ricard leave as part of their talent exodus, and with powerful blocking tight end Durham Smythe lost for the season and with this line struggling and their best lineman Vega Ioane, looking a potential absence due to injury, Jackson is likely going to have to boost this thing with legs more than anything else.
Henry’s body language looks different, during and after Sunday's debacle.
He seems to know holes are going to close before they open and he almost sounds defeated. Whether or not his football mortality is peering back at him remains to be seen, but rookie coordinator Declan Doyle is riding him hard – 147 carries leads the NFL and are second in NFL history through seven weeks for a 32-year-old back since the 1970 merger – and now feels like a good time to scheme up some stuff for his understudies.  Doyle threatened to run Henry 300 times or more – would be first time in Henry’s career he’s done that three years in a row – but perhaps they need a rethink .
“Got to be better,” Henry said after averaging 2.9 yards/carry Sunday. “It's not good enough. Terrible. I'm looking at myself. I think every man can look in the mirror, but as far as myself, I can speak on me.
“It's not good enough at all. We got to figure it out. Everybody evaluates themselves, coaches are going to evaluate and we can go from there. It's just not good enough at all for us to be able to win games and be able to string drives together [and] have an impact on the game as far as the running game."
Henry needs help at this stage of his career and he’s not getting it. Baltimore’s 1.33 yards before contact are the team’s lowest since 2010, their 4.7 yards/carry as a team is the lowest since 2018, before Jackson was the full-season QB. Defenses are picking up keys and tells and shutting down inside runs and the pitch plays. Minter seems to think Doyle needs to find solutions.
“Any time you look at specifically the run game, to me, it's - what are you asking the guys to do,” Minter said Monday. “Can they do what you're asking them to do when you go to the line, to the tight ends, to the wide receivers?
“Obviously, we lost one of our key blocking tight ends a few weeks back, and so it's like, what are we asking some of these younger guys to do? Can they do it? Can we be good at the things that we're asking them to do? So, I think it's just a constant search for the schemes, the plays, what you're asking the guys to do.”
Henry is averaging 3.9/carry – 26th in the NFL and his lowest through seven games since 2019. These three areas beg major questions:
This was a cheatcode for Henry his first two years here. And maybe when Jackson comes back it will be again. But left tackle Ronnie Stanley isn’t special anymore, and the interior offensive line, sans Ioane, has a chance to be one of the worst in the NFL.
The Ravens averaged 5.9 yards/carry running outside zone in 2024-20425, which had a lot do with Henry winning a quadruple crown in that span – most carries (632), most rushing yards (3516, nearly 300 more than anyone else) with 32 rushing TDs and 5.6 yards/carry. That run will not continue this season.
Henry's 3.9 yards/carry is the average for all 32-year-old backs since 1970, and Baltimore is at 4.9 yards/carry on outside zone. The last three weeks Henry has 94 yards on 27 carries on outside zone (3.5/carry). They have faced bad perimeter rushing defenses in recent weeks and bad defenses against outside zone, and been stymied, anyway.
“We (have) to search for those better answers on how people are playing us,” Doyle said after Sunday’s’ game when the offense failed to score again in the second half.
Henry ran more under center than anyone in the NFL in Tennessee before joining the top shotgun offense in the NFL, in terms of usage, in Baltimore. Doyle made getting under center a major emphasis this offseason, but DeCosta let an All-Pro center leave in free agency and replaced him with cheap journeymen who got hurt and now they have no under-center run game.
We’ll see how much Jurgens helps. Baltimore averaged a season-low 0.30 yards before contact Sunday. The last four weeks he is averaging 3.7/carry on under-center runs, 27th in the NFL.
Third-and-1 has been a disaster around here since around the middle of last season. Turns out firing Todd Monken as offensive coordinator – he is a front-runner for NFL Coach of the Year in Cleveland nearing the midpoint – wasn’t a solution there. This is now worse than ever.
The Wild Cat stuff works every once in a while, but I suspect Jackson on bootlegs and keepers will be a calling card when he comes back. The Ravens third-down run conversion rate (40.9) is their lowest since 2003 – yeah, 2003 – and they rank 29th in the NFL in third-and-one and fourth-and-one rushing this season.
A bad offensive line undermined this offense a year ago. It could do so on a much grander scale this year.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: Marvin Lewis Could Help Fix The Ravens' Defense. If Jesse Minter Calls, He'll Listen
full_text:
The Baltimore Ravens badly need someone with NFL head coaching experience on their staff, ASAP, to try to help the franchise pull out of a seven-season funk with a collapsing second-half defense.
Rookie head coach Jesse Minter seems overmatched and bewildered right now – allowing 35 unanswered points to the Bengals Sunday was a nadir for the once-proud defense  – and some alarming missteps from the offseason are already coming to roost. Building one of only two coaching staffs in the NFL that included no one with former NFL head coaching experience was really something, especially for how novice most of the staff was , and there are obvious issues with players being undisciplined to the system once playing with a lead, repeated communication mishaps, pathetic tackling and massive issues with pass rush and coverage.
The general manger is out of his depth, too, and already made a ridiculously desperate trade for a slumping offensive lineman in concussion protocol, and who has been running the team as if his job might be in the balance. Eric DeCosta should have been fired when head coach John Harbaugh was, and he seems to be squirming now . The building in tense, the GM, coach and players have proven to be chokers; the two-time MVP quarterback (Lamar Jackson) is injured, the team can’t manage its messaging about his high-ankle sprain in a coherent manner ( abhorrent PR is very much their brand ) and they’ve blown 13-point leads in successive weeks to division foes.
Worst of all, they have DeCosta-ed – losing a game in which they lead by double-digits in the second half – a record 17 times since the start of 2019 (he is the constant) – and already done it three times this season in Minter’s first seven games. As always, we have a plan to help the perpetually underachieving franchises in this town; the Ravens should have hired Marvin Lewis when they put the staff together and they need to call him now (like I did Monday).
The Commanders just brought in former head coach Steve Wilks to help their overwhelmed young defensive coordinator and the Cowboys brought in Mike Pettine to do the same thing and head coach DeMeco Ryans took over play calling on defense in Houston and the Broncos, who nearly went to the Super Bowl last year and could do so this year, turned things around once head coach Sean Payton took over offensive play calling.
Lewis ran the Ravens defense at its heights, had a great run as Bengals head coach, helped young head coach Antonio Pierce as an assistant head coach with the Raiders in 2024, and follows the league closely doing syndicated calls of NFL games on the radio. He’s watching Ravens film, he knows their culture and history like few could, and he is at a stage in his career where it’s not about his padding resume, but rather helping young coaches succeed in a place he cares deeply for.
So when I tooK the pulse of the Ravens systemic issues with Lewis on “The Daily Flock Show” (a deep dive on their defensive woes) Monday I had to ask if he’d try to help his buddy Ozzie Newsome out and be a resource for Minter if the team reached out. Lewis wouldn’t consider leaving his home in Arizona for much, but this would pique his interest should the Ravens do the right thing.
“Well, I would be remiss in saying I wouldn’t listen,” Lewis said about any hypothetical Ravens interest. “You’ve got to listen. And there are people you want to help, and more important than me; it’s somebody I would want to help and support. That’s what’s important more than anything.”
When former Ravens defensive mastermind Mike Macdonald left to become head coach in Seattle – the one that got away – he didn’t bring in a family member to be his mentor, he secured the services of successful former head coach and defensive coordinator Leslie Frazier. They won a Super Bowl in Year Two. It should have been a prerequisite for Minter’s staff, and the Ravens have a history of doing this sort of thing in-season, be it Dean Pees and Jerry Rosburg rejoining the franchise out of quasi-retirement .
He was invaluable for Pierce, he has recent experience at Arizona State University as well so still understands how to relate to young players and his wealth of experience is unlike anything on this staff currently. He did special projects for Pierce, helped with inactives and was a sounding board for him to sit in on coordinator meetings throughout the week and offer insight to the head coach in private.
“Thursday and Friday he gave me about four minutes in practice where I could go over a special situation that may come up in the game, where it’s a backed-up situation for the offense or the offense threw a big pass and now it has the ball at the 25-yard-line. And I wouldn’t tell those coordinators what the situation was going to be for the day, because we wanted them to think on their feet and be ready to call it that way …
“A lot of things like that I did, and I was a part of the defensive meetings and I’d look at the opposing defense and would go in and talk to the offensive coaches. “When you do this, this is always their response.’ We saw a little bit of that yesterday (in the Ravens game) I think in how Cincinnati kept building their formations.”
The Ravens badly need new eyes and ears in their meeting rooms. Here’s their second half rankings:
Yards Per Play: 6.0 (29th) Passing Yards : 147 (29th) Yds/Att.: 8.0 (30th)
INT/Att .: 0.00% (T-last) First Downs : 12.3 (30th) 3rd Down: 44% (24th)
QB Rating: 117.0 (28th) Comp % : 71.3% (28th) TD-INT : 8-0 (32nd)
Both of Minter’s starting corners were embarrassed by the Bengals Sunday, Lewis noted in our discussion how much Nate Wiggins was attacked, while Marlon Humphrey lost the plot in coverage and suffered in tackling. Their corners and safeties do not have an interception all season; their culture is warped and on Monday Minter hinted at how deep it runs.
“We have guys that care and want to do it right,” Minter said, “but there's also moments in the game where it's like, 'Who's the guy that's going to grab everybody together, get them together on the sideline? I think as a team, we're working through who that is.
“Who is that person? Who are those players? There’s guys that want to do it, and then there's guys that maybe they're dealing with something, or they're not playing the way they want to play, so they don't feel like they can do it in those moments.”
Maybe a former head coach could help the rookie figure out how to bring it out of them.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: Were Ravens Surprised Lamar Jackson Missed Bengals Game? Could He Play Sunday? Jesse Minter Explains
full_text:
Ravens rookie head coach Jesse Minter continues to speak in guarded and cryptic tones about the status of two-time MVP quarterback Lamar Jackson ahead of a critical game at Buffalo in Week 8. The team is nearing the midpoint of the season in a downward spiral and Jackson, recovering from what he called a "high-ankle sprain," has arguably a greater impact on regular-season wins and losses than any NFL player.
Minter’s defense is getting overrun in the second half of games – allowing 114 points in the second half, most in the NFL – with some in rival NFL front offices believing the young coach needs help from a former head coach/defensive coordinator to fix systemic issues in their game-day process. In two straight weeks the offense has failed to score in the second half with back-up Snoop Huntley filling in, while the defense blew a 13-point lead to the Browns and Bengals.
The Ravens have an NFL record 17 losses with a double-digit lead since 2019, the collapses have only gotten worse under Minter – allowing 35 unanswered points Sunday at hom e was a new low – and while general manager Eric DeCosta’s rosters are undoubtedly a major part of the problem ( his job security should be under intense scrutiny after head coach John Harbaugh was already fired for all the late-game debacles), Minter is in the crosshairs now and badly needs his best player back.
After asserting for three weeks – during which Jackson never once practiced fully – that the star was “day-to-day” with an ankle injury that the team was certainly couching as not too severe – Minter stayed away from that wording on Monday. But he uttered it again as recently as Friday, although Jackson made it clear in his remarks on Friday that the injury was extremely painful, saying he still has been unable to run normally since suffering the injury in Week 4.
“I think he’ll be in a decent spot but we'll know a lot more on Wednesday,” Minter said.
It’s fair to assume at this point that Jackson will not play until he is able to practice fully with no setbacks. The CBS broadcast of Week 7’s game referred to “swelling” over the weekend after limited practice Wed-Fri as the cause for Jackson being downgraded to out on Saturday after being listed as questionable on Friday’s injury report.
“I’m not going to speak really on the details of anybody’s injury,” Minter said. “… Look, if he’s able to play and is healthy enough to play and play the way he needs to play, then he will play.”
The CBS broadcast also asserted that the Ravens were surprised that Jackson was not able to face the Bengals. To that Minter said, “I would say a little bit,” pointing to an ongoing feeling-out process with the ankle.
Of course, the backdrop to the situation is the fact that Jackson is the rarest of superstar quarterbacks in his prime who has reached a point in his contract with no future guarantees beyond this season. He carries an untenable $85M cap hit in 2027, with a no-trade clause and a no-franchise tag clause, which gives him NBA levels of leverage over where he plays next season and how much he makes .
Minter continues to say that Jackson is “working his butt off” to return as soon as his body will allow him, and he has repeatedly refereed to this decision as one the team and QB and medical staff would make together. The Ravens win 70% of their regular season games that Jackson starts and are a losing franchise without him since he took over as starter midway through the 2018 season.
His career arc with them has been highly unusual throughout, demanding a trade at one point and getting no interest as a de-facto free agent on a non-exclusive tag, which later become fodder in an NFLPA collusion case. Given the strange backdrop between player and team, calling this a “day-to-day” injury for the better part of a month seems to have been another unforced error by this franchise.
Beating Buffalo coming off a bye would be a stretch and the Ravens have a quick turnaround hosting Jacksonville on Thursday night in Week 9.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: Three Reasons Bills Must Be Careful With James Cook's Workload
full_text:
James Cook is one of the best running backs in the NFL.
However, the Buffalo Bills have fallen into a dangerous trend of relying on Cook more than any other team relies on a single running back, and it could have long-term implications on his play.
Cook has carried the ball 117 times so far this season, the seventh most in the NFL, although four players ahead of him have played an extra game. Regardless, that number in and of itself is not the issue. The problem is the numbers for the other RBs on the team.
Ray Davis has just five carries this year , and Ty Johnson has two. Frank Gore Jr also recorded one attempt in Week 1.
The ratio of Cook's carries to Davis's is 117 to 5, or 23.4 to 1, which is significantly higher than any other backfield in the league.
In fact, it's almost 15 attempts more than the next closest ratio in Detroit or Cleveland's backfields that are around 8 to 1. The league median is 2.6 to 1.
The Bills’ RB1 vs. RB2 usage is crazyyyy James Cook: 117 rushing attempts Ray Davis: 5 That’s a 23-to-1 ratio 👀 pic.twitter.com/iVjfdsDPod
There's no reason not to give the ball to your best offensive weapon more than anyone else on the team. But look at that chart! Buffalo needs to split the backfield up a little differently for a multitude of reasons.
This applies to both the short term and long term. On a game by game basis, the Bills are going to want Cook at his best. But the Bills are also going to want to lean on Cook in the December and January, when the stakes are higher and the weather is colder.
The more carries Cook racks up in the early part of the season, the larger toll that will take on his body. Which brings me to the next reason...
Cook is in the first year of a four year extension, meaning he still has three more seasons making north of $13 million . The back also just turned 27, inching closer to the daunting age 29 falloff seen by many RBs over the years.
If the Bills continue to use Cook the way they currently do, it could fasttrack his decline, shortening the peak of one of the most talented players in Bills history.
Davis and Johnson are not James Cook. But there's a reason the Bills haven't changed the makeup of their RB room for several seasons now.
Josh Allen regularly refers to Johnson as "the best third down back in the league," while Davis was able to display his burst and elusiveness last year as a kick returner, leading to a First-Team All Pro nod. Davis also has four career games with double digit carries, and he's averaged 4.3 yards per carry or better in each of those games.
Not to mention, Davis and Johnson would also be behind one of the best run-blocking offensive lines in the NFL, currently ranked second in ESPN's run block win rate this season.
As the season progresses, the Bills would be wise to take some of the workload off of Cook's plate, choosing to lean heavily on him only when necessary.

title: Bills' First Week 8 Practice Report: Which Injured Players Were Prepping for Ravens?
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills hit the field for their first practice following last week's bye, and multiple key suspects were present and accounted for.
With the team seemingly approaching full strength heading into the November 1 home game against the Baltimore Ravens, wide receiver DJ Moore and defensive tackle Ed Oliver were back in action at One Bills Drive.
Both Oliver and Moore were inactive for the Weeks 5 and 6 road games prior to the bye, so their practice participation is a sign that they're on track for a return to the lineup.
Tight end Dalton Kincaid and edge rusher Bradley Chubb, who were banged up last time out against the Las Vegas Raiders on October 18, both participated on Wednesday.
Wearing red non-contact jerseys ( h/t WGR's Sal Capaccio ), both players are nursing rib injuries. Kincaid and Chubb were cleared to return against the Raiders after in-game evaluations. The former re-entered when the Bills took possession with 8:01 left in the fourth quarter, and he made a 14-yard reception three snaps into the drive.
Initially spraining his AC joint in Week 2 , Moore reaggravated the injury during the Week 4 loss to the New England Patriots, and he's been out of the lineup since.
Having not missed a game since December 2020 with the Carolina Panthers, Moore was apparently not comfortable watching from the sideline.
"It was obviously frustrating for him, but for him, it was the best thing to do," said Bills' head coach Joe Brady .
Moore, who was officially questionable to play heading into the last two games, was still wearing a red non-contact jersey on Wednesday, but it is presumably just for precaution.
Oliver took a hit to the left leg in the knee area during the October 4 game against New England and was subsequently ruled out.
After missing five consecutive official practices , Oliver logged limited participation on Friday, October 16. He was questionable before being scratched on game day against the Raiders.
Believed to have a minor MCL issue, Oliver seemingly had enough rest and recovery over the past 3.5 weeks. Oliver, a 2019 first-round draft pick, is cornerstone up front for Buffalo.
"There's a reason that Ed Oliver is who Ed Oliver is, and getting him out there and being able to play football again is only going to help our defense and our identity," said Brady prior to Wednesday's practice.
It's been more than nine months since wide receiver Tyrell Shavers has played competitive football, but that drought will end soon enough.
Working his way back from an ACL tear that occurred during the first half of a wild-card playoff game against the Jacksonville Jaguars, Shavers finally returned to practice on Wednesday. The Bills officially opened his activation window, meaning he has 21 days before mandated to come off Injured Reserve.
Shavers was a depth receiver and core special teams contributor during the 2025 season. It's worth noting that Buffalo currently has six wide receivers on its 53-man roster.
Starting right tackle Spencer Brown did not practice on Wednesday, but he shed light on his absence while formally addressing reporters after the fact.
"It's good. Just lingering stuff from what's happened to me last couple weeks. What happened in that LA game, just kind of got nicked up. Took enough drugs to sedate a small elephant when I was in LA," said Brown.
A back flare-up forced him out of the October 12 game against the Rams after 16 offensive snaps. Tylan Grable came off the bench to man the RT spot for the remainder of the overtime win, and Brown was back in action six days later in Las Vegas.
Brown, who described the issue as a muscle "freak out" prior two weeks ago, apparently sat out practice as part of his maintenance plan. The vet rest will presumably help ensure his availability in Week 8 against Baltimore.

title: Bills Dealing With Disappearance of Greg Rousseau Again
full_text:
Entering Week 8, the Buffalo Bills are fresh off a much-needed bye after starting the months of September and October with a near perfect 5-1 record.
However, despite the solid overall mark in the standings, there were several areas of concern for Buffalo to clean up over the past several days.
The Bills might be winning, but it hasn’t necessarily been pretty . And, that’s particularly the case on the defensive side of the ball in Western New York under first-year NFL defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard .
Wherever one may look, the stats are damning toward Leonhard’s unit.
And, although some players started out the year on a tear—namely defensive tackle Deone Walker and outside linebacker Gregory Rousseau—the entire unit has been a shell of itself from what it once was under former defensive-minded head coach Sean McDermott over the past nine years.
Now, it also appears that those individual stalwarts mentioned above are also beginning to fade, specifically Rousseau, who started out the year with 19 total tackles, 16 quarterback hits, eight tackles for loss, six sacks, three forced fumbles, and three pass deflections in the team’s first four outings of the 2026 campaign.
It appeared that the player nicknamed “Groot” was finally becoming a dominant difference-maker within a new scheme despite the overall struggles of Buffalo’s defense this season under Leonhard—a unit ranked 31st in total yards allowed entering November—but now it seems as if he’s headed back to his old ways.
Well, when looking back on his past production, the sixth-year veteran defender has a history of hot starts before quickly fizzling out toward the middle and end of the season.
For example, according to Pro Football Reference , in 2022 the 6-foot-6, 266-pound pass-rusher tallied 15 total tackles, six quarterback hits, five tackles for loss, and four sacks during Buffalo’s first four matchups of the season before finishing with just 22 more tackles, only eight more quarterback hits, five additional tackles for loss, and three more sacks over the remainder of the season that year.
Furthermore, in 2024 Rousseau exploded for six total tackles, three sacks, three tackles for loss, two quarterback hits, and one forced fumble in the season opener against the Arizona Cardinals before adding only five more sacks the rest of the way while only averaging 0.86 tackles for loss and 1.47 quarterback hits per game in the final 15 regular season games that he suited up for.
Needless to say, fast starts out of the gate before quickly fading have been a common theme for the 26-year-old former University of Miami standout edge rusher ever since entering the professional ranks back in 2021.
And, now that trend is beginning again as Rousseau has posted just two total tackles, two pass deflections, and two quarterback hits over the past two games against the Los Angeles Rams and Las Vegas Raiders.
Yes, he did have a critical game-altering field goal block against the Rams on Monday Night Football , but he was quiet other than that . . . and he was practically non-existent against the Raiders on a short week.
So, while many players and coaches probably needed a reset during the recent bye week for Buffalo, there’s seemingly no player that probably needed one more than Rousseau.
His 39 quarterback pressures are still second in the league through seven weeks according to Pro Football Focus , but “almost sacks” only account for so much, especially with the way the rest of the defense is performing on a weekly basis.
It’s imperative that—somehow, some way—the Bills’ top pass-rusher returns to his early-season form and avoid yet another year of a major statistical drop-off over the second half of the year.
With quarterbacks like Lamar Jackson, Patrick Mahomes, Drake Maye, and Caleb Williams still on the docket for Buffalo later on in 2026 , as well as plenty of other capable gunslingers like Kyler Murray and Jordan Love, takedowns will be more important than pressures moving forward.
Getting things ramped back up in that department against the Ravens and their ailing offensive line at Highmark Stadium would be a great place to start for Rousseau.

title: Lamar Jackson Wednesday Injury Updates Send Bills Mixed Signals on QB's Week 8 Status
full_text:
With how badly the Buffalo Bills' defense has struggled this season, the hope was that they would avoid facing quarterback Lamar Jackson when they meet the Baltimore Ravens in Week 8.
Of course, Jackson has been nursing an ankle injury for the last three weeks and he has not played in a game in that span as a result.
There was some optimism over the weekend and early this week that Jackson would make it back for Week 8 , but the latest injury updates from Ravens practice are sending mixed signals.
According to ESPN's Jamison Hensley , Jackson was on the practice field with his helmet and pads on Wednesday, so the Ravens signal-caller is taking part.
However, Hensley also noted that Jackson's left ankle is wrapped , which is an indication he might not be 100% yet. He also doesn't appear to be running at full power yet, either.
The Ravens won't drop their injury report until later in the day, so we don't have his exact participation level yet, but clearly he's going to be listed as limited, at worst.
A limited session would be anything but a guarantee that Jackson will play, though, as he was limited all three days last week before sitting out. Until he logs a full practice, Jackson's status remains up in the air.
We'll update this page once we have confirmation of just how much Jackson participated in practice.
The first year of defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard has been a disaster for Buffalo.
The Bills enter the Week 8 contest against the Ravens allowing the third-most points per game. They also sport the second-worst pass defense and are just middle-of-the-road against the run.
If Jackson plays, he may present a challenge the Bills haven't seen yet this season, which is a quarterback who is elite at running the football, so we're not exactly sure how well the 2026 defense will hold up against Jackson's mobility.
We say he "may" present a challenge on the ground because, there's also a chance that Jackson won't be at 100% if he does play, so his running ability may not be a big factor.
But, then again, if he isn't 100%, Jackson might not suit up at all after he made it clear last week he doesn't want to go that route because he might end up hurting his team.
"I'm restricted. Like I can't really do what I do. So I'm not helping nobody if I can just go out there and be a statue and get hit," he said. "No positive. Like that's not helping my team at all. That's just me. I feel like I'm being selfish because it's about me at that point for me to get out there and be hurt. That's dumb."
If Jackson doesn't go, the Bills will face Tyler Huntley instead. He would amount to a significant downgrade for Baltimore and, in turn, a massive boost for Buffalo's defense.

title: Bills' Defense Won't Be This Bad Moving Forward If Jim Leonhard Can Make One Fix
full_text:
With six games in the books, the numbers are ugly.
The Buffalo Bills ' defense has shown occasional flashes of competency under first-year coordinator Jim Leonhard, but those flashes have been too few and far between .
"It's time to be good at something," said Leonhard in the wake of a 37-34 road win over the Los Angeles Rams. "It's too inconsistent to pretend that we're building and working and making improvements."
The Bills are allowing 28.5 points per game to opposing offenses. Their pass defense (285.8) ranks next to last in the NFL. Buffalo has allowed at least 30 points in four of its five wins thus far.
For as discouraging as those numbers are, there's a belief that, even without any personnel upgrades moving forward, the Bills' defense has realistic potential for improvement.
Sharing his hot takes on One Bills Live during the bye week, ESPN analyst Dan Orlovsky attributed the problems to occasional in-game lapses.
“There's four or five snaps a game where there's blown coverage, because one guy is doing something different than 10," said Orlovsky, a former NFL quarterback. "If and when they fix that, I think this has got a chance to be a Top 15 defense. They will not be a Top 15 defense until they fix that. There's not a rhyme or reason to exactly all the time why it's happening.”
Those blown coverages have apparently occurred due to communication issues in the defense's back end.
"Our communication isn't where it needs to be right now," said head coach Joe Brady following the Week 5 win over the Los Angeles Rams.
Defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard, who spent 10 seasons as a NFL safety, acknowledged the failures heading into the bye.
"I would say from a coverage standpoint, we need to be cleaner on communication. There's too many times where we look confused when I don't think there's enough options for us to be that confused, so we'll clean that up," said Leonhard.
When the Bills return to action against the Baltimore Ravens on November 1, multiple adjustments are likely to have been made.
"That's the biggest thing in the bye week. How do I help the coverage just play with more confidence, play faster, play more aggressive, allow them to get vision on the quarterback and break," said Leonhard.
The  Bills' defensive front has shown ability to disrupt the opposing passer while staying true against the run.
“[Deone] Walker, once again, outstanding. I thought [Dorian] Williams was great. [Bradley] Chubb was really good," said Orlovsky. "The next step is cleaning up those four to five snaps a game that right now are killing this defense. And if they don't, you'll come on here every week and people will, all week, continue to make fun of this defense."
If Leonhard can get his defense to communicate adequately, then it can become more of an asset rather than a liability down the stretch.
"If they can figure that out over the next two months, I truly believe this defense is good enough, fast enough, schematically diverse enough to be a top half defense in the league," said Orlovsky.

title: Will Lamar Jackson Return to Face Bills? Doctor's Opinion vs. Ian Rapoport's Report
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills know their next opponent is the Baltimore Ravens.
As to whom the opponent will start at quarterback on November 1 in Orchard Park, it doesn't appear that even the Ravens know that at this point in time.
Two-time NFL MVP Lamar Jackson has missed the last three games due to what Dr. David Chao believes is a left ankle eversion sprain . Conventional wisdom suggests Jackson will return for the Week 8 game against the Bills, but there's certainly reason for doubt.
There was a thought that Jackson, although not 100 percent, could have played against the Cincinnati Bengals on October 25. After limited participation in practice, the QB1 was tabbed as questionable to play on Friday's injury report. On Saturday, the Ravens ruled him out.
Meanwhile, Chao, a former San Diego Chargers' team doctor who now offers expert injury analysis, gave Jackson a one-in-three chance to suit up in Week 7.
This week, Chao has issued a 50 percent probability that Jackson returns to game action against the Bills.
"I don't think he's for sure playing this week yet. I think this is a 50-50 week," said Chao on Monday. "Let's see how it develops. It's a big game, Bills, etc., but I don't think it's a guarantee that he's playing. I think it's 50-50 right now."
Lamar Jackson keeps trending closer to a return. Week 6: I had him at 85% no-go Week 7: 66% no-go Week 8: 50-50 This is his best chance to return since the ankle injury. pic.twitter.com/kxbYA7udrK
On Tuesday, NFL Network insider Ian Rapoport appeared on ESPN's Big Day , and proceeded to make a strong declaration.
"I expect, based on the people I've spoken with, that Lamar Jackson will play this week.  He will be on the field this week against the Buffalo Bills," said Rapoport. "He is believed to be as close to 100 percent as he has been, and the Ravens do expect him to play."
As for Ravens' head coach Jesse Minter, his comments did not reach that same level of confidence.
"Lamar's working his butt off to be back, to be out there," said Minter one day after losing to the Bengals. "I'll think he'll be in a decent spot, but we'll know a lot more on Wednesday."
It's also worth noting that Rapoport called Jackson's ankle sprain "a two-to-three week injury."
Quite frankly, it's foolish for him to speak so matter of factly. There have been plenty of instances where this type of injury, depending upon severity, can take up to four weeks, especially when the player relies as heavily on his legs as Jackson does.
There's also reason to question Rapoport's sources in this situation. Last week, Jackson called out the talking head for apparently mis-reporting the injury.
"Ian Rapoport said that? He part of the training staff?" said Jackson during his media availability .
The Bills are 2-2 against Jackson as a starter in the regular season and 2-0 in the playoffs.
While Jackson is probably more likely to play than not, the Bills must prepare in case backup Tyler Huntley gets the call again.
Huntley, who can also tuck it and run effectively, owns an 8-11 record as a starter. He has 34 career appearances under his belt, accounting for 17 touchdown passes and 11 interceptions.
Last time out against the Bengals, Huntley completed 67.6 percent of passes for 298 yards and one touchdown. He was sacked four times and intercepted once in the 35-13 loss.
While the QB choice is TBD, the Ravens will almost definitely be without starting guard Olaivavega “Vega” Ioane due to injury.
As for the Bills' injury outlook , they appear to be nearing full strength in Week 8.

title: Bills' Next Opponent Receives Worrisome Injury News as Ravens Take Another Hit
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills’ players and coaches may have been on a bye week over the last several days , but that wasn’t the case for the majority of teams in the league in Week 7 as the NFL was jam packed with plenty of exciting action last weekend .
For Buffalo’s upcoming opponent—the Baltimore Ravens—things weren’t so exciting on Sunday, though, as the AFC North squad fell short at home to the Cincinnati Bengals, 35-13, after originally leading 13-0 at halftime. The loss marked the team’s second straight in its division to fall to 4-3 on the season under first-year head coach Jesse Minter.
Furthermore, Baltimore appears to have lost an important member of its offensive line during the last matchup with Cincinnati, as well, as NFL insiders Ian Rapoport and Mike Garafolo reported on Tuesday morning that Ravens’ starting offensive guard Olaivavega “Vega” Ioane, who was selected at pick No. 14 overall in the first round of the 2026 NFL Draft out Penn State this past spring, suffered a MCL sprain against the Bengals.
A 22-year-old native of Graham, Washington, Ioane was the fourth offensive lineman selected in the first round of April’s draft, but he was also the first guard to go off the board.
Seen by many talent evaluators as a sure-fire NFL starter, Ioane seamlessly transitioned into the starting lineup for Baltimore this offseason.
Making starts at right guard and center out of necessity due to various other injured players going down earlier this season up front for the Ravens, the former Nittany Lions’ lineman has been a solid presence along the offensive line during his first season as a professional.
In fact, according to the NFL’s Next Gen Stats , the 6-foot-4, 326-pound thumper allowed only a 4.6% pressure rate entering Week 6, and he surrendered zero sacks in 163 pass-blocking snaps ( 84 at RG, 79 at C ), as well, making him the highest-rated rookie guard in the NFL in that critical department.
For that reason, the news of Ioane being sidelined for at least “a little bit” is certainly brutal information to receive at this juncture of the season, especially considering that Baltimore’s franchise veteran quarterback Lamar Jackson is likely set to return to the lineup after missing the past three games with an apparent ankle injury.
If the rookie stalwart is unable to suit up against the Bills this weekend at Highmark Stadium in Orchard Park, then it will mean that the Ravens will be trotting out their sixth different offensive line combination through the first eight weeks of 2026 campaign.
And, while that’s a sight that Buffalo’s AFC counterpart likely doesn’t want to see this weekend, it’s certainly a situation that the Bills and defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard will have to capitalize on .
Whether it be up-and-coming defensive star Deone Walker or former top-10 pick Ed Oliver on the interior of Buffalo’s defensive front, someone on the defensive line needs to dominate their battle with Baltimore’s backup at right guard on Sunday.
The matchup between the Bills and Ravens has future playoff implications written all over it, so it’ll be imperative that Buffalo takes full advantage of any areas of weakness that their upcoming opponent might have.
The objective for first-year head coach Joe Brady has seemingly always been to reach the No. 1 seed in the AFC during his inaugural season as the head man in charge in Western New York, and that goal appears to be more in reach than ever before entering November 2026, especially after the Kansas City Chiefs just dropped their first game of the season on Sunday Night Football against the Seattle Seahawks.
Out of the bye week, Brady and Leonhard must create a plan of attack to push forward with vengeance over the final 11 games of the season.
Exploiting Baltimore’s shortcomings up front would be a great place to start on Sunday.

title: Quenton Nelson Trade Gives Bills Urgency to Make Deal With Colts Immediately
full_text:
We are two weeks away from the NFL trade deadline but one big move has already gone down and that's a stark reminder for the Buffalo Bills that they can't sit around and wait much longer.
On Tuesday, the Indianapolis Colts traded All-Pro guard Quenton Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks in exchange for a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick.
This obviously shows the Colts are not waiting around to start the fire sale everyone was expecting and this should add urgency for the Bills, who need to immediately call the Colts if they want to acquire players Indy is willing to sell off.
Three Colts players the Bills should have interest in are defensive linemen DeForest Buckner and Grover Stewart and wide receiver Josh Downs, all of whom ESPN's Adam Schefter believes could get moved before the deadline.
"I think the players that could be on the move for the Colts are DeForest Buckner, Josh Downs, and Grover Stewart," Schefter stated on The Pat McAfee Show . "DeForest Buckner is the one that I think will be dealt next."
While the defensive line certainly isn't the most dire need the Bills have on defense, it's still a position group general manager Brandon Beane should consider adding to.
Ed Oliver and Deone Walker are great, but the Bills are lacking a third starting-caliber player at the position and Oliver has been banged up this season , which only makes adding depth more necessary.
Buckner would be the better option of the two because he's not only a plus run defender, but an elite interior pass-rusher, also. In seven games this season, Buckner has posted four sacks.
The Bills have had major issues stopping the pass this season and beefing up the pass-rush is a good way to fix that.
Stewart would be a cheaper option and a fine consolation prize, although he doesn't offer much as a pass-rusher. He would, however, be an upgrade for Buffalo's run defense.
At wide receiver, the Bills don't have a dire need there, at least not yet. Keon Coleman has done a great job stepping up in 2026 and Khalil Shakir and DJ Moore give Buffalo a strong trio.
However, Moore has been battling a shoulder injury and the Bills are just one injury away from being in a precarious spot at the position because Joshua Palmer simply can't be relied upon.
Adding Downs would give the Bills some strong insurance and a player who can do just about everything Moore can.
If the Bills want any one of these three players or someone else on the Colts' roster, they need to strike quickly or else they could miss the boat.
