title: Texans GM Explains Where Things Stand With C.J. Stroud's Contract
full_text:
Throughout the course of this past offseason, one of the major storylines revolving around the Houston Texans was their contract negotiations surrouning quarterback C.J. Stroud.
Stroud, who became eligible to sign his rookie-scale extension earlier this offseason after his third season in the NFL, was in about as interesting of a contract dilemma as we've seen for a quarterback recent NFL history.
While the Texans quarterback had put together a solid first three years in the league, an up-and-down third season, paired with a brutal four-interception outing in a playoff loss to the New England Patriots , added big questions around what he'd would be worth on his second contract, and whether or not he'd be in the team's long-term plans moving forward.
The Texans and Stroud had negotiated over the course of the offseason , couldn't get a deal done, and has led to Houston's quarterback playing throughout his 2026 season with the overarching motivation of boosting the value on his next deal.
And so far, even while the Texans might be 2-5 at the bye, Stroud has met–– and even exceeded–– all of the expectations that had been on his plate heading into the year.
He's averaging over 260 passing yards per game, has got an 11:1 TD-to-INT ratio, is on pace for the highest completion percentage of his career, and has made those upcoming contract discussions for this offseason look perhaps even more interesting than they did earlier this summer.
Now that the Texans have reached their Week 8 bye, general manager Nick Caserio spoke to the media about a variety of topics on Monday –– and one of those discussions revolved around how he felt about Stroud's contract talks after his strong start to the season.
And overall, Caserio felt pretty confident about the situation as a whole. Not only is he not surprised about Stroud's strong start to the season, but he's also not worried about getting a new deal done whenever the time comes to do so.
"We had really good discussions. I mean, I would say we were pretty close," Caserio said of Stroud's contract talks. "We weren't able to consummate an agreement. I don't think anybody's really too worried about it. I'd say he's going out there, and honestly, he's played really good football–– which isn't a surprise of anybody."
"I think there's very few people, other than maybe DeMeco and myself, who supported him all offseason when he was essentially bad-mouthed for like four months about one bad half of football. So, I think the way that he's handled himself, and how he's approached it speaks to who he is, and it's not a surprise to any of us."
"I think the contract will take care of itself, whenever that is. We were close, we didn't get it over the finish line, but I don't think that's going to dissuade anybody moving forward from ultimately reaching an agreement."
The Texans aren't going to get a deal worked out with Stroud in the middle of the season. While Houston is technically eligible to hash out a new contract, Stroud had made it clear before the season that if there wasn't an extension worked out before Week 1, the two sides would table those discussions until next offseason.
And based on Stroud's early sample size, there are very few questions about whether or not the Texans would be interested in getting a new deal done.
But knowing that Stroud has had such a fiery first few games of the year, this type of performance has almost certainly increased the price tag on his next contract compared to where things stood before the season .
Yet, that's the cost the Texans are now forced to pay by deciding not to be more aggressive in their prior discussions.
Caserio also remained very complimentary about how Stroud has started this season off, even when factoring in all of the surrounding turbulence this roster has faced as a whole. And when taking a step back, he correlates that strong start to the year as a credit to the work he did over the course of the offseason .
"The guy's a good quarterback. He's been a good quarterback since he's been in the league," Caserio continued on Stroud. "I know sometimes everybody looks at it through a different lens... but that's just the reality of it. We've talked about that. That's how DeMeco and I feel. That's what we've said."
"I don't know how many times I got asked about it and talked about his professionalism, his performance, his attitude, how he worked this offseason. I think you're seeing a direct correlation between the work that he put in in the offseason and the results on the field... We're glad he's our quarterback."
Now that Stroud has answered the call for a strong start to the season, there should be a whole lot more certainty around what the Texans' plans are regarding a new extension for their QB1 once next offseason arrives in 2027.
However, the value of what that contract might be for Stroud will now be a decent chunk more than what was expected just a few months ago––so it'll be a situation to keep close watch of once we get to the end of this season.

title: Texans Week 8 Consensus Power Rankings: Where Houston Ranks at the Bye
full_text:
The Houston Texans felt like they had all the momentum behind them after they had logged back-to-back wins in Weeks 5 and 6 heading into this past weekend against the New York Giants.
Then, the Texans were quickly hit with a bit of a brutal reality check Houston would fall in overtime fashion to the same Giants team they were projected to beat by more than a touchdown, and now find themselves at a 2-5 record after seven weeks because of it.
With that in mind, let's sort through a new batch of consensus power rankings to see just where the Texans stack up around the league as they head into their Week 8 bye:
Sports Illustrated 's Conor Orr was extremely high on the Texans entering the year, having them as high as within the top five teams in the NFL before Week 1. Fast forward to this week, though, and he's got them all the way outside of the top 20.
"I know great defenses are difficult to maintain from year to year, but the Texans’ fall from grace remains one of the most stunning moments in recent history. J.J. McCarthy would have been ripped to shreds by almost the exact same cast of characters a year ago (no offense). How do you not evolve over the course of an offseason?"
Nick Shook turns out to be the most bullish on the Texans within our consensus power rankings, given that he's the only one to slot Houston inside the top 20––even after the events of this past weekend's overtime loss to New York.
"Another tough loss has landed on the Texans’ ledger, reducing their room for error going forward. It’s fair to say this defense is no longer deserving of its respected reputation -- especially when reflecting on how Devin Singletary ran through the heart of the unit to a game-winning touchdown. I do believe C.J. Stroud will continue to keep them competitive. I’m keeping an eye on that connection with Marvin Harrison Jr. too; Stroud’s touchdown pass to Harrison on Sunday was exquisite."
ESPN 's writers placed the Texans just outside of the top 20 in their respective rankings. D.J. Bien-Aime was tasked with choosing Houston's best offseason addition through seven weeks, and he chose none other than Foster Moreau.
"The Texans didn't have many big offseason acquisitions, but Moreau has provided help in the run game. And he has been a good red zone threat with three total touchdowns. Moreau has played 43% of the snaps, eating into the playing time of tight end Dalton Schultz, who is down from 70% in 2025 to 57% this season. Moreau helps Houston's offense not be predictable when he's in the game. Even though Houston has just two wins, its offense is averaging 24 points per game. And Moreau is a noteworthy part of the unit"
Josh Kendall and Chad Graff have the Texans at the lowest mark on our consensus rankings at 22nd, largely because of the holes this once-elite defense has proven to have all around the unit.
"The Texans were supposed to be Super Bowl contenders. Their defense was supposed to be among the best in the NFL. Instead, the unit ranks 24th in EPA per play and has gone from generating the second-most pressure in the league to the ninth most."
Pete Prisco seems to be a bit more pessimistic on the Texans' chances to rally back from their 2-5 record, noting that this weekend's loss to New York might be a death blow to their hopes of claiming the AFC South.
"Losing at home to the Giants just might be the death blow in their chances of winning the AFC South. The defense just isn't good enough."
Ralph Vacchiano does consider the Texans to be "much-improved" from the state they were at this time three weeks ago. However, it didn't stop him from also throwing them outside of their top 20 teams as DeMeco Ryans' defense continues to show they aren't at their same status from 2025.
"The Texans are undoubtedly a much-improved team over the past three weeks and can take comfort in that as they head into their bye week. But here’s their reality: It was always going to be tough, if not impossible, to rebound from an 0-4 start. The upstart Giants showed them how hard on Sunday by running all over them. The loss was bad enough, but giving up 420 yards to a Giants team starting its third QB this season? This Texans' defense just hasn’t been good enough and now the club is operating the rest of the season with almost no margin for error."

title: DeMeco Ryans Calls Texans' Penalty Issues Ridiculous–– And He's Right
full_text:
The Houston Texans are heading into their bye week with a 2-5 record and a bundle of issues to address in order to come out on the other side looking better than they have through seven games.
One of their most glaring issues focuses on one key factor this team just hasn't gotten right through the first half of the season: penalties.
Within the first seven weeks of the season, the Texans rank within the bottom four of the NFL for penalties called against them (58) and within the bottom two for yards given up from penalties (508).
Those issues really began to surface in a bad way within the Texans' latest loss against the New York Giants ; a game in which Houston saw eight flags called against them for 80 yards. It was their fifth game of this season in which this team gave up 80 yards or more on penalties.
The penalty woes got so bad for the Texans that, after Houston's overtime loss against the Giants on Sunday, DeMeco Ryans would have some strong criticism for the team's consistent accumulation of flags, calling them "ridiculous" and hinting that there could be some personnel changes in store if it cuts down on those errors and miscues.
"Yeah, the penalties are ridiculous," Ryans said post-game. "It keeps happening over and over again. So, we've got to find a way to fix it, or get different people in so we don't have the same mistakes over and over again."
It's really tough to argue against Ryans here, because this has been a consistent problem for the Texans now, even dating back to last season.
Through seven games of the Texans' 2025 season, they had accumulated a slightly less 52 penalties for a total of 427 yards.
It's a similar rate of mistakes that Houston has inflicted upon themselves at the same point in the season. But after an entire 12 months have passed since the Texans were at that point in 2025, combined with the improvements that the team has made around the roster in the offseason , their miscues have only increased.
Really, that's inexcusable. And it's not any type of winning formula that'll get the Texans back on track from the three games under .500 that they sit at right now.
So how does Ryans plan to address those mistakes moving forward?
Well, the Texans head coach re-approached those penalty issues during his Monday press conference after Houston's loss to New York, where he emphasized the team's need to be both clean and smart–– particularly on the offensive line.
"We just have to make sure we're clean, especially when it comes to blocking. Knowing when to let up, knowing we can't, you know, hold guys."
"You can't do that. So, you have to be smart there. You got to know when to let up, especially when you're at the point of attack."
When taking a step back to look at those 58 penalties in total for the Texans on the season, a large chunk of them reside on the shoulders of their offensive front, or simply because of a miscue pre-snap.
19 of those 58 penalties have stemmed from the offensive line; roughly one-third. A combined 26 of them are coming from offensive holding or via false start, according to NFLPenalties.com .
Will the Texans need to switch up their personnel upfront to limit those problems moving in to the second half of the season? Does there need to be a change within the coaching staff to try and spark better results?
Honestly, everything needs to be on the table for the Texans to get things right here, most importantly on the offensive line. Houston does have close to two weeks before their next game against the LA Chargers arrives, so there's at least time on their side to make the necessary tweaks to avoid a repeat of this weekend.
But if that lack of discipline continues after the bye week, and those penalties keep continuously setting Houston's offense back at the start of drives, it's going to be even tougher to have any sense of optimism that this group can climb out of the 2-5 hole they're in right now.

title: Are Texans Trade Deadline Buyers or Sellers? Nick Caserio Weighs In
full_text:
The Houston Texans head into their bye week at a 2-5 record after the events of this weekend's overtime loss against the New York Giants .
The next time the Texans will be taking the field in Week 9 will be just two days out from the NFL trade deadline, where there's bound to be several moving pieces around the league.
But when it comes to the Texans' situation, it's hard to really determine what their plan of attack at the deadline may be.
On one hand, Houston's lost five games in the first seven weeks. Both sides of the ball have real issues to address, they're winless at home through four tries , and there might not be a realistic pathway to improving this roster much from where things are at right now.
On another, the Texans did just make a trade to acquire Marvin Harrison Jr. in exchange for a second-round pick in this year's draft only two weeks ago, so it's hard to say that this team has folded its hand for this season moving forward.
So which direction will the Texans go as it pertains to their trade deadline plans? Will they go out to sell some pieces on their current roster, or will they try to go out and be buyers to make further improvements?
Well, Texans general manager Nick Caserio spoke about where the team stands on the day after Houston's Week 7 loss that might offer a bit more clarity on what to expect.
When Caserio was asked about whether or not the Texans were preparing to be buyers or sellers at this year's trade deadline, he left the door open for really any possibility.
He notes that the Texans have talked to most of the league over recent days to gauge what the market is looking like, and the team won't be eliminating any possibility.
"I mean, every opportunity, you know, we'll look at it," Caserio said. "If it makes sense, great. If not. We're always open. We've had conversations. We've talked to most of the league here. Teams have started to reach out here a little bit, trying to figure out, like, 'Alright, where are teams? What are you looking for? Where's the surplus? Where do you potentially have a need?"
"So, we'll always be open-minded. We're not going to eliminate anything. We'll listen, and ultimately, we'll do what we feel makes the most sense."
Overall, the Texans and Caserio don't seem to be forcing a particular move to their roster. They'll simply be taking what the market gives them.
If a team comes to the table with an intriguing offer for a position of need on either side, then perhaps Houston and their front office will take it. If no move comes to fruition, then the focus for any changes can be directed to the coming offseason.
But the sense you get here is that the Texans feel a little more likely to stay put with their current roster rather than making any big roster shake-ups.
Caserio had noted earlier in the press conference that the team wasn't going to make any "knee-jerk decisions" after their loss to New York, which likely includes their approach to the trade deadline.
"We'll look at it," Caserio said of whether the Texans will make any personnel changes. "I mean, if they feel it's appropriate, great. And then what's the alternative? So, we'll look at everything. We're not going to make any knee-jerk decisions on the heels of what happened yesterday."
"So, we'll go through the week we'll take inventory. DeMeco will spend time with the coaching staff, kind of talk through some different things, whether it's schematically, whether it's personnel-wise, and then we'll kind of try to figure out what's the best formula moving forward."
So as always, with an executive like Caserio , an unexpected trade could be in play if the price is right. However, it certainly doesn't seem as if a big move is imminent for Houston––whether that be to sell off some existing talent or to add even more to their existing group on hand.

title: Fire Sale: Potential Trade Packages for 3 Remaining Colts Stars
full_text:
Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner are gone. Two pillars of the Indianapolis Colts over the past decade were shipped out on Tuesday , and nobody feels untouchable anymore.
Indianapolis received a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-rounder for Nelson, plus a 2027 fourth-round pick for Buckner. Both were on expiring deals, but that return still hurts.
At 2-5, the rest of this season could get brutal. All Colts fans can do is appreciate what these guys gave us, collect draft picks and hope the next regime gets it right.
With the Nov. 10 deadline approaching, here are three hypothetical trade packages these Colts might demand.
Proposed Trade: Denver Broncos send a 2027 first-round pick and 2028 fourth-round pick.
I'm not trading JT for a couple of mid-round picks. Unlike Nelson and Buckner, Taylor is under contract through 2028 after signing a two-year, $44 million extension in August.
Through seven games, he has 587 rushing yards and a league-leading eight touchdowns. He's 27, still the centerpiece of this offense, and by far Indianapolis' most valuable trade asset.
Denver is among the teams ESPN has linked to Taylor, although no offer has been reported. Shane Steichen said Wednesday that Taylor hasn't requested a trade, and Adam Schefter reports that owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon wants to keep him .
"[Carlie] Irsay-Gordon views [Jonathan] Taylor as a key part of the organization and a likely mainstay in their rebuild," Schefter said.
Fine by me. But if somebody wants JT, I'm demanding a massive haul. Ideally, you'd send him to an NFC team, but if an AFC contender comes calling with an offer you can't refuse, you have to consider it.
Also, the Colts don't own their 2027 first-rounder, so I want one back for the league's best RB.
Taylor netting a first-round pick would certainly be unprecedented and would no doubt be considered an overpay, but if the Colts play their cards right, they may just convince a potential suitor to pull the trigger.
Taylor's most comparable trade package is that of Christian McCaffrey's blockbuster haul from 2022.
In exchange for McCaffrey, the Panthers received a 2023 NFL Draft second-round pick, a 2023 third-rounder, a 2023 fourth-rounder, and a 2024 fifth-round pick.
The bidding for Taylor likely starts with multiple Day 2 (Rounds 2-3) draft selections, but if a contender comes calling with what they believe will be a late first-round pick, the Colts would be irresponsible to turn it down.
Proposed Trade: Pittsburgh Steelers send a 2027 fifth-round pick and 2028 sixth-round pick.
This one stings. Josh Downs has been one of my favorite young players to watch, and I never expected him to be part of this teardown.
ESPN's Jeremy Fowler reported Wednesday that Downs requested a trade , confirming that his days in Indianapolis are numbered.
Sources: Colts WR Josh Downs is requesting a trade from Indianapolis. pic.twitter.com/rwGaVGMTFf
The 25-year-old has 26 catches for 307 yards and no touchdowns through seven games, and his rookie contract expires after this season.
Multiple AFC teams, including the Pittsburgh Steelers, are reportedly interested in trading for Downs, according to NFL Insider Jordan Schultz .
Two Day 3 picks aren't exciting, but they're better than gambling on potential compensatory help down the road.
I still believe Downs can become one of the league's best receivers in the right offense.
Proposed Trade: Green Bay Packers send a 2027 sixth-round pick.
Big Grove has been holding down Indianapolis' run defense since 2017. He deserves plenty of appreciation for that, but at 33 and on an expiring contract, it's probably time to part ways.
His value is primarily against the run, not as a pass rusher. That limits the market, but I think a sixth-round pick is a reasonable return for a veteran who can still contribute against the run.
Moving Stewart would leave another hole along this defensive line. But a rebuilding team needs those draft picks, and getting something now beats watching another veteran walk in March.
None of this is easy to watch. If Tuesday taught us anything, it's that nobody's legacy guarantees they'll finish their career in Indianapolis.
The memories aren't going anywhere. The front office just needs to turn these departures into future Colts legends.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: Biggest Colts Winners of Fire Sale: Two Young Players Get Massive Opportunity
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts may be punting on the 2026 season, but their future has some bright spots on the roster.
Colts' Owner/CEO Carlie Irsay-Gordon has kicked off the team's rebuild with a fire sale of the roster's best players , trading away longtime franchise pillars Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner on Tuesday.
The Colts are aiming to add any draft capital they can for the next era by shopping their top players, and this exodus began with the trading of the franchise's most pivotal staples.
Indianapolis's immediate outlook looks bleaker than ever before, but there are two players who have been granted a massive opportunity as a result.
If these two Colts can prove their worth, the next regime's year-one outlook may not be as dire as these trades suggest it'll be.
The biggest winner of the DeForest Buckner trade is Colts defensive tackle Adetomiwa Adebawore.
The fourth-year interior defensive lineman has been an intriguing player since the Colts drafted him in the fourth round (110th overall) of the 2023 NFL Draft.
Adebawore's absurd athletic profile was enough to entice, but his pass-rush potential excited most.
The talented young pass rusher flashed his intriguing skills across his first two seasons in the NFL, but he still had a long way to go in run defense before he could be considered for a bigger role.
Of course, the longtime interior duo of DeForest Buckner and Grover Stewart made it nearly impossible for any defensive tackle to carve out a three-down role in the Colts' defense, but Buckner's departure changes everything.
Not only is the opportunity there, but Adebawore has earned the increased role in question.
Adebawore's first two seasons suggested that he'd likely be a designated pass rusher for the foreseeable future, but a quiet, mini-breakout in his third season single-handedly changed his trajectory.
Below are Adebawore's pass-rush numbers throughout his first three seasons (2023-25) in the NFL:
2023 (rookie): 20.7% playing time, 1.5 sacks, 7.6% pressure rate, 3 defensive stops 2024: 17.9% playing time, 1.0 sacks, 6.7% pressure rate, 4 defensive stops 2025: 46.8% playing time, 4.0 sacks, 10.2% pressure rate, 24 defensive stops
The upward trajectory was apparent, and Adebawore has locked in to fully break out after seven games in the 2026 regular season.
Adebawore struggled to find playing time to start the new year, but has since earned the trust of defensive coordinator Lou Anarumo and the rest of the staff.
After seven weeks, Adebawore is undeniably the Colts' best pass rusher. He is currently tied for second with the most sacks among interior defensive linemen league-wide and leads the team in most major pass-rush statistics.
#Colts DT Adetomiwa Adebawore has the 2nd-most pressures (12) on the team (excl. Buckner) after seven weeks despite only playing 35.9% of snaps. He leads the defense in sacks (4.0), pressure rate (13.0%), and quick pressures (6), and has the second-most stops (13). pic.twitter.com/cqamb6tThI
We've known that Adebawore has some nasty pass-rushing chops, but the biggest development has been his improvement in run defense.
Adebawore has blossomed into a legitimate starting defensive tackle, and it comes at no better time as the Colts have parted ways with their longtime pillar across the defensive line.
However, the Colts' newfound star is on an expiring deal. Adebawore is playing in the final year of his rookie contract, so a big payday is set to come his way.
The Colts are understandably busy shopping their failed era's best assets, but if they want to truly maximize the next regime's early outlook, extending Adebawore should be near the organization's top priorities moving forward.
A similar big opportunity has presented itself for one of the Colts' players still on a rookie contract: first-year guard Jalen Farmer.
Unlike Adebawore's situation, Farmer still has to prove himself as a legitimate NFL player
The Colts drafted Farmer in the fourth round (113th overall) of the 2026 NFL Draft, envisioning that he'll become OL Coach Tony Sparano Jr.'s next installment of successful draft-and-stash projects .
Indianapolis was prepared to treat Farmer's rookie season like a redshirt year as they roll with their proven veteran unit, but Quenton Nelson's departure has changed the trajectory entirely.
Instead, a Hall of Fame-sized hole now sits across the Colts' interior offensive line, and Farmer is set to take over as we approach the midway point of the 2026 regular season.
Although he is an unproven rookie, Tony Sparano Jr. has the utmost faith in Farmer's ability .
As Sparano Jr. famously said following the Colts' combine interview with Farmer, "Let me tell you this much. Draft him, and I'll make it work."
Sparano Jr.’s conviction in Jalen Farmer is so apparent, not only by his own words, but also by the #Colts war room’s reaction when he arrives to celebrate said draft selection. 🎥: @Colts https://t.co/RxH86gKHkC pic.twitter.com/EFmmsUSYYe
In just a few short years with the Colts, Sparano Jr. has successfully developed the likes of LT Bernhard Raimann, RG Will Fries, RG Matt Goncalves, and C Tanor Bortolini.
Second-year tackle Jalen Travis has had an up-and-down start to his first season as a full-time starter, but there's still hope that he can become the ideal longtime Braden Smith replacement.
And it's easy to see why Sparano Jr. believes that Jalen Farmer will be his next successful project.
Farmer sports a strong athletic profile, has ample experience at the position (although he's mainly played right guard), and possesses a ton of raw power.
The Colts' rookie guard will be going from special teams duties to filling the void that Quenton Nelson left.
Even though this season is lost, the Colts have granted themselves a promising evaluation period of pieces that could stick with them through this ongoing fire sale and kick off the new era.
Farmer and Adebawore have a 10-game trial period to prove that they deserve to be long-term pieces of the rebuild.
Noah Compton is the Publisher of Indianapolis Colts On SI. Noah is from the Indy area and has been covering the Colts since 2022, including stops at FanSided, The Blue Stable, and SBNation.

title: Josh Downs' Trade Request Pushes Colts Further Toward Full Rebuild
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts ' roster teardown is gaining momentum, and Josh Downs could be the next player out the door.
The fourth-year wide receiver has officially requested a trade, according to ESPN's Jeremy Fowler, as Indianapolis continues its roster renovation following the departures of Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner .
Downs' request presents another pivotal decision for a team that's already begun looking towards the future. With the Nov. 10 trade deadline approaching, the Colts must do right by Downs and get him into a better situation while picking up assets for the future simultaneously .
Downs' trade request, his comments Wednesday and the frustration he's shown in recent weeks all point toward a receiver who wants a change of scenery.
Asked about the possibility of a trade, Downs told reporters, "I'm open to whatever. Whatever comes my way comes my way, and we go from there."
He was also asked whether he would have preferred to sign an extension before the season, responding, "I mean, if it came my way, it came my way, but like I wouldn't say that."
Josh Downs talks potential trade + if he wanted a contract extension: pic.twitter.com/w2KuKEmym3
Downs' frustration is understandable. He's in the final year of his rookie contract and has watched the Colts' season spiral while struggling to influence games himself. Despite Alec Pierce missing significant time, Downs has recorded just 307 receiving yards and no touchdowns through seven games.
With Indianapolis trading away established veterans and shifting its focus toward the future, Downs has little reason to wait around for the franchise to find its footing. A trade would give him a chance to finish the season in a better situation and increase his market value heading into free agency.
The Pittsburgh Steelers have emerged as one potential destination for Downs, with NFL insider Jordan Schultz reporting that multiple AFC teams have expressed interest in the Colts receiver. While a deal wasn't considered likely this week, Schultz reported that a trade is expected to happen eventually.
#Colts WR Josh Downs has received interest from multiple AFC teams, including the #Steelers , and while a deal is not considered likely this week, the expectation is a trade will eventually happen, per sources. pic.twitter.com/lZ5rH5YyIF
The Kansas City Chiefs are another team worth watching.
Kansas City has dealt with injuries to its receiving corps and could use another reliable target for Patrick Mahomes. Downs' ability to work underneath and create separation from the slot would give the Chiefs another option in the passing game. The New England Patriots could also make sense given Downs' familiarity with quarterback Drake Maye from their time together at North Carolina.
Downs is in the final year of his rookie deal, and an acquiring team would have about 10 games minimum to decide if Downs is someone they want to retain, or if he's just a rental.
As for compensation, a Day 3 draft pick seems like a reasonable target for Indianapolis.
Downs hasn't established himself as a No. 1 receiver, and his modest production this season could limit what teams are willing to offer. Still, his age and remaining upside should give the Colts a chance to recoup an asset before he potentially leaves in free agency.
Trading Nelson and Buckner sent a clear message to the rest of the league: Indianapolis is willing to move on from the core it spent years building.
Downs' request makes it even harder for the Colts to justify holding onto players who may not fit their long-term plans.
There are other decisions to make before the deadline. Grover Stewart and Keenan Allen are among the players whose expiring contracts could make them trade candidates, giving interim general manager Ed Dodds more opportunities to recoup assets. Neither move is a foregone conclusion, but both deserve consideration as Indianapolis evaluates what comes next.
The goal shouldn't be to tear down the roster without a plan. It should be to identify the players who can contribute to the Colts’ next competitive window and determine what the others are worth on the trade market.
Downs has made his preference clear, and Indianapolis has already shown it is willing to make moves. The decisions made over the next week and a half should reflect the same commitment to the future.

title: What the Quenton Nelson Trade Means for Colts' Future
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts made a major move Tuesday, trading six-time All-Pro guard Quenton Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks as the franchise looks to find its footing after a disappointing stretch.
Nelson's departure marks a significant change of direction for the Colts, who have gone from attempting to contend for a playoff spot earlier this season to now gearing up for a rebuild.
But there are questions surrounding where the Colts can go from here.
The Colts have a potential replacement for Nelson waiting in the wings already.
Rookie Jalen Farmer could get his first opportunity to fill the void at left guard, giving the team a chance to evaluate whether he can become a long-term starter. Indianapolis selected Farmer in the fourth round of the 2026 NFL Draft, initially as a depth and developmental piece.
Former general manager Chris Ballard said the Colts had targeted Farmer earlier in the draft and compared him to Bernhard Raimann, another offensive lineman the organization developed into a starter.
Offensive line coach Tony Sparano Jr. was equally enthusiastic about the Kentucky product, praising his power, ability to anchor, and run-blocking skills. You may remember Sparano telling fellow staff members, "Let me tell you this much. Draft him and I'll make it work," after the Colts met with Farmer at the NFL Combine.
#Colts OL Coach Tony Sparano Jr.’s combine interview with G Jalen Farmer showcased a match made in heaven of sorts. “Let me tell you this much. Draft him and I’ll make it work.” 🎥: @Colts pic.twitter.com/WH9HDbSy7S
With Nelson now in Seattle, Farmer has a clearer path to playing time. He spent his college career at right guard, so transitioning to the left side would present a new challenge, but not an impossible one.
Still, the Colts' investment in him and their confidence in his potential make him an intriguing option to fill the position beyond just this season. Farmer will have to prove he can handle the responsibilities of an NFL starter, and there will undoubtedly be some bumps at first, but the opportunity is significant.
Rather than immediately searching outside the organization for Nelson's successor, Indianapolis can use the remainder of the season to evaluate whether Farmer can be a part of the plan moving forward.
Losing Nelson creates another challenge for an Indianapolis offense that needs to find more consistency in the run game.
The six-time All-Pro was the team's most reliable blocker - arguably one of the greatest run blockers in NFL history - and his departure leaves a significant hole in the interior of the offensive line.
The Colts have already seen how difficult it can be to establish the run when their blocking struggles. Indianapolis managed just 66 rushing yards against Pittsburgh in Week 5, despite relying heavily on Jonathan Taylor to carry the offense. Nelson was one of the few bright spots in that performance, earning an 81.9 run-blocking grade from Pro Football Focus.
Taylor showed what he can still do against Minnesota, rushing for 95 yards and a touchdown in Sunday's loss, but maintaining that production will become more difficult without Nelson in front of him.
The adjustment also creates an opportunity for the remaining linemen to prove they can handle larger roles. Assuming Farmer gets the chance to start at left guard, his ability to open running lanes for Taylor will be one of the biggest things to watch.
The Colts need to see whether their younger linemen can fill the void left by Nelson without the ground game taking a step backward. And if Taylor is also dealt as part of the Colts' ongoing fire sale, the next era will be fully embraced, but the run game will bring forgotten lows.
By moving off Nelson and his contract, the Colts are giving their next general manager some flexibility as the organization looks to reshape the roster.
The trade compensation gives Indianapolis additional resources to work with. The Colts acquired a third-round pick in the 2027 NFL Draft and a fifth-round selection in 2028, giving the next general manager more draft capital to address the team's needs.
Indianapolis is also projected to have roughly $88 million in salary cap space next offseason, giving the next general manager considerable financial flexibility. Nelson's departure won't directly increase that figure, as his contract was already set to expire after the 2026 season. However, the trade allows the Colts to move forward without having to negotiate a new deal with one of their longtime stars while bringing back valuable draft capital in return.
Nelson's departure gives the next general manager more freedom to evaluate the roster and establish a new direction---his or her own direction. With additional draft picks, significant projected cap space and the opportunity to assess younger players like Farmer, the remainder of the season will help determine who the Colts want to be a part of their rebuild.

title: Colts' Future Comes Into Focus After Parting Ways With Two Trench Staples
full_text:
When it rains, it pours. And it's coming down in buckets over Indianapolis.
The Colts have made two major changes to their roster, trading away two of their most recognizable players as the franchise looks to chart a new course after a disappointing season.
After sending eight-time Pro Bowl guard Quenton Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks for a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick, Indianapolis also traded defensive tackle DeForest Buckner to the San Francisco 49ers in exchange for 2027 fourth-round pick.
With both veterans gone, Indianapolis faces significant questions about both its immediate and long-term future. Let's attempt to answer what the next several months may look like.
The Colts have little time to adjust after trading away two of the most established players on their roster. There's still football left to play, but with Nelson and Buckner gone, Indianapolis is officially headed for a lost season.
Rather than mail it in, the Colts should use the remaining games to evaluate the players who are still there. The departures create opportunities for younger players to take on larger roles and show whether they belong in the team's plans moving forward.
Indianapolis could also make more moves before the Nov. 10 trade deadline. Veterans such as Keenan Allen, Grover Stewart and Charvarius Ward could attract interest from contenders if the Colts decide to pursue additional draft compensation for their next general manager to work with.
By the end of the season, Indianapolis should have a clearer picture of which players can contribute to its next competitive roster and where reinforcements will be needed.
Trading Nelson and Buckner leaves significant holes on both lines. Each was an established starter and leader at his position, making their departures consequential beyond the immediate impact on the depth chart.
Offensively, Indianapolis must find a replacement for Nelson at left guard. Rookie Jalen Farmer, a fourth-round pick in the most recent draft, is one option. He should receive a 10-game trial run the rest of the season so the Colts can determine whether he can be part of the team's long-term plans.
Buckner's departure creates a similar challenge on the defensive line. More responsibility will fall on the remaining interior defenders, including Stewart and Adetomiwa Adebawore. The Colts have to find out if Adebawore, a free agent at the end of the season, is a pillar they want to build around.
How Indianapolis handles those vacancies will be a crucial part of its roster evaluation. The goal isn't necessarily to find direct replacements for two established stars, but to build offensive and defensive lines capable of supporting the team's next competitive window.
The Colts' longer-term outlook will depend heavily on who takes over as general manager and how that person chooses to approach the roster. Indianapolis still has talent, but the new decision-maker will have to identify which players he or she deems as viable options moving forward.
The trades also provide additional draft capital. Indianapolis acquired a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick for Nelson, adding to the compensation received for Buckner. However, the Colts still don't have their 2027 first-round pick after sending it to the New York Jets for cornerback Sauce Gardner.
That makes the team's remaining draft assets especially important. The next general manager will need to weigh the value of adding young talent against the opportunity to address immediate needs through free agency.
Moving veteran contracts could also create more financial flexibility, depending on the details of each deal. That would give the next GM more options to retain key players, pursue outside additions or continue reshaping the roster.
Ultimately, Indianapolis has created an opportunity to take the team in a different direction. The next general manager will have to decide how much of the current foundation is worth keeping around. Those deemed to not be worth retaining must make their way out of the building one way or another.
Needless to say, primary owner and CEO Carlie Irsay-Gordon has a big hire to make in the not-so-distant future.

title: Thank You, Big Q: Remembering a Colts Legend
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts traded their longest-tenured player to the Seattle Seahawks on Tuesday for a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-rounder. Two mid-round picks for one of the greatest offensive linemen in franchise history.
I always thought Big Q would retire in Indianapolis. I thought he would spend his entire career wearing the Horseshoe, walk into the Hall of Fame one day and have the Colts attached to his name forever.
Instead, one of the best players to ever put on a Colts uniform is heading to Seattle.
Nelson was the No. 6 overall pick in 2018, and it did not take long to realize Indianapolis had something special. He became the first guard in NFL history to win Offensive Rookie of the Month and immediately helped change the identity of an offensive line that desperately needed one.
From there, the accolades became almost automatic.
Nelson made the Pro Bowl in each of his first eight seasons, becoming the first player in Colts history to accomplish that and only the second offensive lineman in NFL history to do it, joining Hall of Fame tackle Joe Thomas.
He was also a three-time First-Team All-Pro from 2018-20 before adding three Second-Team selections in 2021, 2024 and 2025.
That is six All-Pro selections in eight completed seasons.
And somehow, the awards still do not tell the entire story.
Nelson brought an edge to this offense that is hard to quantify. He didn't just block defenders; he punished them, played through the whistle, and made sure everyone around him played with that same intensity.
Seriously, how many offensive guards have a highlight tape you would willingly sit down and watch? Big Q was different.
The consistency was just as ridiculous. Nelson started 136 games for Indianapolis and missed only four, all during the 2021 season.
Even at 30 years old, he was still playing like one of the best guards in football. Through seven games this season, Nelson had allowed zero sacks and only six pressures, while his 86.6 PFF grade ranked third among qualified guards.
I understand the business side. Nelson is in the final year of his contract, the Colts are 2-5, Chris Ballard is gone and this franchise is clearly looking toward what comes next.
But some players mean more than the draft picks attached to their name.
Nelson was toughness. He was consistency. He was the backbone of this offensive line for nearly a decade and represented everything you could ask for in an Indianapolis Colt.
In my eyes, Big Q is a future Hall of Famer and one of the best Colts to ever wear the Horseshoe.
Man, I am going to miss watching No. 56 in Indianapolis.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: Next Colts Player Most Likely to be Traded After Quenton Nelson
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts have started their trade deadline activity with a major move , sending left guard Quenton Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks in exchange for a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick.
With the team sitting at 2-5 and facing questions about its direction, more changes could be on the way.
Jonathan Taylor, Josh Downs and Grover Stewart are among the other players who could draw interest from contenders. However, DeForest Buckner stands out as a particularly intriguing candidate, especially with a familiar NFC contender potentially in the picture.
The San Francisco 49ers have already emerged as a potential landing spot for DeForest Buckner.
San Francisco has a clear need up front after dealing with injuries along its defensive line. The 49ers have also been one of the NFL's best teams this season, starting 6-0 despite those absences. Adding Buckner would give them an established interior pass rusher as they look to maintain that success.
As for the financials, San Francisco entered the trade-deadline period with approximately $41.3 million in salary cap space, the most in the NFL. That flexibility puts the 49ers in a strong position to pursue a veteran like Buckner without having to make significant financial sacrifices elsewhere on the roster.
And of course, there's familiarity between the two parties. The 49ers selected Buckner with the No. 7 overall pick in the 2016 NFL Draft, and he spent the first four seasons of his career with the organization, playing a key role in their run to Super Bowl LIV.
San Francisco traded him to Indianapolis in March 2020 in exchange for the 13th overall pick, which became defensive tackle Javon Kinlaw. Now, six years later, the two sides could reunite under very different circumstances.
Buckner is 32 and in the final year of his contract, while the Colts are gearing up to start a rebuilding phase. A return to San Francisco would give Buckner an opportunity to compete for a championship while allowing Indianapolis to recoup draft capital for a veteran who could leave in free agency next offseason.
The Colts are actively shopping Buckner, whose connection to San Francisco makes the 49ers seem like a trade partner of destiny.
Buckner isn't the only Colt who could be dealt before the Nov. 10 deadline.
Jonathan Taylor is the biggest name among the Colts' other potential trade candidates, although Indianapolis appears more inclined to keep him than move him. Ownership reportedly views the star running back as a key piece of the team's future, but that shouldn't make him untouchable.
If the right offer comes along, the Colts should be willing to pull the trigger. The 2022 Christian McCaffrey trade offers a useful benchmark, as Carolina received second, third and fourth-round picks in 2023 along with a fifth-rounder in 2024 from San Francisco.
Taylor remains one of the NFL's top running backs, and Indianapolis should demand a substantial return rather than trade him simply for the sake of moving him. At the same time, the team shouldn't pass up a significant package of draft capital just because Taylor is a player it wants to retain.
Josh Downs is another possibility as he enters the final year of his rookie contract. The 25-year-old receiver could appeal to contenders looking for a reliable slot target, although moving him would leave Indianapolis with fewer established options in the passing game.
Defensive tackle Grover Stewart could also draw interest from teams seeking help against the run. Like Buckner, the veteran defensive tackle is playing on an expiring contract, making him a potential rental for a contender and another opportunity for Indianapolis to add draft capital.
Either way, Nelson’s trade is just the first of a few to come as Indianapolis strips its operation down to the studs, ready to start fresh.

title: Let the Fire Sale Commence: Biggest Domino in Colts Rebuild Falls First
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts are staring down a full-fledged organizational reset after parting ways with longtime general manager Chris Ballard following their Week 6 loss to the then-winless Tennessee Titans.
After assistant general manager Ed Dodds took over for Ballard to become interim GM for the remainder of the 2026 season, the mission from ownership was clear: start shopping the entire roster ahead of the NFL Trade Deadline .
A near decade of mediocrity left the Indianapolis Colts at a crossroads, and they've decided to tear the roster down to its studs as they embark upon a new era.
This rebuild has officially kicked off a fire sale of sorts, with the departure of longtime future Hall of Fame guard Quenton Nelson being the first domino to fall.
The Colts traded Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks for a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick, according to NFL insider Tom Pelissero.
So, how did we get here, was the compensation fair, and where do we go from here?
I break it all down below.
Quenton Nelson has been one of the league's most consistent, productive, and accomplished players since the Indianapolis Colts drafted him sixth overall in the 2018 NFL Draft.
Nelson has earned Pro Bowl honors in each of his eight seasons in the NFL and has added six All-Pro selections (3x First-Team, 3x Second-Team).
On top of that, Nelson has only missed four games in eight seasons.
Nelson has epitomized what it means to be a future Hall of Fame candidate, so why on earth did the Colts let him walk out the door?
For starters, it's more than likely that Quenton Nelson was fed up with how the organization continues to find itself in rebuilding scenarios and wanted no part in running it back.
Nelson is 30 years old and is in the final year of his four-year deal, so not wanting to sign up for a full-blown rebuild in what could very well be his final NFL contract is understandable.
Of course, the Colts would love nothing more than to have Nelson around for their first official rebuild in over a decade, but unfortunately for them, it's a two-way street.
It takes two to tango, after all.
Nelson likely wanted to start fresh elsewhere, particularly with a contender, before he entered his first free agency as an unrestricted free agent.
Given what the Seahawks gave up for Nelson, I think it's fair to assume he was not interested in re-signing with the Colts.
Some may feel strongly about the Colts not netting at least a second-round pick for Quenton Nelson's services, but at the end of the day, Indianapolis's hands were tied.
The Colts have been famously inching towards a fire sale of their roster, and Nelson's pedigree has revealed him as a popular trade candidate.
In theory, a future Hall of Famer should at least net a first-round pick in return, but it's not quite that simple.
The offensive guard position is one of the biggest examples of non-premium talent, and even though Nelson sports some of the best talent said position has ever seen, teams across the league remain hesitant to value it that way.
A current third-round pick and a future fifth-rounder may seem scoff-worthy at first glance, but when you break down the history of traded compensation for other guards across the league, Nelson's haul starts to make more sense.
You may not like it, but the Colts did as best they could.
Indianapolis' return of a 3rd and a 5th for Quenton Nelson is the most pure draft capital for a guard since at least 2011, per Spotrac. only 4 have netted a 4th: 2013: G. Carimi, 4th 2014: L. Mankins, 4th + player 2021: B. Bredeson + 5th + 7th, 4th 2025: J. Thuney, 4th
I think this is both the best example of why the return for Quenton Nelson isn’t as irresponsible as some are suggesting, and also why the Chris Ballard era needed to end: non-premium positions.
It's precisely why Nelson's return seems so weak, but also why star running back Jonathan Taylor will not be netting a first-round pick in return.
Not only were the Colts dealt the tough task of netting worthwhile compensation for one of the league's least-valued positions, but they also had the added layer of Nelson's expiring contract to deal with.
Unless they re-sign him, the Seattle Seahawks have signed up for 11 weeks of Quenton Nelson.
When you consider Nelson's age, expiring contract, and unwillingness to sign up for a true rebuild with the organization that's failed him, this seems like one of the best-case scenarios for Indianapolis.
The only argument against this process I can think of is that the Colts could have potentially netted more compensation if they had waited closer to the deadline.
In theory, this would've driven up the price, but realistically, how much of an overpay could the Colts have gotten out of this hypothetical hard bargain?
Nelson leaving in free agency would've netted a third-round compensatory pick; therefore, it's almost as if the Seahawks rented his services for a future fifth-round pick.
This may sting on the surface, but you also can't guarantee that the Colts would not have made any deals in free agency that would've negated their compensatory return.
Again, it's more than likely that Nelson didn't want to be here, so it makes sense that the Colts wanted to do right by their longtime offensive pillar and ship him somewhere that's best for both parties.
It's borderline disgusting to watch a homegrown future Hall of Famer get dealt elsewhere, but this is the bed the Colts have made, and now they must sleep in it.
As far as the 2026 regular season goes, the Colts have admitted that playoffs are no longer an option.
Nelson's departure lowers the offense's floor more than you can imagine, so trying to maintain playoff aspirations while preparing for the future is no longer a feasible outcome.
The Colts will continue selling off as many assets as possible as they look to enter a new era, but at least their future can get a good look for the rest of this season.
The left guard spot will likely see rookie Jalen Farmer fill the void at some point in the near future, and this is a massive opportunity for OL Coach Tony Sparano Jr. to turn his most recent draft crush into yet another successful project across the Colts' offensive line.
Sparano Jr. has churned out successful draft-and-stash projects in recent years, such as LT Bernhard Raimann, G Will Fries, G Matt Goncalves, C Tanor Bortolini, and RT Jalen Travis, and Farmer could become the next installment of sorts.
Sparano Jr.'s conviction in the former Kentucky guard led the Colts to draft him in the fourth round of the 2026 NFL Draft.
Sparano Jr.’s conviction in Jalen Farmer is so apparent, not only by his own words, but also by the #Colts war room’s reaction when he arrives to celebrate said draft selection. 🎥: @Colts https://t.co/RxH86gKHkC pic.twitter.com/EFmmsUSYYe
Farmer has yet to play this season, given the Colts' offensive line has been held down by a veteran unit, but with Quenton Nelson's departure leaving a gargantuan-sized hole, the rookie now has a huge opportunity to prove himself as a building block for the next regime.
Noah Compton is the Publisher of Indianapolis Colts On SI. Noah is from the Indy area and has been covering the Colts since 2022, including stops at FanSided, The Blue Stable, and SBNation.

title: Colts Week 7 Stock Report: 2 Risers, 3 Fallers as Offense Falls Apart
full_text:
A third straight loss leaves the Indianapolis Colts facing an uncomfortable reality: the season is slipping away, and the offense is now a major reason why.
For once, the defense held up its end against the undefeated Minnesota Vikings. Indianapolis still walked away with a 16-10 loss and a 2-5 record.
There aren't many players trending upward right now, but a couple deserve some credit. Here are my two risers and three fallers from Week 7.
With Sauce Gardner sidelined, Walley stepped into a bigger role at outside corner and delivered his best performance of the season.
He earned a 94.2 coverage grade from Pro Football Focus, the highest in the NFL in Week 7. Walley allowed just 16 receiving yards and forced a fumble.
Unfortunately, he suffered an injury and never returned. That's a tough way to end a breakout game, because outside corner looks like exactly where he belongs.
Facing one of the NFL's most aggressive defenses, Raimann was one of the few Indianapolis offensive linemen who didn't look overwhelmed.
He posted an 89.5 pass-blocking grade, the third-highest among NFL offensive linemen in Week 7, and helped spring Jonathan Taylor's 38-yard touchdown with a downfield block.
The Daniel Jones situation is getting more concerning by the week.
He finished 13-of-22 for 108 yards, zero touchdowns and a game-sealing interception, earning a 46.5 PFF passing grade.
Through seven games, Jones has 1,398 passing yards, four touchdowns and seven interceptions while completing just 59.6% of his passes.
Yes, he's missing weapons, and Minnesota's pressure was absurd. But his mobility has vanished, the missed throws keep piling up.
The calls for Anthony Richardson are only getting louder.
This is a name I never expected to see on the fallers list.
Shrader entered Sunday without a missed field goal this season, then missed from 56 and 48 yards in the second half. Both were long attempts, but Indianapolis desperately needed those points in a six-point loss.
He's been too reliable for us to panic after one game. Still, this was an uncharacteristically rough afternoon for a guy who has made a habit of drilling everything.
Minnesota's pass rush was a nightmare for this offensive line, and Travis had his share of struggles at right tackle.
He allowed six pressures and finished with the 134th-ranked pass-blocking grade among 157 offensive linemen who played in Week 7, according to PFF.
That's simply not going to cut it, especially with Daniel Jones already struggling to operate under pressure.
Indianapolis finally got a defensive performance good enough to win. If this offense doesn't figure things out soon, that won't matter much.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: Trades and BTJ: 3 Most Important Things Jaguars' Liam Coen Said About Week 8's Colts Matchup
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars do not need any extra motivation heading into Week 8's battle with the Indianapolis Colts.
Jacksonville knows what Week 8's tilt with the Colts means moving forward, especially as it pertains to the race for the AFC South title. They also know that it is paramount to rebound from their last game, a 34-31 loss to the Houston Texans in Week 6 before they went on their bye week.
"When you go on a bye, it's the hardest thing to be on a bye, especially coming off of a loss and you just want to get back out there and compete, get back out there and practice," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said Wednesday.
"As I said, I didn't sleep a ton Sunday night because you're just wanting to get back at it, and you want to get back in the building with the players. And that's kind of been my sense of enjoyment, or any sort of sense of, I guess, confidence comes from being able to get back to work with these guys.”
So, what are the most important things Coen said on Wednesday as the Jaguars prepare for their next step in the race to the AFC South mountain top? We break it down below.
While the Jaguars are still riding relatively high entering Week 8, things are a little different with the Colts. The Colts have already begun a fire sale to concede their place in the AFC South race, opening the door for the Jaguars to have a potentially easier path. That fire sale has included trading away All-Pros like Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner to the Seattle Seahawks and San Francisco 49ers this week, making the Colts a weakened team entering Sunday.
“Yeah, obviously really good players that I have a lot of respect for. [Seahawks OL] Quenton Nelson was playing arguably some of the best football of his career as was Buckner [49ers DT DeForest Buckner] in a lot of ways, extremely disruptive in both the run and the pass, batting a lot of tipped balls and created some issues inside with he and 95 [Adetomiwa Adebawore] in there rushing inside, who do you slide to, stuff like that. Obviously, it's two good players. We can't deny that, right?" Coen said.
With that said, Coen has once again stressed that the Jaguars can not put any energy or focus into what is going on across the sidelines. For the Jaguars to beat the Colts and build post-bye momentum, they will have to focus on what they do and their own improvements. It is easy to fall into the trap of underestmating a team, but the Jaguars have already seen what that looks like after their battle with the Philadelphia Eagles.
"But, knowing what this team is, knowing what that team's going to want to do, this has to all be about our improvements, us getting back on track," Coen said. "Got a good division opponent that we're playing at home and the focus level getting in pads today has to be about our execution, our fundamentals and technique because you just can't control that stuff and if you think about it too much, it typically doesn't help.”
While the Jaguars have been one of the better teams in the NFL at generating pressure (quickest time to pressure in NFL, No. 8 in pressure rate) they rank just 24th in sack rate. They are impacting the passer, but not bringing him down enough. At the same time, the coverage and the pass-rush have not been on the same page at the rate that they were a year ago, making the pass defense one of the biggest area of focuses coming out of the Jaguars' bye.
“I think it's a combination between hand usage, continuing to put guys in the spots with the right combinations of guys to help create some of those matchups and get the favorable matchup that we really want to hunt up out of the group," Coen said.
As things stand today, it does not feel as if there is some magic fix the Jaguars can find without adding someone before the trade deadline. The Jaguars are where they are in terms of the pass-rush, and the solution is to play better on multiple fronts.
"It starts with get off, it starts with hand usage, it starts with mixing in pressure looks to help get the back eaten up, or now we got one-on-one matchups, different spots. It has to get better," Coen said. "We need it to get better, but also, the back end's got to help, the second level of the defense has to help with some of those things. When you get the ball thrown over your head, then it doesn't help the rush. So, that’s been a combination of things.”
There has certainly been a lot of outside chatter and debate when it comes to embattled Jaguars wide receiver Brian Thomas Jr., who has not caught a pass since Week 4 against the Cincinnati Bengals. Thomas did not play a single snap in the second half of the Jaguars' Week 6 loss to the Houston Texans after two first-half drops, and his future with the team will remain in doubt until either they trade him or until he starts producing.
Coen took several questions on the Thomas front on Wednesday, though he once again stressed the belief that Thomas will help the Jaguars move the ball and score points when it comes to Sunday's game against the Colts. Coen has said that at several different poiints before, but the heat has never been turned up on Thomas quite like this.
“I mean, every player has ups and downs and it’s just week to week in the NFL. I fully anticipate he's going to make plays for us this Sunday," Coen said.
"It's just every week different guys step up, different guys make plays, and you've got to be able to be consistent with their approach as a coach to say, okay, you got to keep giving people opportunities. But also, when there's a hot hand going, you got to go with the hot hand a little bit here and there, and that's just the way the game flows.”

title: Jaguars-Colts Wednesday Injury Report: It Is Time to Unleash Jalen Huskey
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- There should be one clear reaction to the Jacksonville Jaguars' first injury report of Week 8: it is time for Jalen Huskey.
Huskey, the No. 100 pick in April's NFL Draft, has yet to log a snap on defense and has only been active for one game. But the Jaguars should use this week to push Huskey toward some real playing time considering starting safety Antonio Johnson missed Wednesday's practice with an ankle injury.
Johnson was the only Jaguar who did not practice Wednesday, which is not a great sign coming off a bye week. Johnson injured his ankle in the Week 6 loss to the Houston Texans in London, and the Jaguars very well may be without their best safety once they kick off against the Indianapolis Colts in Week 8.
With second-year safety Caleb Ransaw on injured reserve and not looking close to returning anytime soon, the Jaguars' options at safety while Johnson recovers are starting safety Eric Murray, backup safety Kaevon Merriweather, second-year special teamer Rayuan Lane, or Huskey. The Jaguars leaned toward Merriweather getting playing time over Huskey at previous points, but it is time for the Jaguars to unleash their rookie.
Merriweather has played 45 NFL games and has been in the NFL since 2023, so naturally he has more experience than Huskey does just a few months into his NFL career. But the Jaguars need to see what they have in their young safety, especially as injuries continue to hit the safety room. Even if the Jaguars start Merriweather over Huskey, they should deploy their third-round defensive back as their No. 3 safety.
Simply put, Jacksonville has a young, athletic and talented safety who has been waiting in the wings, and it is time to see what he has. That is not to say Huskey would be the solution to the Jaguars' issues with explosive passes allowed, but he would give the Jaguars a dynamic at the safety position that Lane and Merriweather likely would not.
Johnson not playing on Sunday would be a significant blow for the Jaguars' defense considering the impact he has made this season, both in coverage and as a blitzer against the run and rushing the passer. But the Jaguars drafted Huskey for situations like this, and it is time to let him play.
With that said, there was some good news for the Jaguars on the injury front. Cornerback Montaric Brown was a full participant after missing time with a hamstring injury that has sidelined him for all but six snaps in the Jaguars' last three games.
Brown was struggling at times before his injury, but a healthy Brown would help change the math in the cornerback room and potentially allow the Jaguars to play Jarrian Jones in the slot more than he has played since Brown started missing practice and game reps due to injury.
"Buster's not only a pro’s pro, consistent, communication and can make plays on the football. He stabilizes things and also is a really good tackler in space," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said on Wednesday.
"Anytime we can be at full strength, it's a benefit to our defense. It allows those four specific DBs to be able to stay fresh, stay healthy, rotate in spots and play in different areas of the field in which we feel as though they're a strength for us and situationally as well. Anytime you go down at corner, which a lot of teams do, right, it just gets thin quick.”
Limited in practice for the Jaguars were four players: linebacker Jalani Tavai (hamstring), wide receiver Jakobi Meyers (hamstring), long snapper Ross Matiscik (shoulder), and defensive tackle Ruke Orhorhoro.

title: Walker Little Can Answer One of the Jaguars' Biggest Questions, Starting in Week 8
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- Few Jacksonville Jaguars have as much to gain over the next three months as Walker Little.
Little is set to step in at left tackle for the rest of the season following the season-ending knee injury sustained by starting left tackle Anton Harrison, giving Little a chance to not just once again prove his worth, but also givng him a chance to answer one of the Jaguars' biggest and most looming questions entering future seasons.
Simply put, the future of the Jaguars' left tackle spot is a complete coin toss right now. While there has been hyperfocus about the Jaguars' pass-rush and defensive front in general, it is clear that the Jaguars' biggest 2027 need as of today is left tackle. Harrison was supposed to be the long-term answer at the spot, of course, but his injury has created quite the question mark for whether he has done enough to prove himself as the answer.
“Yeah, bummer for Anton and our team, really. I've been very proud of Anton, and he will be sorely missed. I really felt like Anton had been playing really good football, really all in with the group, his buy-in, his attention to detail, the way he'd been playing. I was very proud of Anton and the way he was playing for us," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said about Harrison's injury earlier this week.
The Jaguars would have loved to see Harrison establish himself as the left tackle of the future this year, but the injury means we will not get that answer until potentially next season when Harrison is coming off a serious injury. Could Little, once thought to be the Jaguars' left tackle for years to come, now reclaim his spot and ease the Jaguars' minds at the most important position on the line?
"We'll miss him without a doubt but was extremely proud of [OL] Walker Little and the way that he played on Sunday against Houston and stepped up in both the run and the pass," Coen said about Little filling in against the Houston Texans. Did some really good things for us and, no flinch, no blink, next man up mentality. Excited about him and his opportunity and there's not many guys that care more than Walker in a lot of ways about this team and about this group of guys.
If Little can provide the consistency the Jaguars need in Week 8 and beyond to help set up a run toward another AFC South title, the math on the Jaguars' left tackle spot might change. Little would be entering a contract year in 2027, but the Jaguars could see enough out of him this year to know that they have two different options to be their left tackle of tomorrow instead of just waiting to see if Harrison can become that player.
Little has been waiting for a chance like this for most of his career. He has had limited stretches of play where he has been seen as the guy at left tackle, but the Jaguars have no other option but to view him as it for the rest of 2027.
"I've learned a lot over my career and watched guys that have kind of been in my position as that sixth O-lineman, and how they've done it, how they stay ready for the moment," Little said this week.
"And I also think getting that game experience, having played in a lot of games it lets you refine what you need to do during practice. And just honestly, more than anything, it's just staying locked in, not letting things slip through the cracks even though you may not get the opportunity to play, so that when your number is called you can jump in and flow with the offense.”
The loss of Harrison is a significant one, and it causes a lot of questions for the Jaguars moving forward. But Little has the next 11 games to start answering some of those questions.

title: The Biggest Swing the Jaguars Can Take at the Trade Deadline is Clear
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The NFL Trade Deadline is just 13 days away, and there is one clear swing the Jacksonville Jaguars can take.
No, there isn't a pass-rusher or defensive back worth sending a first-round pick for in an attempt to take control of their wide-open window in the AFC. This isn't the kind of deadline that will see a Jalen Ramsey or Myles Garrett type of trade,  but it is one where the Jaguars could surely improve.
So, who is the true big swing the Jaguars can try to land before Nov. 10? It is clear, and it is a player the Jaguars have already faced: Philadelphia Eagles defensive tackle Moro Ojomo.
Simply put, there is no player who makes much more sense for the Jaguars at the trade deadline than Ojomo, the Eagles' talented fourth-year defensive tackle. There are a few different reasons why, but it starts with what Ojomo would naturally bring to the middle of the Jaguars' defensive line. Would he move the needle enough compared to Arik Armstead and the Jaguars' other interior pass-rushers? All evidence, from the film to the metrics, indicate the answer is yes.
Let's start with the fit. Ojomo plays in a similar defensive front to the one the Jaguars and Anthony Campanile employ, getting snaps both at three-technique and at nose tackle. Ojomo isn't simply an upfield three-technique who is trying to shoot into the backfield off the guard's outside shoulder on every play, and he has displayed the ability to two-gap that defensive tackles must thrive at in Campanile's system.
#Eagles DT Moro Ojomo is going to get $100 million-plus next spring pic.twitter.com/RHzxzK0L1x
Ojomo is a talented run-defender, but where he would really help the Jaguars is in terms of the pass-rush. As things stand today, the Jaguars' defensive tackles (DaVon Hamilton, Arik Armstead, Matt Dickerson, Ruke Orhorhoro, and Albert Regis) have recorded 33 pressures and an average pressure rate of 8%. This year by himself, Ojomo has 18 pressures and a 10.2% rate, which would make him far and away the Jaguars' most effective and effecient pass-rusher from the inside.
Ojomo, who has zero sacks this year, had six sacks last year but has been a significantly better player in 2025. He looks like the second coming of Milton Williams, serving as the most productive of the Eagles' big three at defensive tackle despite being the odd man out for the long-term. The Eagles have already paid Jalen Carter and Jordan Davis, and Ojomo is now guranteed to play for a new team next season.
With Ojomo's Eagles career ending later this season, and with the Eagles' season officially lost, there is no reason for Philadelphia to hang onto him at the trade deadline. They could be stubborn akep hind hold onto him since, chances are, they would get at least a fourth-round compensatory pick for him if they keep him before letting him walk in free agency in March.
The difference is that the Eagles wouldn't get that pick until 2028. If the Jaguars were to offer the Eagles a similarly valued pick but in 2027 instead, the Eagles would be a bit foolish to not let go of their talented defensive tackle. The writing is already on the wall that he won't return, so why not get a pick for him now instead of a year from now?
As for the Jaguars, Ojomo is exactly the kind of player they should target. He turned 25 in August and has his best football ahead of him, with many defensive tackles truly hitting their peak around 26/27. He is an ascending player who should continue to get better moving forward, which would not be the case if the Jaguars added an older veteran like Daron Payne.
The Jaguars would have nearly three months to see if Ojomo is a long-term piece and the future of their interior defensive line before they had to make any future decisions. With Armstead and Hamilton in contract years, Ojomo could easily be re-signed to be a key piece moving forward, which is the move the Jaguars made with Jakobi Meyers once it became clear that he was set to be a building block.
If the Jaguars feel like Ojomo is nothing more than a rental who can help them over the course of the 2026 playoff run, then they could then plat the comp pick game the Eagles would be interested in. If Ojomo helped the Jaguars win some big games this year and then helps net them a third- or fourth-round pick in the future, is anyone complaining?
Ojomo may not be a household name yet, but he is one of the most talented and impactful players whose odds to be traded are near guranteed. There is no reason the Jaguars shouldn't take a swing when it comes to adding him to their defense.
