title: NFL Power Rankings Roundup: Jaguars Enter Week 8 With Massive Opportunity in AFC South
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- Week 8 is set to be an important week for the Jacksonville Jaguars.
After the amount of losing and tomfoolery that has transpired in the AFC South since the last time the Jaguars were on the field in London in Week 6, the Jaguars have quite the opportunity on hand when they face the Indianapolis Colts in their return from the bye week on Sunday at EverBank Stadium.
With the Colts now conceding the AFC South with the trades of Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner, and with the Texans sitting at 2-5 and still not quite figuring things out, the divisional race is there for the taking as long as the Jaguars take care of business. And if that is how things play out, the Jaguars can shift their focus to bigger and better things across the AFC.
So, where do the Jaguars stack up against the other AFC contenders entering an important Week 8? We break it down below with this week's roundup of power rankings.
The Jaguars do not take a step backward or forward in SI's weekly power rankings, with Liam Coen's squad sticking firm at the No. 8 spot. The Jaguars have a chance to raise their profile a good bit in the weeks and months to come with battles against the Baltimore Ravens and Chicago Bears both down the road.
The bye week gave the Seahawks the chance to jump in front of the Jaguars but, otherwise, there is not much here. The Minnesota Vikings will have to lose a game eventually, and that is likely when the Jaguars can really start getting a rise. Otherwise, most of the teams in front of the Jaguars here can be expected to stay there.
I am going to talk about the Cincinnati Bengals being ranked above the Jaguars a few times here, but that is the biggest question mark in terms of where the Jaguars are ranked here and which teams are above them. The Jaguars already beat the Bengals in Cincinnati, but alas.
There is almost zero movement in this week's power rankings, and the same applies for the Jaguars at No. 8. If the Chiefs keep slipping, though, the Jaguars could easily take their spot in the weeks and months to come considering their strength of schedule.
There isn't much to say here. The Jaguars are behind a few risers like the Chicago Bears who are coming off strong Week 7 performances, which means the Jaguars and their bye week brings them down a spot. If the Jaguars are going to rise, it will need to happen over the next few weeks as they play some key AFC South games.
The Jaguars drop out of the top-five here in favor of ... the Cincinnati Bengals? The Bengals defense is still not very good, and the offenses needed the score 35 unanswered points in the second-half to make up for an absolutely putrid first half against the Baltimore Ravens in Week 7. Putting the Bengals anywhere near above the Jaguars is off, I would say, but that is where the Jaguars find themselves in this week's rankings at a few different spots.
The Bengals jumped the Jaguars in this week's power rankings, which seems ... odd. The Jaguars were clearly the better team when they faced off against the Bengals in Week 4, with the Jaguars having two touchdowns and an interception all negated by questionable judgement calls from the officials. The Jaguars are better than the Bengals, and I would imagine they are better by quite a bit, too.
The Jaguars climbed this week after the San Francisco 49ers and Kansas City Chiefs lost their first games of the season. It is fair to say the 49ers and Chiefs each can't say they are surely a tier above the Jaguars after mistake-filled and middling performances against the Atlanta Falcons and Seattle Seahawks, which makes it clear that the Jaguars belong here.

title: The Jaguars' Perfect Trade Target Isn't Actually Even an Option
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- There is one NFL Trade Deadline target that makes perfect sense for the Jacksonville Jaguars ... who also seemingly has zero chance of landing in Jacksonville.
The Indianapolis Colts are in a complete tailspin , and their fire sale began on Tuesday as they sent future Hall of Fame guard Quenton Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks for a third-round pick and a future fifth-round pick. As a result, it only makes sense for the Colts to make the perfect trade deadline target available: defensive tackle DeForest Buckner.
With that said , Buckner's talents should not be expected to land in Jacksonville for a simple reason: the Colts and Jaguars do not do business with each other when it comes to trades.
There are a million reasons why Buckner would make sense for the Jaguars. Even at 32, he is still one of the best interior pass-rushers in the NFL, and he would lead the Jaguars in both pressures and sacks. The Jaguars have lacked any sense of an interior rush for years now, and Buckner would be a more appealing option to boost the Jaguars' pass-rush than most other interior defenders. He is also in a contract year and would likely help the Jaguars earn a compensatory draft pick in March if he serves to only be a rental for the rest of 2026.
Buckner is exactly the kind of player the Jaguars need in the middle of their defense, the Colts are seemingly set to be willing to move on from all top players, and the Jaguars have the picks to make a compelling case and offer. With that said, there just isn't a chance the Jaguars are going to land the veteran defensive tackle. Whenever Buckner is traded (likely to the San Francisco 49ers or Chicago Bears), one should not question why Jaguars general manager James Gladstone didn't make it happen.
Sources: The #Colts are also actively shopping DT DeForest Buckner. I expect him to be moved soon if the right offer comes in. https://t.co/U36PCN9an3
Instead, it is clear that the Jaguars' AFC South connection with the Colts makes them disqualified from the Buckner sweepstakes to start. Buckner looks like he is bound to be the next player the Colts and placeholder general manager Ed Dodds deals, but that does not mean the Colts are going to help Jacksonville anytime soon.
Yes, the Colts have already conceded their place in the AFC South race. And yes, the Colts will likely lose to the Jaguars twice in 2026 even if Buckner wasn't on the Jaguars' defense. But history says that a Buckner trade to Jacksonville isn't just unlikely, but it it would break all historical precedents the AFC South has set over the last few decades.
The Jaguars have engaged in player trades in the AFC South just twice: in 2025 when they traded Christian Kirk to the Houston Texans for a seventh-round pick, and in 2020 when they traded the Tennessee Titans a sixth-round pick for linebacker Kamalei Correa, who played six games for the 1-15 Jaguars and made seven tackles.
So trades have happened, but it has only been trades that contain absolutely zero consequences. The Jaguars knew that Kirk was never going to impact their race for the AFC South title, just like the Titans knew that giving Correa to a bad Jaguars team would make no difference. A Buckner trade wouldn't fall into this category at all, though. It would be a legit game-changer in the short-term, and Dodds doesn't want to be the interim general manager who helped the Jaguars find playoff success in a wide-open AFC.
In a perfect world, Buckner would make a ton of sense for the Jaguars. He fits everything they need on and off the field. But in this world, Buckner to the Jaguars is nothing more than a pipedream and a wish upon a star.

title: Ranking the Jaguars' Top NFL Trade Deadline Targets: From Realistic to Delusional
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The NFL Trade Deadline is officially two weeks away, and the Jacksonville Jaguars are certainly a team to watch once Nov. 10 rolls around.
Part of that is due to the situation surrounding wide receiver Brian Thomas Jr., who could draw interest from teams in need of an offensive spark. Part of it is also due to the fact that the 4-2 Jaguars look ready to go on a run, which would mean it makes all the sense in the world for them to be buyers once the deadline is officially here.
So, which trade deadline targets make the most actual sense for James Gladstone's front office to go after? And which are, well, pipedreams? We break it down below.
If there is one move that just makes sense for the Jaguars, from fit to need, it is likely Khalil Mack. The Jaguars have a talented pair of defensive ends in Josh Hines-Allen and Travon Walker who should get more productive as the year goes, but their pass-rush depth behind the duo is minimal. The Jaguars have not gotten much production from backup defensive ends Danny Striggow and Bryan Thomas Jr., while Dennis Gardeck might be better off as a rotational piece than as a key part of the pass-rush rotation.
Mack makes a ton of sense for a contender like the Jaguars, he is cheap and in a contract year, and likely would take what amounts to a fifth-round pick to land in a trade. He is getting up there and his production has taken a small dip as a result, but he can still get the job done. He would fit the Jaguars' culture and mentality on defense, while also allowing Travon Walker to play pass-rushing snaps inside more frequently.
While Moro Ojomo did get sidelined with an injury against the Dallas Cowboys on Monday Night Football, he still makes a ton of sense for a team like the Jaguars as long as it wasn't anything overly serious. The Eagles are sitting at 2-5 and their season looks closer and closer to being over with each passing week. With big money tied up to Jalen Carter and Jordan Davis, it has always been clear the Eagles would not re-sign Ojomo, making him an easy trade candidate.
Ojomo is young, can give the Jaguars a boost both against the run and the pass, and would allow the Jaguars to have time to figure out whether he is just a rental and a compensatory pick formula chess piece, or if he is instead a long-term option. Not many players, if any, make more sense for the Jaguars to call about.
While Zach Sieler has been a productive player for a long-time, he is in a different stage of his career than Ojomo. He is older, less productive as a pass-rusher right now, more expensive, and is under contract for several more seasons. With that said, he has connections to the Jaguars' staff, would improve their depth at defensive tackle, and likely would not take much to pry from the Dolphins considering where they are at with their rebuild.
Do the Jaguars actually have a use in their scheme for a true designated pass-rusher who is more of a speed threat than anything else? That remains to be seen considering the traits the Jaguars have been adding at EDGE over the last two years. With that said, both Will McDonald and Josh Uche are guys who can really go off the edge, and they would give the Jaguars the fastball pass-rusher off the edge that would mesh well with Hines-Allen and Walker.
This would be all about cost, both in terms of draft compensation and cap space needed. The Jaguars would need to create a few million in terms of cap space to fit Payne's deal on the books, while he is also closer to being a blue-chip player than most others on this list. Payne would make a big, big impact for the Jaguars due to his production as both a pass-rusher and a run-stopper, but this seems unlikely unless it is something like a straight Payne for Brian Thomas Jr. swap.
We already mentioned one Los Angeles Chargers pass-rusher as a trade option. Tuli Tuipulotu is another gifted Chargers defender who could be shopped as they continue to lose games due to his status as a contract-year defender at a premium position. With that said, chances are he would cost a good bit more than Mack due to the fact that he is a much younger player at the same position. He would also be more of a starter-type, while Mack can be more rotational.
Outside of Jacksonville, the AFC South is a mess right now. All three other AFC South teams lost in Week 7, bringing the combined AFC South record for non-Jaguars teams to 5-16. The 2-5 Indianapolis Colts look like they could be major sellers ahead of the Nov. 10 trade deadline, and the result of their battle with the Jaguars in Week 8 could play a big role in that. The Houston Texans seem unlikely to be sellers since they will believe they can make a run, while the Tennessee Titans have the NFL's best defensive tackle once again playing on its worst team
With that said, do not expect for the Jaguars to land any potential departures from the AFC South such as DeForest Buckner, Grover Stewart, Quenton Nelson, or whomever else. In-division trades do not happen often unless they are ones of little-to-no consequence, like the Jaguars trading Christian Kirk to the Texans last season. That is just how these things go, and the only real way the AFC South's movement at the deadline will impact the Jaguars is by weaking the division as they try to go on their run.

title: Liam Coen Has 1 Simple Solution for Jaguars to Avoid NFL's Referee Debacle
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- As the Jacksonville Jaguars surely know by now, the NFL has a referee problem.
The Jaguars have seen officials make some dramatic, and even simply flat-out wrong, calls against them during their 4-2 stretch in the first six weeks of the season. This includes five touchdowns negated by penalties since Week 3, including a Bhayshul Tuten touchdown in Week 6 against the Houston Texans on a phantom hold. A few plays later, Trevor Lawrence threw a red-zone interception and the Jaguars failed to score, eventually losing 34-31 on a walk-off field goal.
With the NFL's officials under more fire this week after a complete debacle of a performance in the Green Bay Packers' loss to the Detroit Lions, it is only natural for the focus on the NFL's penalty problem to once again shift toward its officials. As a result, Jaguars head coach Liam Coen has one simple solution for the Jaguars to avoid penalty issues at they look to make a run: l eave no doubt.
“Leave no doubt is really what it comes down to. Play above it, leave no doubt," Coen said Monday when asked about what he preaches to his locker room when it comes to recent penalty issues.
That is of course easier said than done, especially with some of the calls that have gone against the Jaguars this season. But no matter how valid the penalties are, the flags are the biggest reason the Jaguars are 4-2 right now and not 5-1. The numbers make it clear that, outside of the Packers, no team has been impacted more by judgement calls from officials than the Jaguars.
What you are feeling is real weezy The Packers rank last in penalty "luck" through 7 weeks. Mostly due to defensive holding and roughing the passer calls on the defense https://t.co/CytDRjyAhP pic.twitter.com/g42tXv7wWG
"Fundamentals, and you guys hear me say it ad nauseam, but regardless of results, right, the fundamentals and techniques in which we coach, teach… We’ve got to continue to detail those even when fatigue sets in and whether it's mental or physical fatigue that sets in, we have got to be at our best in terms of detail, fundamentally sharp, disciplined in order to leave no doubt that we control our destiny," Coen said.
"We control the outcomes of games at the end of the day in terms of win or lose, and we can live with those results. You just can't go there. It's hard not to. It's human instinct and nature to do so, but it really doesn't do anybody any good to go down that path. Trust me, I've been there.”
Coen, of course, is right. There is nothing the Jaguars can do about the called-back Tuten touchdowns or Josh Cameron's negated kickoff return against the Eagles or Travis Hunter's negated interception against the Bengals, or any of the several questionable pass interference calls against the Texans. All the Jaguars can do is play through it, starting with Week 8 against the Indianapolis Colts.
Penalties are a huge reason the Jaguars lost to the Texans in London, but they are not the only reason. The Jaguars still made their fair share of self-inflicted mistakes that they must avoid in the weeks to come, which is the message Coen and his staff has stressed.
"We got to be on our P's and Q's, and that just makes us better football players," Jaguars cornerback Jourdan Lewis said on Monday.
"And I think that's what kept me in the league a long time, is just understanding how to adapt to different styles of how the game is being played and called just understanding the rules, because at the end of the day we got to go out there and play. Regardless of how it's being officiated or things are being called, we got to be out there and give it our all and play our best.”

title: Jaguars Know The Magic Number in the AFC South, and Now They Can Make Their Run
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are ready to make their run.
The bye week turned everything around for the Jaguars a year ago, and the comparisons to this year can certainly be drawn. Jacksonville was 4-3 and coming off a tough loss in London at last year's bye week, and this year the Jaguars were 4-2 entering their bye and coming off an emotional last-second loss to the Houston Texans in London.
Adding Jakobi Meyers at the trade deadline certainly helped, but overall the Jaguars were a different team post-bye last season. Jacksonville went 9-1 after last year's bye week to set themselves up with a 13-4 record, an AFC South title, and a home playoff game.
Now, they will need to make the same thing happen now that they know what the magic number in the AFC South is : 13 wins.
The math is simple. If the Jaguars go 9-2 over the next 11 weeks, they will win the AFC South. With the Houston Texans and Indianapolis Colts sitting at 2-5 after Week 7 , the Jaguars can ensure an AFC South title with 13 wins ... a number the Colts and Texans can not reach. Now, winning 9-of-11 games is difficult and something most teams do not do over the second-half of a season, but the Jaguars will be coming out of their Week 7 bye hoping to not be like most teams.
It helps that the Jaguars got quite a bit of help from the AFC South in Week 7. The AFC South went 0-3 on Sunday, and the Jaguars' three rivals have just five wins combined this season. The Texans have made runs before, and nothing is ever secured, but the Jaguars' chances of winning the south increased on a Sunday where the Jaguars were at home.
“It helps. It definitely helps. I did keep some eye on some of the opponents that we will be seeing in the future. To see the type of game style that they play and how they're doing," Jaguars cornerback Jourdan Lewis said Monday. "The AFC South helped us. We’re still number one in the division and just trying to make sure that we don't have any skids to where we let anybody get any opportunity to take that from us.”
To ensure the Jaguars avoid those skids and make a run, the Jaguars have a few clear areas to improve. Head coach Liam Coen noted some of these areas Monday, pointing out red-zone penalties on offense, explosive plays allowed through the air on defense, and kickoff and punt coverage units.
Each of these aspects of their team came up big in their lone two losses, especially in the Week 6 loss to the Texans. That is where the Jaguars' bye week comes into play. Last year, the bye week was about improving Trevor Lawrence and the passing game, and the Jaguars did exactly that. Now, their focus moving into Week 8 against the Indianapolis Colts and beyond is clear.
"Anytime you get a little bit of an opportunity to reset, gather your thoughts, also get away from it a little bit. Sometimes absence makes the heart grow fonder in ways, and no different in football. I couldn't sleep last night," Coen said Monday.
"Excited about getting back in the building and getting back with these guys and attacking these next 11 games together and really getting after it. It also came a little earlier this year than last, if you will, right, in terms of the way it played out and how many games we've played. But six weeks in and you see all the stuff that happens on any given Sunday, specifically within our division, it should only allow you to have a mindset and mentality to come in here and attack this thing with a division game up this week.”
The Jaguars have one of the NFL's easier schedules over the next 11 weeks, facing the Colts and Titans twice, the 2-5 Texans once more, the Washington Commanders, and some other very winnable games against the Dallas Cowboys, Baltimore Ravens, New York Giants, and the Pittsburgh Steelers. The toughest game left looks to be the Chicago Bears in Week 13.
But the Jaguars, more than anything, need to avoid those skids that Lewis mentioned. They can't take anything for granted, and they are still facing their own injury questions and pre-trade deadline chatter. It is, however, clear what it will take for the Jaguars to reach their goals.
Nine more wins, and the Jaguars will play a playoff football game in Jacksonville. It is time for the Jaguars to make their run.

title: The Colts Have Already Given the Jaguars the Perfect Week 8 Blueprint
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars have a big game coming up in Week 8, and they may have been given some early help in the form of the Minnesota Vikings.
The Jaguars are set to host their AFC South rival Indianapolis Colts in Week 8 as Jacksonville comes off their bye week, and they will be getting a Colts team that is fresh off a 16-10 loss to the Vikings. But beyond the fact the Jaguars are getting a slumping Colts team at the right time, the Jaguars also got a boost from the Vikings via a blueprint for disrupting the Colts, Shane Steichen, and Daniel Jones.
No team in football is blitzing more than the Vikings, who are led by defensive guru Brian Flores. Flores is going to send the house every single week, and he made sure to really turn up the pressure against the Colts and Jones. The plan clearly worked, with Jones going 11-of-18 for 101 yards and an interception against the blitz: giving him a passer rating of 53.2 and just 5.6 yards per attempt. Jones was one of the worst quarterbacks in the NFL this week against the blitz by most metrics, numbers that track with season-long averages.
The Vikings defense blitzed on 85.2% of Daniel Jones' dropbacks, the highest blitz rate by a defense in a game in the Next Gen Stats era (since 2016). Minnesota generated pressure on 60.9% of those blitzes, with all four its sacks coming when blitzing. #INDvsMIN | #Skol
This season, Jones ranks No. 21 out of 33 qualifying quarterbacks in EPA/Dropback against the blitz, No. 26 in passer rating, No. 33 in sacks, No. 27 in pressure rate, and No. 29 in air yards per attempt. In short, he gets sacked a ton against the blitz and, when he does throw it, he isn't exactly pushing the ball downfield. Jones is not accurate enough or a quick enough processor to consistently win as a quick-game passer, and Flores was able to get after this flaw on Sunday.
Simply put, the blueprint has been out on Jones for some time. But the performance he put together against the Vikings, combined with the fact that the Colts have the NFL's slowest receiver room with Alec Pierce injured, makes it clear that to secure a win on Sunday, Jaguars defensive coordinator Anthony Campanile should take a page out of his former bosses' playbook.
Campanile has worked for a number of top defensive minds, including Flores, Vic Fangio, and Jeff Hafley. While there is no coach quite like Flores, he has certainly made an impact on how Campanile sees the game and structures his defense, which means it might not be overly difficult for Campanile to attempt to replicate some of the things the Vikings did against the Colts.
“I think a lot of people had a huge influence on me. I'd say recently, obviously working with Jeff Hafley, I thought we had a very similar belief system and style. We see things very similarly and then Vic Fangio is probably a guy who—he had a tremendous impact on me, just in seeing certain things in the game and how you call the game," Campanile said last year. "And even in terms of how you practice things, so he's been somebody that has been a great resource for me, was a huge help to me. And he definitely had a big effect on me as well. Jeff's one of those guys and Flo [Vikings Defensive Coordinator Brian Flores] too. Coach Flores had a huge impact on me. And you can probably see a lot of the things that we do,  they may show up  for some of those teams as well.”
There are different factors to work in, of course. The Jaguars have an elite shutdown cornerback in Travis Hunter who can impact the math when it comes to blitzing and the defensive approach. The Jaguars have also not blitzed anywhere near as much as the Vikings, with Minnesota blitzing on 68.9% of passing plays (No. 1 in the NFL) compared to 30.5% from the Jaguars (No. 14). The highest rate of blitzing the Jaguars have done in a game this season was 45.2% against the Denver Broncos in Week 2, which would still fall below the Vikings' lowest blitz rate of the season (54.35).
But the blueprint is there, and the Jaguars can spin things in their own way to get home. Against the Colts a year ago, the Jaguars blitzed Jones twice on seven drop backs in his limited time on the field. Expect that number to go up after the success that Flores and the Vikings had, because it is clear that Jones and the Colts' offense as a whole simply can not handle it.

title: Patrick Mahomes Voices Thoughts on Josh Simmons Situation; Optimistic About 2026 Return
full_text:
One of the more concerning storylines in what has otherwise been a strong 5-1 start to the season for the Kansas City Chiefs has been Josh Simmons' back injury. A bulging disc in his lower back has kept the left tackle off the field the entire campaign, and the team placed him on Injured Reserve last week after his recovery stalled despite a brief return to practice in limited capacity.
Up until a few days ago, there was still optimism around the fanbase regarding Simmons' situation, as the training staff reportedly doesn't believe he'll need surgery for his injury and thinks he can heal with rest. However, the perception of Simmons took a turn for the worse when Mike Garafolo and Ian Rapoport revealed a dispute that went down in practice. According to the report, Simmons was in a team meeting with his feet propped up. Head coach Andy Reid took exception to this, and so did quarterback Patrick Mahomes. The superstar signal-caller allegedly asked Simmons to put his feet down and told him to leave the meeting in order to get treatment.
The latest development was bound to come up when the two-time MVP spoke to the media on Wednesday. He didn't directly confirm or deny the details of the exchange, but acknowledged that difficult conversations had taken place and that the team needs to do a better job of keeping those things in-house moving forward.
"Stuff like that doesn't really bother because I'm so in the moment. I think we've had the right conversations now," Mahomes stated. "We're moving in the direction. You have to have hard conversations at some point... We've built this culture of coming together as a family, and kind of doing whatever we can to make sure that not only the player but also the person is going in the right direction. You want to keep those conversations in the building, and so that's something we'll be better at moving forward."
Patrick Mahomes was asked about the story that came out Sunday morning between him and Josh Simmons. He told @Leabonics , "You have to be able to have tough conversations so that you can have better conversations going forward." pic.twitter.com/95NrEXWX4d
Rather than a hostile back-and-forth, Mahomes insisted that this was more of an open dialogue typical of the culture Reid has built throughout his years as head coach. He made sure to clarify that there was nothing malicious about the altercation and that things like that happen fairly often in the locker room.
Mahomes' outlook is far different from the one some Chiefs fans have taken amid the growing uncertainty surrounding Simmons. With the former first-round pick yet to play this season and now facing at least four more games on IR, questions about his future in Kansas City have grown. KCSN's very own Tucker Franklin and Matt Verderame recently pondered whether Simmons has played his final game in the red and gold. That isn't the perspective Mahomes has, though. He remains steadfast in his belief that Simmons has been working hard during this recovery process and will be back to help the team at some point.
"I'm extremely confident because I've seen the work he puts in," Mahomes said, according to 96.5 The Fan . "He's doing his rehab, he's doing his work, he's doing everything he can to be back on that field. He'll have a couple weeks here now while he's on IR where he can get himself back to the physical shape that he can be in. He'll be mentally confident to go out there and be the best version of himself, when he's able to do that, he'll be back on the football field."
Much has been said about the situation, and it certainly hasn't been a good look for the Chiefs. They invested a first-round pick in Simmons in last year's draft, and he was solid when he played across his eight starts as a rookie. However, he dealt with personal issues and a wrist injury that forced him to miss extended time, and it's starting to feel like his absence in 2026 is for something beyond football as well. In the meantime, undrafted rookie Kahlil Benson has been filling in at left tackle . He's stepped into a difficult role early in his career, but Simmons was drafted to help protect Mahomes for years to come. It is no secret that the Chiefs' best version of themselves includes Simmons on the blind side of KC's franchise cornerstone.
The public narrative surrounding Simmons has become increasingly negative, which is why Mahomes made sure to tread carefully with his words. While his comments don't put to rest the rumors about the tackle's long-term future in Kansas City, they do shed light on how Mahomes saw things through his own lens.

title: Andy Reid, Patrick Mahomes React to Chiefs’ Controversial Justin Tucker Signing
full_text:
Amid Kansas City Chiefs kicker Harrison Butker's ongoing struggles, the franchise made a surprising move this morning by signing Justin Tucker to the practice squad . The former Baltimore Ravens standout hasn't kicked in the NFL since the 2024 season after serving a suspension for violating the league's Personal Conduct Policy.
Many Kansas City fans thought it was well overdue for the team to bring someone in to make Butker's job less secure. However, the signing has already faced significant backlash from the media. He was cut by Baltimore in May 2025 due to a combination of his declining performance and the allegations of sexual misconduct involving 16 massage therapists . When head coach Andy Reid stepped to the podium for his press conference today , he fielded questions about Tucker for approximately five consecutive minutes. One of the more notable questions he faced was about the message Tucker's signing sends to female Chiefs fans.
"He's done his suspension. Took care of that business there," Reid responded. "I'll leave it at that for you."
Reid emphasized that he and the front office had done extensive homework on Tucker's past before they decided to offer him a spot on the practice squad. He wouldn't quite elaborate on what this "homework" entailed, but insisted the team had spoken with multiple people before making its decision.
"We try to do our homework the best way we possibly can," Reid said. "Talked to a lot of people to make sure things are okay." KC's head coach said that the team brought in three kickers earlier this week to try out for a spot. Reid believes that Tucker was the best of the bunch by a long shot. He wasn't exactly effective in his last full season when he finished with a subpar 73.3% field goal percentage (22-for-30), and it's been a while since he's kicked in live action.
If there's anything this signing does, it makes it clear that Butker's future with the team is no longer guaranteed. He's cost the Chiefs too many points in recent years for this situation to be ignored any longer. Since the start of the 2025 campaign, Butker's 15 missed kicks and extra points are the most of any player in the NFL.
Even after bringing Tucker on board, Reid maintains that he is still confident in his longtime placekicker and believes Butker's recent shortcomings stem from inconsistent form and technique rather than a mental issue. "Listen, we love Harrison. I've told you before, he's one of my favorite guys," he said about Butker. "Sometimes, things don't go quite the way you want them, and you work on that. He understands the business and how it works. We had a practice squad position open, so for security, we brought [Tucker] in and put him in that spot. Butker gets it and he knows that's part of the business."
He also confirmed that the "up-and-down" Butker will receive most of the first-team reps in remaining practices leading up to the Broncos game and that he should be the only kicker active this Sunday.
Coincidentally, Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes and Tucker have a history that goes beyond their time spent on opposing sidelines. The two (and Travis Kelce) were famously involved in a brief pregame confrontation over warm-up space in the 2024 AFC Championship Game, where KC would advance to Super Bowl LVIII in a 17-10 victory.
While there appeared to be bad blood between the two parties at the time, Mahomes chalked it up to competition and brushed the tension aside. "We haven't had a lot of conversations because he was on the Ravens, but it wasn't like we ever had any beef," Mahomes confirmed today. "At that moment, it was just competitors being competitors. He's been a big-time kicker for a long time... At the end of the day, we're just playing a game, and you want to compete and win."
Mahomes, who has always done an excellent job avoiding controversial answers to the media, wouldn't go in-depth on his thoughts about Tucker's signing and reaffirmed his trust in the front office. "We have a lot people that have been added in and out," Mahomes stated. "I try not go get too high or low or anything. I know [Brett] Veach does a great job of bringing players in."
There was always going to be an uproar over the Chiefs signing a shunned player whose NFL career appeared to be all but over. We'll soon find out whether Tucker is ever elevated to the 53-man roster and if he'll be an outside distraction moving forward.

title: Omarr Norman-Lott Taking Next Step in Return to Chiefs From ACL Tear
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs have been paid multiple visits by the pesky injury bug this season, although Week 8 presents one bit of good news on the defensive side of the ball.
Just over a year removed from sustaining a torn ACL , tackle Omarr Norman-Lott is being designated to return from the physically unable to perform (PUP) list. Sam McDowell of the Kansas City Star first broke the news on Wednesday.
The Chiefs designated Omarr Norman-Lott to return to practice today, a source told The Star.
Norman-Lott, the 63rd overall pick in last year's NFL Draft, originally suffered the knee injury during a Week 7 contest against the Las Vegas Raiders. That ended his rookie campaign after the Tennessee product logged all of 73 snaps, recording five tackles and a sack in the process.
With the door for a potential regular-season debut now propped open, Norman-Lott is set to begin a 21-day window in which the team can evaluate his progress. At any point during that period, Kansas City can move Norman-Lott to the active 53-man roster. If he isn't ready to return, he'll remain on the shelf for the rest of the 2026-27 season.
Speaking to the media two weeks ago to the day, head coach Andy Reid briefly acknowledged that the sophomore tackle was inching closer to a potential return to action in some capacity.
"He is getting better, yeah," Reid said. "He is getting better. He's out working out with the trainers and doing that, but he's getting closer.”
This process seems to have taken longer than initially thought, as general manager Brett Veach shared back in April that he expected the former second-round pick to " be ready to rock and roll " for training camp. He was technically with the team at the Missouri Western State University campus, albeit to continue rehab and keep moving along at a slower pace.
Given the presence of All-Pro Chris Jones, the offseason signing of Khyiris Tonga and the first-round NFL Draft pickup of Peter Woods, there's no imminent pressure for Norman-Lott to get back on the field quickly. He'd presumably fill the role of someone like undrafted rookie Bryson Eason once ready, but Eason's played just 18 defensive snaps in four games.
According to Pro Football Focus , Norman-Lott logged six pressures in 48 pass-rushing opportunities as a first-year player. Considering his athletic profile during college compared to the seemingly bulked-up version the Chiefs fielded early on, it'll be interesting to see what role he assumes on defense when and if he plays down the stretch.
For a team that's been ravaged by recent injuries, this is a positive midweek development for Kansas City.

title: Chiefs Put Harrison Butker on Notice With Reported Justin Tucker Signing
full_text:
Despite their 5-1 record, the Kansas City Chiefs have experienced their fair share of issues throughout the 2026-27 season thus far. Getting consistent play out of the special teams unit, particularly regarding kicker Harrison Butker, is at or near the top of the list.
Following another rough outing for the club's longtime star kicker, Kansas City is bringing in another one to light a fire under Butker. It just so happens to be someone whose resume and track record blow Butker's out of the water.
First reported by Sam McDowell of the Kansas City Star on Wednesday morning, the Chiefs are bringing in former Baltimore Ravens kicker Justin Tucker on a practice squad basis.
The Chiefs are signing kicker Justin Tucker to the practice squad, a source tells The Star.
Ian Rapoport of NFL Network and ESPN reports that the Chiefs also worked out two other kickers, including former Los Angeles Rams man Harrison Mevis.
Speaking to the media following Sunday's 20-3 loss to the Seattle Seahawks , a game in which he went 1-for-3 on field goals, Butker tipped his cap to special teams coordinator Dave Toub for having his back through some recent struggles.
"I appreciate it," Butker said. "He definitely supports me. I'm in my 10th season here. I'm very thankful to have been with him for such a long time. He's my biggest supporter and always pushing me to do my best. Every kick matters, every day at practice, every game. I've got to be better."
Butker stated his pre-game warmup leading up to Sunday Night Football "wasn't great," although he couldn't pinpoint one specific thing that led to him missing his kicks.
Harrison Butker (Kansas City) ranks dead last in field goal pts over expected at -7.69, behind Trey Smack -7.28 (Green Bay) & Harrison Mevis -6.87 (Free Agent) Leaders: Will Reichard +9.47 (Minnesota), Chase McLaughlin +8.78 (Tampa Bay) & Ka'imi Fairbairn +8.56 (Houston) https://t.co/zIndx0hYoV
Tucker, a seven-time Pro Bowler and career 89.1% kicker on field goals, trails only Los Angeles Chargers standout Cameron Dicker (92.6%) as the most accurate player ever. Still, the move isn't necessarily as clear-cut in value as it appears on the surface.
First and foremost, it's been two seasons since Tucker's even kicked in an NFL game. He was suspended 10 weeks during the 2025 offseason following allegations of sexual misconduct, deemed a violation of the NFL's personal conduct policy. That followed Tucker being released by the Ravens, the only other NFL franchise he's ever known, on May 5 of the same year.
The veteran was reinstated on November 11 , only to remain unsigned for nearly a full calendar year thereafter. Tucker did get brought in for tryouts with the New Orleans Saints, Indianapolis Colts and New York Jets during that window.
Off-the-field developments aside, the Tucker signing comes with plenty of additional questions to answer. He's now several years removed from his last Pro Bowl campaign in 2023, and he left a trail of poor results on his way out of Baltimore. Kicking in all 17 regular-season games in 2024, he converted on just 22 of 30 field goal attempts, good for a 73.3% mark.
That includes a 6-of-11 ledger from 50-plus yards, which has been an issue for Butker lately as well.
Can someone who turns 37 in a matter of weeks, hasn't played in a game in 21 months and wasn't good the last time we saw him provide enough for the move to be worth it? That all remains to be seen.
At the least, it's a message to Butker that he must improve his level of play. Otherwise, his Chiefs tenure could be on ice.

title: Chiefs On SI Mailbag: Were the Chiefs Actually Exposed in Seattle?
full_text:
Things couldn't have gone much worse for the Kansas City Chiefs in their Sunday Night Football loss against the Seattle Seahawks . Still, KC remains at the top of the AFC with a 5-1 record and a lot of football still to be played.
What questions rose to the top of the Chiefs' list of uncertainties after their first loss of the year? Let's answer a few in this week's edition of the Chiefs On SI mailbag.
After this Seattle debacle, how bad have the Chiefs been exposed? - @MrEd315
I like the phrasing of this question, and I think I may surprise some people with my answer. How badly were the Chiefs exposed on Sunday? I'm not sure they were exposed at all!
The Chiefs' flaws in that game were glaring. Xavier Worthy, Jalen Royals and Andrew Armstrong are not a legitimate 1-2-3 trio of wide receivers, and the Chiefs know that. The Seahawks knew that.
The injuries at offensive tackle—down to OT3 on the left side and OT4 on the right—were no secret either. The Seahawks may have "exposed" the fact that if you can stop Kenneth Walker, you can stop that version of the Chiefs' offense , but we talked about that issue all week, leading up to the game.
The pass rush wasn't nearly good enough at rattling Sam Darnold, but it was the fourth game this year where they failed to record a sack; that's not a new issue either.
This whole winding road leads me to a potentially unsatisfying point: the Chiefs lost that game more dramatically than I would have expected, but not for any reasons that weren't already top-of-mind. Is that enough to soothe all of your Chief concerns? Absolutely not. But it is a silver lining, and better than losing a game for some surprising, unforeseen reason.
How would you divvy up blame for the poor offensive performance between QB play, personnel, and scheme? I feel like the QB play is not a given to be Tier 1 like it was prior to 2024. - @broccolirabe.bsky.social
Patrick Mahomes has been excellent this season, but I do think the Seattle loss included his worst game of the year . With memories of the way he's been caught "pressing" in the past as he's tried to overcome his surroundings in recent years, I think the uncertainty at offensive tackle and lack of any legitimate separation from his pass-catchers allowed Mahomes to rediscover some bad habits in Seattle .
Still, late in the game, Mahomes seemed to find his groove again before being let down by his supporting cast. The quarterback is, by far, the least of my worries.
I do think the coaching staff could have given Kenneth Walker a few more tries on the ground before completely giving up on the running game (though it was unproductive when they did try it), and I'd love to see Cyrus Allen get a longer look when none of the other pass-catchers are standing out. Ultimately, I think that the deficiencies of the players who were thrust into action on Sunday night played the biggest role of the three options presented in the question.
How do they get to 10 wins? - @joeybeckley.bsky.social
Keep playing the games. They're 5-1. They have plenty of issues to solve, and this mailbag has detailed several, but I'd be absolutely floored if they're not a playoff team with double-digit wins.
With the injuries at WR and tackle and the lack of any sort of pass rush, could the Chiefs actually do a little selling at the deadline instead of adding? - @mrproctober.bsky.social
If some team wants to acquire a non-vital piece from KC, Brett Veach should hear them out, sure. In the meantime, they're currently the No. 1 seed in the AFC. Even if that seems unlikely to hold, a 5-1 team quarterbacked by Patrick Mahomes will not and should not be "sellers" at the deadline.

title: Chiefs Rookie and Sophomore Power Rankings: Several Young Players Drop in Week 8
full_text:
Seven weeks into the 2026 NFL campaign, the Kansas City Chiefs finally suffered their first loss . There are no moral victories in this sport, although one potential silver lining is that the defeat came at the hands of an NFC club that very well could contend for the Super Bowl once again.
In the aftermath of an ugly showing on the road, Kansas City is sent back to the drawing board prior to a critical Sunday showdown against the Denver Broncos. The club's young players will surely be asked to contribute in an AFC West clash — which ones are trending in the right and wrong directions?
Following Week 7, let's break down the Chiefs' rookies and sophomores by ranking each qualifying 53-man roster member in tiers. Be sure to return to this series each week to see who's moving and shaking.
Defensive tackle Omarr Norman-Lott isn't included due to him currently being on the physically unable to perform list . Left tackle Josh Simmons isn't included after going to injured reserve . The same applies to running back Brashard Smith .
When you notch an interception to potentially save a touchdown, you get kudos. When you do so in a game that was bordering on getting out of hand and your return sets up the team for an end-of-half field goal try, you get mentioned in this group. Cornerback Nohl Williams' impressive season rolls on thanks to his pick of Seahawks quarterback Sam Darnold in Week 7.
NOHL WILLIAMS END ZONE INT AND A BIG RETURN KCvsSEA on NBC/Peacock Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/K42foMAhQy
First-round corner Mansoor Delane had a couple of rough reps against last season's Offensive Player of the Year, wideout Jaxon Smith-Njigba, although one was simply a remarkable throw and catch. There's no need to worry about the LSU product moving forward. His third-down pass breakup and separate nice play on Smith-Njigba on a second-and-10 in the second half provided plenty of reason for continued optimism.
Rookie pass rusher R Mason Thomas and sophomore defensive end Ashton Gillotte were both shouted out in this week's stock watch story for their performances at Lumen Field. Thomas flashed more of his ability to put pressure on opposing signal-callers, whereas Gillotte's run defense was one of the few bright spots on Sunday Night Football .
Dropping down after temporarily being bumped up a tier are undrafted rookie offensive tackle Kahlil Benson and first-round defensive tackle Peter Woods. The former had one of his worst showings as a pro, albeit against a ruthless defense, but he was partially responsible for quarterback Patrick Mahomes being pressured at a top-five rate for his career. The latter played 33 snaps, good for nearly 48% of those available, but made a minimal impact.
First-year halfback Emmett Johnson didn't receive a single carry on offense for the second time in three games, but he did make a pair of nice plays in the passing game. One was a critical catch on a seemingly lost drive, and the next was a block that allowed Mahomes to pick up a rushing first down.
Wide receivers Jalen Royals and Cyrus Allen both had moments that reminded those in Chiefs circles why they have yet to break out to this point. Allen, in particular, is a fan-favorite piece who many want to see the field more, but he's occasionally had trouble even navigating plays correctly.
UDFA defensive tackle Bryson Eason logged five snaps on defense and had an assisted tackle. He doesn't play special teams, so he can't move down a tier, but he's the least-noticeable player in this group.
The split of special teams versus offensive reps for tight end Jake Briningstool is up to 84-52 in 2026. In the last three games, it's 39-23. In Week 7, it was 12-5. Among this "primary special teams tier," he's the player it's easiest to see getting a promotion with a bit more involvement in future contests. Without someone above him getting hurt, safety Xavier Nwankpa's role seems capped, which is a shame considering the juice he brings to the field.
Linebacker Jeffrey Bassa is moderately similar to Nwankpa, although his role for special teams coordinator Dave Toub is more significant as a trusted option who's also made some plays this season. Given the shuffle at his defensive position, though, an increased snap count appears unlikely.
With Simmons on IR, UDFA tackle Diego Pounds technically was active for Week 7 but didn't play a single snap. He's here until further notice, joined by fourth-round rookie corner Jadon Canady , seventh-round rookie quarterback Garrett Nussmeier and UDFA defensive end Jack Pyburn . Nussmeier has routinely been the club's emergency third field general, but him not getting any live reps is a good thing.

title: Chiefs Stock Watch: Multiple Risers and Fallers After KC's First Loss vs. Seahawks
full_text:
No good run lasts forever, which the Kansas City Chiefs learned the hard way in Week 7 against the Seattle Seahawks. Going on the road to face the defending Super Bowl champions proved to be too tall a task for head coach Andy Reid's crew, resulting in an embarrassment on the Sunday Night Football stage.
Multiple players on both sides of the football struggled to make a positive impact. On the flip side, others' arrows might be pointing in the right direction despite the 20-3 defeat.
Let's dive into the good and bad from Week 7's Chiefs loss against Seattle and single out three players whose stock is trending up, as well as three who could use a better showing in Week 8 and beyond.
These players stood out for positive reasons over the weekend, potentially changing the trajectory of their seasons in the process.
Coming into the regular season, many had questions about how viable of an option second-year defensive end Ashton Gillotte would be. After all, he was on the heels of an underwhelming debut campaign and also sustained a plantar fascia injury in August. After a quiet start to 2026, those concerns were only amplified, but Gillotte's been improving since then.
According to Pro Football Focus , the former third-round pick logged three pressures in back-to-back games against the Las Vegas Raiders and Los Angeles Chargers. The outlet didn't credit him with one in Week 7, but he logged a season-high four "stops" on SNF . For reference, that's a quarter of his 2025 total.
Speaking of pressures, rookie D-end R Mason Thomas racked up four of them against a tough Seattle squad. He was one of just four Chiefs to notch a statistic in that category and trailed only fellow pass rusher George Karlaftis' six on the night.
Thomas, a second-rounder out of Oklahoma , is the best athlete in the room and wins quicker than anyone else. He's an excellent change-of-pace piece whose sack numbers aren't there yet, but there's no denying his raw ability. He has 14 combined pressures in his last three games and isn't getting washed out in run defense as often as he did earlier in the season.
Not all tackles are created equal, especially in the modern NFL. Elements like depth in relation to the line of scrimmage, pursuit versus crashing downhill, whether a player was in coverage and so much more go into the value of that box score stat. Linebacker Nick Bolton knows that better than anyone, evidenced by him sitting in the double digits in four of his last five contests. The Missouri product had another 11 tackles on Sunday, but this game felt a bit different.
Bolton was a huge factor in run support in Seattle, including a TFL on halfback Velus Jones Jr. on the club's fifth possession and a couple of other stops. He did whiff on an attempt that comes to mind, but this was the fully realized version of the heat-seeking missile Kansas City needs. Add in that Bolton was fighting through some obvious discomfort down the stretch, and you get a bang-up job for the leader of the defense.
This group of three didn't meet the standard in Week 7 and desperately need to recover moving forward if the team is to remain successful.
No one — and I mean no one — had a rougher Week 7 for the Chiefs than cornerback L'Jarius Sneed. I almost feel bad for him, as this shouldn't have been the plan for him when the club reunited with him on a one-year deal during the offseason. His rough year continued on Sunday night, even on just 14 defensive snaps, which underscored just how colossal of a failure this stint was against wideout Jaxon Smith-Njigba.
Sneed routinely lost to the reigning Offensive Player of the Year on in-breakers, including a third-and-7 on Seattle's second possession for a gain of 33 yards. At that point, Sneed had been targeted three times in coverage and surrendered 53 yards. The aging Cooper Kupp, too, got his game off against Sneed by way of a third-and-9 conversion on that same drive.
The bad moments didn't stop there for Sneed, who ceded a nine-yard reception despite committing defensive holding on a play with less than a minute left in the first half. This was a game to flush for the veteran defensive back; only time will tell if his play improves.
Back to the theme of all good things coming to an end. With how otherworldly impressive he was to begin the year, running back Kenneth Walker III was eventually bound to stumble. There's no shame in doing so against a defense that, according to RBSDM , ranks second in rush success rate (32.1%) and third in EPA per carry (-0.196) allowed. Walker rushed for 36 years on Sunday, and each of them was about as hard-earned as it gets.
A 2.6 yard-per-carry average was nothing for a player who's averaging 4.10 yards after contact per tote in 2026. Walker's patented wiggle didn't allow him to break strings of tackles in tight spaces in prime time, nor was he able to escape around the edge and record explosive rushes. His longest carry was seven yards, easily his worst in a single contest this year.
Better days are ahead for Kansas City's best player this season.
Week 7 was an ugly one for quarterback Patrick Mahomes, seeing him complete just 19 of his 33 passes for 165 yards, no touchdowns, an interception and a 58.3 passer rating. The two-time MVP looked like anything but that under the bright lights at Lumen Field, missing multiple throws in various fashions and also bailing on a couple of clean pockets.
Mahomes admitted following the loss that he can be better, and everyone expects him to. It's also difficult to place too much blame on him considering he was down both starting offensive tackles and perhaps his two best receivers. Running an offense at a high level while shorthanded and being under duress roughly half the time is virtually impossible.
We'll honor the stock watch component and list Mahomes here, but don't expect to see his name too many times.

title: What Matters (and What Doesn't) from the Chiefs' Brutal Loss in Seattle
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs' Sunday Night Football loss to the Seattle Seahawks was a drubbing in all three phases, leaving plenty of questions unanswered about how the Chiefs can recalibrate for the next act of their season.
However, not all of the Chiefs' issues that were exposed in Seattle are worth worrying about. Following a loss that thorough, let's take a look at some issues that do matter and some that don't—at least until further notice.
For the fourth time in six games, the Chiefs' defense failed to record a sack of the opposing quarterback. Even though some of the underlying metrics have supported the KC pass rush due to better performances in statistics like pressure rate , they've allowed opposing quarterbacks to be too comfortable, too often. With Sam Darnold as the target on Sunday night, the Chiefs just needed enough pressure to rattle Darnold, forcing him to start making characteristic mistakes. Instead, he threw and ran for several long third-down conversions.
Meanwhile, the Chiefs' only sacks since Week 1 came against a completely battered Los Angeles Chargers O-line last week.
Chiefs rookie cornerback Mansoor Delane had a couple of "welcome to the NFL" moments against Seahawks wide receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba, but nothing about Delane's losses indicate that he's anything other than an excellent young player who got beaten by a superstar.
JSN WHAT A CATCH FOR A TOUCHDOWN KCvsSEA on NBC/Peacock Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/bN6IT22fM4
Similarly to the long completion Delane allowed last week to Chargers wide receiver Quentin Johnston, the rookie was in excellent position, had his hand between the ball and the receiver's hands, and just couldn't land the final fingernail to break up the pass. Delane would love to have those plays back, I'm sure, but even elite cornerbacks lose to the best receivers at times. Delane looked like a near-peer to Smith-Njigba, not like a rookie out of his depth.
If you would have told me before the game that rookie Cyrus Allen would lead the Chiefs' wide receivers in receiving yards, I would have been thrilled. Allen has seen very limited work to begin his first year in the pros, and a chance to break out through a heavily injured Chiefs WR room would have been well-timed.
Well, he did lead Chiefs wideouts in receiving yards, but he only had one catch for 18 yards—reeled in on the second play of the game.
With Rashee Rice (hamstring) sidelined again and Tyquan Thornton (ankle) remaining on IR through at least the vast majority of the regular season , the Chiefs needed someone to step up. Tight ends and running backs led the receiving box score with paltry stats, while Allen's 18 yards narrowly outpaced Xavier Worthy's three catches for 11 yards, Justin Watson's one for seven, Andrew Armstrong's one for three and Jalen Royals' zero for zero.
The Seahawks' defense is excellent, but those are not the stat lines of a functional unit.
Rice is the Chiefs' most reliable wide receiver, while Thornton was the most explosive. Worthy's role is murky, as his blazing 40-yard dash speed doesn't quite seem to translate to game speed, and much of his potential remains theoretical. Royals and Armstrong may have roles as "dirty work" receivers, but the Chiefs still need to find significantly more firepower in the passing game.
As disappointing as Kenneth Walker's 14-carry, 36-yard performance was, there's no reason for his underwhelming stat line to overshadow his impact on the Chiefs' offense or what can be expected of him going forward.
With O-line uncertainty and the aforementioned woes in the passing game, the Seahawks knew what we all knew: the Chiefs' best chance for offensive success (and explosive plays) came with Walker, so the Seattle D played accordingly. While the star running back has shown that he can jump-start the Chiefs' offense against middling opponents, it's too much to ask for him (or any individual player) to thrive as the focal point of an otherwise-struggling unit against an excellent defense.

title: After Flopping vs. Seahawks, Patrick Mahomes Knows Chiefs' Offense Must Bounce Back
full_text:
No matter how you slice it or what you chalk it up to, there's absolutely no denying that the Kansas City Chiefs' offense did nothing short of flop against the Seattle Seahawks.
Add in that KC came into Week 7 with an undefeated record and had a chance to extend that streak on Sunday Night Football , and you get an even bigger disappointment in terms of performance.
From opening kickoff until the final whistle, head coach Mike MacDonald and his Seahawks defense completely bottled up a Chiefs offense that rolled into the evening as one of football's best per-play, per-drive and per-game units. There's tons of blame to go around, although it's no surprise that the team's best player spent the first moments after the 20-3 loss reflecting.
Quarterback Patrick Mahomes didn't sugarcoat Sunday's shortcoming, but he knows it's time to get right back to work and right some wrongs.
"You got your tail kicked," Mahomes said. "Didn't execute offensively, especially around that midfield area. Kept us away from a lot of points, or at least enough points to be competitive. But it's stuff you've got to learn from. That's obviously a really good defense, and we didn't execute at a high enough level to have success."
By Mahomes' normal standards, he delivered a terrible showing at Lumen Field. On 38 plays, per RBSDM , he averaged -0.13 EPA and had a -9.8% completion rate over expected. Over his last three contests, No. 15 has completed just 61.3% of his passes with an 81.0 passer rating, two touchdowns, two interceptions and an average of 220.7 passing yards each week.
It didn't really matter what the situation was, either. On early-down passes, Mahomes led Kansas City to -0.08 EPA/play (25th percentile) compared to -0.21 (37th percentile) on late-down passing plays. Ahead of Monday's Week 7 finale between the Dallas Cowboys and Philadelphia Eagles, the two-time MVP is 14th among all quarterbacks in adjusted EPA/play (0.139) but is just 25th out of 35 players with 50-plus plays in the same metric (0.023) in Weeks 4-7.
The Chiefs are the only NFL team in the Super Bowl era to have a game with: no 10+ yard rushes no 20+ yard passes no red-zone drives no touchdowns multiple missed field goals
Has pressure factored into Mahomes' lackluster play? Outsiders would argue yes; he thinks on Sunday it was more so him not setting the right tone from the start.
"Obviously a little bit, but I thought especially early in the game, I thought my feet were kind of getting me into trouble where I could have maybe sat in the pocket and made some of the throws down the field," Mahomes said. "I got better a little bit later in the game. But at the same time, when you play a team like that, you can't let them get ahead and get into a game they want to play. Obviously they've had a lot of success doing that, and so [we've] got to be better starting faster — especially with me — and then try to do better throughout the entire game."
According to TruMedia , Kansas City has allowed the sixth-lowest pressure rate on the year at 31.4%. In Weeks 4-7, though, that's 19th at 37.6%. The club is actually being blitzed at a lower per-dropback share (22.8% versus 24.2%) in that sample, so it's a reflection of poor tackle play through and through. Jaylon Moore missing Week 7 and Josh Simmons missing all season hasn't helped.
As currently constructed, the Chiefs' passing attack simply isn't dynamic enough. It owns football's third-lowest average in yards to the sticks on throws (-2.6), and that's down to -4.5 yards in the last two weeks. Injuries can again be at least partially credited here, as Tyquan Thornton ( ankle ) is on injured reserve and Rashee Rice ( hamstring ) hasn't played in weeks.
At the end of the day, not everything falls on Mahomes. He can only put his Superman cape on so frequently, and it's impossible to do others' jobs for them. With that said, he undoubtedly could be playing better, which might just in turn raise the floor of a suddenly struggling offense.
Whether he can do so, fair or unfair, will determine whether Sunday was a blip on the radar or a reason to slam the panic button.

title: Biggest Winners and Losers From the Chiefs’ 20-3 Loss to the Seattle Seahawks
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs suffered their first loss of the season Sunday night in Seattle, and it wasn't close.
The 20-3 final score told the story of a night when the Chiefs struggled in all three phases against a Seahawks team that reminded the country exactly why they held the Lombardi Trophy eight months ago.
Seattle came in at 3-3 and struggled on offense, but their play felt much more dominant and urgent than Kansas City's. The Chiefs were outplayed from start to finish, and the winners column is notably short this week.
Here is the full breakdown.
If there was one moment Sunday night when it felt like the Chiefs might have something going, it came with seconds left in the first half. Seattle led 10-0 and lined up on a second-and-goal from the three, with the ball set to return to them to open the third quarter. A 17-0 halftime deficit would almost certainly have been insurmountable.
Instead, Sam Darnold targeted Rashid Shaheed, and Nohl Williams jumped the route, picked it off, and took it 65 yards the other way. His only mistake was not finding the end zone, which loomed large when Butker missed the ensuing field goal as time expired.
It was Williams's first career interception, notable for a corner known as a ball-hawk coming out of California. He finished the night as the Chiefs’ best defender by a wide margin, recording double-digit tackles, including a tackle for loss, and allowing just two catches for 22 yards on three targets, according to PFF’s preliminary grades. In a game short on positives, Williams stood out.
With tight end Travis Kelce dropping two passes and Patrick Mahomes missing him badly on the opening drive, his backup led the Chiefs in receiving. Noah Gray caught all three of his targets for 44 yards, including a 19-yard reception, continuing what has quietly become a bounce-back season for the six-year veteran.
He is now just nine catches and 20 yards away from surpassing his 2025 season totals, and he has caught 12 of his 14 targets this year, making him one of Mahomes’ most reliable options in a season where reliability has been hard to come by at receiver. On a night with little to celebrate, Gray’s consistency was a welcome constant.
The Chiefs generated just nine pressures on Darnold all evening, and Karlaftis accounted for five of them. That he was the lone bright spot along the defensive line says more about how poor the rest of the group was than it does about how good he was, though he was good.
He hit Darnold twice, batted down a pass, and recorded a tackle for loss, becoming the only Chiefs pass rusher to register a quarterback hit all night. Former All-Pro Chris Jones had zero pressures on 24 pass-rush snaps, according to PFF’s preliminary grades.
The other four pressures belonged to rookie R Mason Thomas, leaving a goose egg for the rest of the group. Karlaftis has been this defense's more consistent performer all season, and Sunday was no exception, even if the unit around him was subpar.
The matchup was billed as strength-on-strength, and Seattle won it in a landslide. Kenneth Walker , who had rushed for 665 yards in his first five games and topped 100 yards in four of them, was held to 36 yards on 14 carries, both season lows by a wide margin.
He averaged just 2.6 yards per carry and forced only one missed tackle, compared to nearly double digits in every previous game this season. The Seahawks bottled him up all night, and without the run game generating momentum, the play-action attack never materialized. Mahomes finished with just 165 passing yards, his lowest output of the season.
To make the optics worse, Seahawks running back Emanuel Wilson ran for 100 yards and a touchdown on the other side of the ball, flipping the entire pre-game narrative on its head. The Chiefs will learn from this, but it was a humbling night for the NFL’s No. 1 offense.
The kicking situation has moved from a concern to legitimate alarm territory. Harrison Butker now sits at just 69 percent on field goals this season after missing two more Sunday night. The first was a 45-yarder, the shortest miss of his season, that went wide right. The second was a 58-yarder at the end of the first half that he hit straight down the middle but left short of the uprights.
The latter is the more troubling miss because it raises questions about leg strength, not just accuracy. The Chiefs never reached the red zone all night, so two made kicks likely wouldn't have changed the outcome, but 13-9 midway through the fourth quarter rather than 13-3 with two missed kicks makes the game look entirely different.
Dave Toub and the Chiefs need to determine quickly whether this is a physical issue, a mental one, or both. For a three-time Super Bowl champion and one of the most decorated kickers in NFL history, the decline has been sudden and significant.
It is hard to single out one defender on a night when Jaxon Smith-Njigba caught nine passes for 150 yards, and the Chiefs allowed 11-of-16 third-down conversions, many on third-and-medium or longer. But cornerback L’Jarius Sneed stood out for the wrong reasons, and Spagnuolo clearly noticed.
Sneed allowed all five of his targets to be caught for 83 yards in just 14 defensive snaps before being benched for Chris Roland-Wallace in the second half, when the defense performed considerably better. Smith-Njigba piled up 129 yards in the first half, with Sneed on the field for much of it.
Sneed surrendered four first downs, three of them to Smith-Njigba and one to Cooper Kupp. The fact that Darnold was actively targeting whoever Sneed was covering in a game that was never particularly close suggests the league has begun to view him as a liability in coverage, and that Roland-Wallace may need to be the answer moving forward.

title: Eagles’ Disaster Could Lead to Chargers’ Blockbuster NFL Trade Deadline Gain
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers are the most obvious NFL trade deadline sellers yet to admit they’re actually sellers.
These things take time, though. The Chargers need to trade Khalil Mack to the Chicago Bears . They might want to consider shipping Quentin Johnston to a contender .
Interestingly, the Chargers could also make a buy or two at the deadline. There are realistic and unrealistic trade targets . But the general theme around this idea is that the Chargers wouldn’t look to buy for right now , but to buy long-term assets to help a rebuild.
And right on cue, the Philadelphia Eagles sure look like an obvious team the Chargers should be calling at the deadline.
The Eagles, like the Chargers, have bellyflopped in the face of big expectations. Jalen Hurts is out with an injury and they're 2-5.
While writing that offensive lineman Landon Dickerson is the No. 12 trade candidate in the NFL, ESPN’s Matt Bowen and Jeremy Fowler noted that “something feels off” between the team and player.
Bowen and Fowler added this: “He recently took what appeared to be a passive-aggressive shot at the front office over his long-term outlook with the franchise. The Eagles are in a position to recoup draft capital for the future and are going younger on the offensive line.”
The Chargers should be more than happy to swoop in here for a solid 28-year-old guard who has a few years left on his current deal. His outlook isn’t perfect, but the Chargers aren’t exactly good at finding quality starting offensive linemen these days.
At this point, the Chargers need to address two or three of the interior offensive line spots yet again next offseason. Yes, they signed Tyler Biadasz and used four of their eight picks in last year’s draft on the unit.
But it’s not enough. There’s developmental talent there, but the Chargers need help now . They’re limping to an offseason in which the fate of the entire coaching staff, Mike McDaniel and Jim Harbaugh, is very much up in the air. That would mean yet another coordinator change for Justin Herbert. They need to cobble together steady veterans who can constantly be on the field in front of them and there’s not even a guarantee that Biadasz will be all the way back from his injury.
The Chargers might have something with second-rounder Jake Slaughter. But they need veterans in the door to stabilize things so he can actually, you know, stay at one spot and develop. Trading for Dickerson isn’t perfect, but it would be a step in the right direction for a franchise that can’t keep failing Herbert while playing an endless waiting game.

title: Quentin Johnston Trade Rumors, Updates Should Have Chargers Calling Steelers, 49ers
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers have a pretty appealing trade deadline candidate with Quentin Johnston .
Granted, Khalil Mack going back to the Chicago Bears comes to mind first.
But Johnston is right there as someone who might have value. He’s still 25 years old and on his rookie deal through 2027. At face value, he’s a guy who has scored eight touchdowns in a season two times.
Granted, some of this boils down to the Chargers’ list of actually appealing trade candidates being…pretty small. But Johnston coming up in NFL trade rumors from insiders at this point makes sense, all things considered.
Let the insiders tell it, the NFL considered Johnston a trade candidate dating back to at least last March, even before the Chargers picked up his fifth-year option.
According to ESPN’s Matt Bowen and Jeremy Fowler , Johnston’s name is now “resurfacing his name in league circles.” They give him a 25 percent chance of being traded while listing the San Francisco 49ers, Las Vegas Raiders and Pittsburgh Steelers as possible fits.
Let’s throw out the Raiders because the AFC West tax might prevent a deal. Shipping Johnston elsewhere in the AFC to the Steelers might make some sense. DK Metcalf headlines the receiving bunch over there, but it’s all running backs and tight ends doing the bulk of the work in the passing game otherwise.
Even more appealing might be sending Johnston to the NFC. The 49ers continue to feel like a buy-happy team but the biggest stars on the offense don’t play wideout, even if Mike Evans and Deebo Samuel are big names.
Point is, the Chargers should have options when the NFL trade deadline arrives. And they’re at the point where they need to largely blow up the depth chart. Ladd McConkey can’t stay healthy. Names like Tre Harris and KeAndre Lambert-Smith haven’t developed. Brenen Thompson is a rookie.
There’s a reality where the Chargers draft Jeremiah Smith at No. 1 in the draft and pair him with McConkey. Everything else would be in flux. Years of miserable roster-building at the skill positions and interior offensive line have ruined things.
The Chargers getting anything back at all for Johnston’s very obvious departure would be a win at this point. Not moving him would simply continue more of the same problems and prevent those other wideouts from, at the very least, getting some developmental reps and putting something on film the rest of the way this season.

title: Should Chargers Be Sellers or Buyers at NFL Trade Deadline?
full_text:
The Chargers have reached a point in the season where Joe Hortiz and the front office need to make a decision and it has to be as soon…as the trade deadline is approaching.
Should the Bolts start looking at ways to improve the roster, or would it make more sense to sell off players and focus on the future?
They should be buyers, not to save this season necessarily, but to build for the future. Meaning both instances in that question could possibly be fulfilled. Sometimes, opportunities to acquire certain players only come once in a blue moon. So taking the chance and helping the future makes the most sense.
I understand why some fans might want to see this team sell at the deadline. When things aren’t going the way you expected, it’s easy to start thinking about draft picks and next season. Wanting to clean house is a natural reaction when a team is not doing the greatest.
But I don’t think that’s where this organization should be looking right now. There is still too much talent on this roster to start treating the season like it’s already over. Even if it is, buying in on playmakers for next season could work out in their favor.
At some point, the front office has to look at the roster and ask itself what can actually be done to make this team better. Maybe that means adding help along the offensive line. Maybe it’s finding another dependable target in the passing game . Depending on how the defense is playing, there could be an opportunity to bring in somebody who makes an immediate impact on that side of the ball, too.
Giving away valuable draft capital for a player who doesn’t solve an actual problem would be a mistake. But if a legitimate opportunity comes along, I don’t think the Chargers should be afraid to take it. There is also something to be said about the message a move like that sends to the locker room. Players want to know that the organization believes in what it’s building. Bringing in somebody who can help right away shows that the front office is still invested in competing instead of simply looking ahead to the offseason.
Of course, buying at the deadline doesn’t guarantee anything. One trade isn’t going to magically fix every issue, and the team still has to prove it can put everything together on the field.

title: Chargers Preseason Star Gets Claimed, Shutting Down Kimani Vidal Trade Rumors
full_text:
While the Los Angeles Chargers had their first week without adding an L to their record, as it is their bye week, they still found a way to lose something. That being their preseason star running back, Greg Desrosiers Jr., the same runner who had 166 yards on 23 attempts in three games.
The Chargers were lucky that Desrosiers Jr. was able to be stashed on their practice squad after his preseason. The hope was that he would be called upon during the season if any of their top three backs, Omarion Hampton, Keaton Mitchell and Kimani Vidal, were to get injured.

He dealt… pic.twitter.com/10F4xbyU26
With John Harbaugh and the New York Giants cutting former Chargers RB Najee Harris and placing role player Tyrone Tracy on injured reserve , they had a need for another RB on their roster, choosing to go with Desrosiers Jr., the practice RB for the other Harbaugh brother, Jim.
bummer, thought he had potential! would've been tough to put him on the 53 in LA to be a healthy inactive every week though so that's just the risk you run https://t.co/mMBEj9Ockd
While it sucks to see someone as talented as Desrosiers Jr. go, this allows the Bolts to have an extra practice squad spot. This has already been filled, with it going to former Arizona Cardinals sixth-round selection, Tejhaun Palmer taking the spot. Palmer worked out a few weeks ago for the squad, seemingly beating out former star JuJu Smith-Schuster for the opportunity.
With the NFL trade deadline around the corner and trade rumors buzzing heavily, names like Khalil Mack and Donte Jackson have been floated around as veteran trade candidates , especially if the Chargers are selling, contrary to what they have told the media.
One name that has picked up steam recently is Kimani Vidal . It has been reported by Steven Haglund that he has heard Vidal is an option for the Chargers to move on from, as teams have called with interest in him.

The 25-year-old Vidal has arguably been the best Chargers running back this season, this coming after his impressive 2025 season. In 2025, he started on the practice squad, ending the season as the team's leading rusher with 643 yards.
With Vidal garnering interest, it began to make sense why the Chargers would move on from him to gather more draft capital, looking to build for the 2027 and beyond seasons. However, a "small" move of losing their preseason and practice squad star, Desrosiers Jr., could allow the Chargers to keep Vidal for the future, as losing two RBs in a short span is a lot, especially for a bottom-of-the-league offense.
