title: Tre Tucker's Latest Emergence Has Raiders Excited for Potential
full_text:
Amid a four-game losing streak, a player on the Las Vegas Raiders offense has begun to re-emerge into the spotlight.
Wide receiver Tre Tucker has been one of the most consistent elements of the Raiders roster over the past few seasons, including this year. The former Cincinnati standout is one of the fastest players on the field each Sunday. Las Vegas head coach Klint Kubiak has noticed that as his involvement in the offense has expanded.
After catching five passes for 103 yards and a touchdown, Tucker is seeing his role grow before his very eyes. The chemistry with starting quarterback Kirk Cousins has been a big reason for the sudden jump in production.
It's always important for your No. 1 wide receiver and quarterback to have good chemistry. While there have been bumps along the way, I believe Cousins and Tucker are starting to find the right balance, even if last week's game against the Los Angeles Rams didn't always produce consistent results (five catches on 12 targets).
As mentioned, Tucker's expanded role within Kubiak's explosive passing offense has allowed him and Cousins to build more connections. The veteran quarterback is encouraged by what he's seen.
"Tre’s done a great job. Even more importantly, the chemistry is good," Cousins said. "It’ll keep getting better. But I think just expanding his role and just allowing him to do more and more. As we’ve given him more, he keeps showing that he can do it. I’m encouraged by it and would love to see him keep doing more up ahead."
Tucker has always been known for his speed, and the Raiders are showing he can wear multiple hats on offense, lining up out wide, in the slot, in motion across the formation, orbit motions, and shifts. In the fourth and final season of his rookie contract, Tucker is showing more than usual; you can call it a job interview for the Raiders brass and 31 other NFL teams. Cousins said as much on Wednesday:
"Well, I think we’ve just given him more to do, more routes, more ways to contribute, and I think he’s taken advantage of those opportunities," Cousins said. "I think he traits were always there. Sometimes when you’re really, really fast, it’s tempting to only have him do the fast things and have the slower guys do the slower things."
"There’s nothing wrong with having Tre do those things too and wear different hats. He’s shown he can do a lot. He doesn’t just need to be the fast guy.”
To Cousins' point, Tucker certainly doesn't need to be the fast guy. It's been delightful to see his role expand in the Raiders' offense and the production that comes with it. However, it doesn't take away from the fact that Tucker is still more of a role player and No. 2 wide receiver in most offenses.
To Tucker's credit, he has been great for Las Vegas in recent weeks and past seasons, developing into a dependable pass-catcher. I still believe the Raiders need to add more upper-tier talent at wide receiver, or a high-ceiling pass-catcher with the potential to be one.
They could still pair one with Tucker, assuming he returns next season and beyond. For now, the production continues to prove critics, myself included, wrong while building more chemistry with Cousins.
Jared Feinberg, a native of western North Carolina, has written about NFL football for nearly a decade. He has contributed to several national outlets and is now part of our On SI team as an NFL team reporter. Jared graduated from UNC Asheville with a bachelor's degree in mass communications and later pursued his master's degree at UNC Charlotte. You can follow Jared Feinberg on Twitter at @JRodNFLDraft

title: 3 NFL Trade Deadline Deals Raiders Should Explore Right Now
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders made a significant number of roster additions this offseason, leaving little room for more additions midseason. However, their four-game losing streak and the upcoming trade deadline make it fair to wonder if the Raiders will make a move before the deadline.
Several players at positions where the Raiders could use help have been traded in recent days. Las Vegas hasn't been tied to many, if any, of the players who were traded. This may indicate that the Raiders will not be active in the trade market.
More specifically, it could mean the Raiders are more likely to sell than buy at the trade deadline. Below are three players the Raiders should consider trading for before the trade deadline, which is less than two weeks away.
Las Vegas got a firsthand look at what Thomas can do when playing his best football. In 2024, Thomas registered nine catches for 132 yards and a touchdown against the Raiders. Thomas has had a decline in his play, but it is hard to believe all the talent he showed last season and before is gone.
The Raiders may feel they have enough with Jalen Nailor's recent return and Jach Bech's expected return. Still, Las Vegas could look to swing a trade for Thomas, who would definitely add a much-needed wrinkle to a limited Raiders offense.
Like all trades, whether it would realistically happen would likely come down to the asking price.
The Raiders need all the help they can get at wide receiver. There likely are not many offensive linemen worth Las Vegas trading away assets for. It would also take any lineman they potentially traded for time to get acquainted with a new offense midseason, which is a tall ask.
Downs is not a world beater, but he is no worse than some of the receivers Las Vegas currently has on its roster. The Raiders' plan of addressing the receiver position by committee does not require top-tier wide receivers; they simply need dependable pass-catchers.
Downs only has 307 receiving yards this season, but he could quietly be an addition the Raiders could use. More importantly, he could be an affordable option for Las Vegas' front office that may be hesitant to invest more resources in this season's roster.
Ridley's route-running skills alone would be a solid addition to the Raiders' roster, especially if they could get him at the right price. His overall skill set would be unlike any that the Raiders currently have. All of the Raiders' current receivers have a different skill set. Ridley could add another.
Ridley, Bech, Nailor, and Tre Tucker would be a serviceable committee of wide receivers. However, the Raiders' front office could decide they have invested enough in the offense and not add any players at all. Time will tell what they decide, but their need for additional roster help is clear.
Although the Raiders could add receivers before the deadline, Tucker's importance cannot be underestimated. In the right system and with the right quarterback, he could blossom into the No. 1 wide receiver many do not believe the Raiders have.
He has shown glimpses of what is possible multiple times throughout his career and this season under Klint Kubiak. Adding other receivers who could help take even more attention off of Tucker could be just what the Raiders need to unlock the unit. Kirk Cousins recently raved about Tucker.
“Going back to training camp, going back to OTAs, he was a guy who could run, run, run, and when other guys started dragging, he still kept his speed up. He was still getting open and still separating in coverage, and he’s shown that on game day as well. But similar to Trey Zuhn [III] moving around, we ask a lot of him,” Cousins said on Wednesday.
“When a guy’s really well-conditioned, we tend to punish him for it. We say, ‘Well, you’re so well-conditioned, we’ll just make you do it again.’ It can be tough, because you still have to understand he’s human, and even though he’s really well-conditioned, let’s not run him into the ground either. So, you try to find that balance, but he can go for a long time.”
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: How Raiders Are Looking To Rebound, End Four-Game Skid
full_text:
After sustaining a 10-game losing streak in each of the past two seasons, the Las Vegas Raiders retooled their roster as much as they could this offseason. Still, everyone knew Las Vegas had more work to do on what was arguably the league's worst roster last season.
John Spytek and the Raiders' front office swung for the fences, handing out over $300 million in new contracts during free agency this offseason. Still, the Raiders' four-game losing streak puts them nearly halfway to another 10-game skid. Luckily, they face the New York Jets this week.
The Raiders' three wins this season have come against teams with a combined 3-16 record. Las Vegas' current losing streak has been against four of the league's best teams, including the Los Angeles Rams, despite their record.
Las Vegas' 3-4 record reflects how inconsistent they have been through the season's first seven games. As they prepare for Week 8, the Raiders have more than a few things to work on. This is true on both sides of the ball, as Las Vegas looks to end its current skid.
The Raiders hit the practice field on Wednesday for the first time in preparation for their road matchup against the Jets. The matchup will pit the Raiders against several former players, including quarterback Geno Smith and offensive lineman Dylan Parham.
Las Vegas undoubtedly misses Parham, as he has had a productive season so far for the Jets. Still, Las Vegas has enough on its end after its fourth straight loss. As the Raiders look to win for the first time in four weeks, Klint Kubiak said his team's focus is solely on the next game.
“I think from our perspective as players and coaches, that’s not something that’s on our minds. What’s on our mind is win the next game, and we’ve played very talented teams and played much more competitive games than that, being the [Kansas City] Chiefs and the Bills. hen you start the game that slow, you put yourself in position to be behind that much, you don’t give yourself a chance to win," Kubiak said earlier this week.
Although the Raiders have played several of the league's best teams, they also hurt themselves in several ways in each loss. That is an area of focus for Kubiak's Raiders heading into Week 8 against the Jets. It will be tough enough to beat the opposing team.
Las Vegas must do a better job of not beating themselves. They have the blueprint to win games, regardless of how good the other team is. The Raiders went toe-to-toe with the Chiefs and the Bills. Both losses featured several positives they displayed in wins.
However, those losses against the Chiefs, the Bills, and their other two losses displayed a team largely beating itself while playing against a much better roster. Las Vegas is 3-4 this season and still has a legitimate shot at a successful campaign.
Given the fact that they have already matched last season's win total, they have already confirmed they are better than they were last season. However, their current four-game skid proves just how big the remaining gap is between Las Vegas and the league's elite.
Sunday's matchup against the Jets will help further determine whether the Raiders are closer to the teams they have beaten or closer to the top of the food chain, like the four teams they have lost to this season.
It is hard to say any team should beat another since anything can happen on any given Sunday. Still, if the Raiders have improved as much as first believed when they went 3-0, they should beat the Jets on Sunday. It is not necessarily a must-win, as it is unclear what Las Vegas' end goal is this season.
However, a loss to a Jets team gunning for the No. 1 overall pick will spark some interesting conversations about the 2026 Raiders and the team's direction for the rest of this season. A five-game losing streak, with a loss to the lowly Jets, would be far from expected.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: NFL Execs React: Raiders, Spytek Pass on Trade Opportunity
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev.—The Raiders (3-4) go to New Jersey this weekend, where they hope to return to their winning ways against the New York Jets (2-5).
The Silver & Black are in the first year of a calculated Raiders rebuild led by GM John Spytek and guided on the field by Klint Kubiak, and they’ve shown admirable discipline in sticking to the plan.
The Raiders need help. We knew before the season even started that this team has positions where the Raiders don’t even have a player, are woefully inadequate (DL), thin (Multiple Positions), or simply young (DB).
This is not a franchise void of talent. Still, they certainly have voids, and the discipline isn’t recognizing them; it’s noticing that one player, or even two, wouldn’t project them into a Super Bowl contender, so don’t overpay for temporary headlines that cost championships in the future.
The Raiders’ guard play has been inconsistent, if we’re being nice, and terrible, if we’re being blunt, from game to game.
With the NFL trade deadline l ooming on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, at 1 PM PT, rumors suggested the Raiders were interested in then-Colts G Quenton Nelson, a perennial Pro Bowler-caliber player (eight times in eight years).  I confirmed the Raiders were interested.
So why not make a deal?  The defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks did.  Believe it or not, the answer is simple.
The Raiders plan all along, as we have reported multiple times, is to use 2026 as a rebuild year, get everything into focus as far as the roster, reload and make more adjustments in 2027 via trades, free agency, and the NFL Draft, and then starting in 2028, be a perennial contender in the NFL Playoffs every year.
Nelson is no doubt a good player; he is terrific.  He is 30, and in the last year of his contract.  The Raiders are not contenders this season; with an expiring contract, the Seahawks paid an exorbitant price: a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick.
We reached out to three NFL executives to ask about the cost the Seahawks paid and their thoughts on Spytek’s decision not to make the move.
Executive No. 1:  “That cost makes sense if you are the Seahawks and think you could be one guy away, and you feel pretty good about resigning him.  I can tell you this: if I am John [Spytek] looking at his roster and so many needs, I’m not doing it.  Those two picks could be two players, and what will his contract be?  If you could get some assurances on a contract, and I’m sure the Seahawks had those talks before swinging this deal, I would have done a third if I were the Raiders, but no chance in hell I would do that Seahawks deal if I was him.”
NFL executive No. 2: “I wouldn’t have made the deal.  That deal went higher than the Hawks wanted, thanks to the Raiders, but they are in need there. Spy [John Spytek] isn’t.  He knows what he has. That move would have gotten him some good press, but it would have also slowed the rebuild; it would have cost him two players [two draft picks] and a lot of cap, on a 30-year-old.”
Finally, executive number three was even more direct.
NFL executive No. 3:  “I don’t know Johnny [John Spytek] well, but not doing that deal tells me a lot about his style, and the Raiders’ thinking.  They aren’t afraid to be bold; [Tyler] Linderbaum proved that, but they aren’t going to be dumb.  That deal makes a lot of sense for Johnny [Seahawks GM John Schneider], but not for the Raiders.  They have a lot of needs, and if Q [Quenton Nelson] were 27, you could do a new deal, maybe not two picks.  But not 30, the cost in picks and salary, and the remaining holes.”
Fans want action; I respect and understand it.  So do Spytek, Tom Brady and Kubiak.  But the Raiders also understand that action for action’s sake has doomed them for over 20 years.
The Raiders want long-term action that makes sense. That is why Marvin Harrison Jr. isn't here.  Nelson, ultimately, didn’t make sense inside the Silver & Black paradigm, and the NF agrees.
Hondo S. Carpenter Sr. is an award-winning sports journalist with decades of experience. He serves as the Senior Writer for NFL and College sports, and is the beat writer covering the Las Vegas Raiders. Additionally, he is the editor and publisher for several sites On SI. Carpenter is a member of the Pro Football Writers Association (PFWA), the Football Writers Association of America (FWAA), and the United States Basketball Writers Association (USBWA).

title: What It Would Cost Raiders To Trade for Top Targets
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders' four-game losing streak has put any and all options back on the table moving forward. That is, if Las Vegas is focused on winning games this season. If they are, there is a possibility they could be active at the trade deadline.
If they are more concerned with the future, which they have a right to be, Las Vegas could not make a move at all by the deadline. Should that be the route they go, Las Vegas' front office has every right to do so, considering the slew of moves they made this offseason.
There simply may not be much more Las Vegas can do trade-wise that would be worth risking valuable future assets for. However, it is far from out of the question.
The average going price for players worth trading for has been at least a second-or third-round draft pick, if not both. Quenton Nelson was traded for a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick. However, the Indianapolis Colts may be in the midst of a fire sale and willing to make deals.
Indianapolis also traded DeForest Buckner to the San Francisco 49ers for a 2027 4th-round pick, but that was a unique situation, as the 49ers originally drafted Buckner. It likely would have cost more without that prior connection.
Other trades may give insight into where the Raiders stand in the market and their willingness, or unwillingness, to strike a trade. The Pittsburgh Steelers traded cornerback Joey Porter Jr. to the Dallas Cowboys in exchange for a 2028 second-round pick and a conditional 2027 sixth-round pick.
The Arizona Cardinals traded receiver Marvin Harrison Jr. to the Houston Texans in exchange for a 2027 second-round pick and a 2027 sixth-round pick. The chances of the Raiders being in on either of these players were relatively low. However, the fact that they were not in on them speaks volumes.
It is debatable whether or not the Raiders should have been in on Nelson, Porter, and Harrison. However, it is not debatable that offensive guard, cornerback, and wide receiver are Las Vegas' top three roster needs at this point in the season.
If they are out on all three of those players at positions of dire need, it is fair to wonder if they are actually in the trade market at all. The Raiders' front office has had a plan all along, and trading away draft capital right now may not be a part of that plan.
Trading away future draft pieces to aid in a season where Las Vegas did not have realistic playoff hopes seems counterproductive considering the progress the Raiders' front office made on the roster during the offseason.
Landon Dickerson would be a solid addition to the Raiders' offensive line, and Brian Thomas Jr. would be a solid addition to their receiver group. However, Las Vegas may be better off keeping their draft picks and betting on John Spytek's drafting abilities instead of trading away resource s for a retread.
Dickerson and Thomas would help the Raiders run the ball better and open up passing lanes for a struggling Raiders offense. The Raiders would be wise to move cautiously on any potential trade, but they undoubtedly need help on that side of the ball, whether before the deadline or after the season.
“I think the number one thing guys is when teams can play that much man against you it's because we're not a threat running the football right now. So, we’ve got to make teams more – we got to be more of a well-rounded offensive football club right now. And again, those are things that we're working on,” Kubiak said earlier this week.
“But when you are down multiple scores, it is not a running game, and we've been giving up way too many points right now to put ourselves in position to be balanced in the fourth quarter, to be balanced in the third quarter. So, I like the strides that our guys have made in practice. I've seen it in the games, I've seen how our runners are breaking tackles. I do like that, but we've got to call runs and be in competitive games in the second half."
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: The Plays That Highlight What Is Holding the Raiders Back
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders' four straight losses have quickly turned an encouraging 3-0 start to the season into an afterthought. Las Vegas' hot start against three of the league's worst teams was followed by four straight games against the league's best.
Despite their record, the Los Angeles Rams are one of the league's best overall rosters, as they should be, since they thoroughly beat the Raiders even though they were significantly shorthanded. The New England Patriots were significantly shorthanded as well, and still routed Las Vegas.
For as much as the Raiders improved their roster this offseason, it was well known that the roster still needed additional work. After four straight losses, they need work at a position they thought they had figured out after starting 3-0.
Awful play call ? Tre Tucker is immediately wide open for a TD. This was a great play call. Cousins just refuses to look for his WRs If Jeanty runs out of bounds it would have been 3rd & ~4 with about 14-16 seconds left. The Raiders would have had to get the first down/TD on the… https://t.co/Uz6UbpiSDf pic.twitter.com/P3PRJ8YoZM
Understand, the topic of whether or not Fernando Mendoza should start, or when they should choose to do so, is an issue in itself. They can decide to not start Mendoza until they are out of playoff contention, or not start him at all this season. That is their prerogative.
However, that is a completely different issue from Kirk Cousins' repeated mishaps on game days. Those are two different issues. Regardless of whether or when Mendoza starts, Cousins is making costly mistakes. He is missing out on plays that are there to be made.
That doesn't even account for the multiple near-interceptions he's thrown this season that defenses couldn't reel in. Watch the film, or a few of the plays below, and decide for yourself. These are just a few. Plenty more plays like these exist from Cousins this season. PLENTY.
Those who know the game and have been around it cannot watch plays like the ones below and credibly absolve Cousins of all blame. Whether they say it or not, his teammates certainly are not watching the film and absolving him of all blame. We shouldn't either.
Slant/flat with a seam from Tucker on 3rd and 5 in the first half. Thought Cousins stayed on the seam too long. If he didn’t like it get to the flat with Mayer for the first. Instead he kind of panics. pic.twitter.com/xIkfPKv1e1
A lot of things can be said about this and about that, but what a player does on the field speaks louder than anything that can be said after a game. There are multiple instances of Cousins missing wide-open receivers, rushing passes, and overall hindering the offense.
For all of the positives he brings to the table, the mistakes Cousins is making are holding the Raiders' offense back. Sure, the unit has several other positions that need further help, but Las Vegas also has a quarterback on the roster with the skill set to work around the unit's other shortcomings.
That quarterback is not Cousins, which is really no fault of his own. In their Week 7 loss to the Rams, the veteran quarterback routinely missed opportunities on well-drawn-up plays; Las Vegas' offensive line held up, and receivers got open. Cousins missed.
It is okay to be honest about what is going on. Even if one chooses not to be, the plays are on film. The guys in the locker room know what they see. Las Vegas' defense sees Cousins holding the offense back, and their coaching staff doing nothing about it.
Does Cousins try to thread it over the top to Bowers ? Nope. Does Cousins throw it to the wide open Connor Heyward ? Nope. Did you guess the check down to Jeanty ? If so, you are correct pic.twitter.com/U8IFSRpQgV
Understand, this is just from the game against the Rams. Las Vegas also had several similar missed opportunities and mistakes from their quarterback in previous games. They were there even when the Raiders started 3-0, but their undefeated start masked those issues.
After four straight losses , it is hard to keep pretending that what is on film isn't. That is the beauty of film! Film does not care what anyone thinks. Film speaks for itself, and it says Cousins routinely does things that are holding Las Vegas' offense back.
“I think from our perspective as players and coaches, that’s not something that’s on our mind. What’s on our mind is win the next game, and we’ve played very talented teams and played much more competitive games than that, being the [Kansas City] Chiefs and the [Buffalo] Bills. Yesterday, when you start the game that slow, you put yourself in position to be behind that much, you don’t give yourself a chance to win,” Kubiak said the day after the game.
“Eventually, Fernando [Mendoza] is going to play football. We have a plan. We don’t have a timeline for that. Kirk [Cousins] is playing really well, and we’re in the hunt. It’s really important that we keep playing really well behind him and continue to develop Fernando, but Fernando is going to play at some point. It’s not going to be this week.”
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: 'We Have A Plan': Raiders Face Future Dilemma With Cousins, Mendoza
full_text:
A month ago, the Las Vegas Raiders were sitting at a surprising 3-0, having faced the Miami Dolphins, New Orleans Saints, and Arizona Cardinals. Since then, they have been winless, losing to some of the NFL's most talented teams.
After Sunday's 35-21 loss to the Los Angeles Rams, head coach Klint Kubiak was asked if he and the staff would consider starting Fernando Mendoza , prompting an answer that still has Raider Nation in a frenzy.
"Yeah, I think we have to go watch the film, and I think at this point we're thinking about everything: how to fix our problems, how to fix our issues in the red zone, in the third quarter, and personnel, scheme," Kubiak said. "We've got to talk about all of it."
While Kubiak clarified on Monday that veteran starter Kirk Cousins would remain there with no controversy, it doesn't resolve the discussion as the Raiders continue to lose games. In the coming weeks, whether they win or lose, the team faces a dilemma about who the starter will be, and it will only get louder as the losses mount.
You might be asking why there is a dilemma. Cousins is third in the NFL in passing yards (1,877) and leads the league in touchdown passes (16) while throwing only five interceptions. The Raiders' passing game has been impressive despite not having a difference-maker at wide receiver and two of them at tight end with Brock Bowers and Michael Mayer.
Cousins is playing well, and he knows it, too. Yet, the losses keep raining down, and the struggles are apparent on both sides of the ball , especially in the trenches and behind a young secondary. Cousins knew when he signed with the Raiders back in April that being benched for Mendoza was a serious possibility at some point during the season.
"I mean, nothing changes in the sense that if I'm not the best option, then I don't want to be out there either. I want our football team to have the best chance to win games. And if the first OTA, if that had become apparent, I would have been the first one to say, 'Yeah, you can't play me.'
"So nothing changes and the organization will do what they feel is best. But I feel that Fernando's done a great job and has a bright future ahead. I'm going to try to go out there and play as well as I possibly can, help us win, and give him a great example to learn from until he does go out there eventually."
Cousins can only do so much at age 38, and he doesn't exactly move well either. He is not as great as his minority owner, Tom Brady, was at this stage of his career, and Cousins has shown regression in some areas of his game, despite his incredible production at the start of the year. Yet, he continues to produce, hasn't had a game where he outright cost his team the game, and has been consistent.
In more ways than one, Cousins has been exactly what you want in a bridge quarterback. He is allowing Mendoza to learn on the sideline, where he consistently has a helmet on, listening to the play calls and the operation pre- and post-snap.
Yet, the dilemma remains with Cousins' consistency and Kubiak pursuit of wins. The Raiders could win this weekend against the New York Jets and move to 4-4, returning themselves to the mix for at least a wild card spot midway through the year. It would be hard to make a change if the momentum shifts with a much-needed win on the road.
Mendoza needs the reps, though. It would be great if he didn't play the rest of the way, but that's not why the Raiders drafted him, and they expect to play him this season. It is rare nowadays that the No. 1 overall draft selection doesn't play an entire regular season regardless of the results of the campaign.
No. 15 offers incredible traits and tools that could make him one of the league's best passers and take the Raiders to places they haven't been in decades. His arm, arrogance, willingness to work through progressions and find answers, and size are due to see the field and not just in relief late in the fourth quarter down multiple scores; to start and play games.
"Yeah, eventually Fernando is going to play football. We have a plan," Kubiak said. "We don’t have a timeline for that. Kirk is playing really well, and we’re in the hunt. It’s really important that we keep playing really well behind him and continue to develop Fernando, but Fernando is going to play at some point. It’s not going to be this week.”
Kubiak and general manager John Spytek need to see what their future holds and where Mendoza needs to grow. I think starting him at some point this season is the right direction to go, even if Cousins continues to play well and doesn't make bad decisions in this offensive system.
The Raiders want to see Mendoza at some point, as do fans. When Kubiak knows it's time, we'll know.
Jared Feinberg, a native of western North Carolina, has written about NFL football for nearly a decade. He has contributed to several national outlets and is now part of our On SI team as an NFL team reporter. title: Why Raiders Missed Out on Opportunity to Improve Future Roster
full_text:
Just a month ago, we were talking about the Las Vegas Raiders as a legitimate playoff contender.
Fast forward to the present day, and the Raiders have had a rude awakening, losing four consecutive games and falling to 3-4 in the blink of an eye. Because Las Vegas was off to such a hot start in the first month of the season, it was featured in discussions of a team potentially being a buyer at the trade deadline. Now, with the current losing streak, the Raiders could be sellers at the deadline . That being said, it doesn't mean Las Vegas shouldn't consider acquiring a player for now and the future.
On Tuesday, the Indianapolis Colts traded eight-time Pro Bowl guard Quenton Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks for a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick. Based on that information, here's why it was a missed opportunity for general manager John Spytek to improve the offensive line .
Yes, the Raiders' draft picks will be much higher on the board than Seattle's, but giving up a Day 2 2027 pick and a Day 3 2028 pick is not expensive at all for one of the best guards in the league. Yes, Las Vegas is trending toward not competing this season, but that doesn't disqualify them from making moves in the near future.
Let's say the front office and coaching staff still believe this team is playing for something this season; then vastly improving the offensive line, especially the interior, isn't the worst idea. Pairing Nelson with Tyler Linderbaum would be an excellent start to rebuilding the interior of the offensive line. Now, Spytek may really value picks in this upcoming draft, especially if the Raiders are picking near the top of each round. However, it never hurts to negotiate and assess the market.
As we've seen countless times over the years, without a formidable offensive line, it's virtually impossible to operate cohesively as an offense. At times, we’ve seen that with Las Vegas, as their run game has been inept due to struggles up front.
It's important to note that Nelson is in the final year of his contract and is a pending free agent. So, you may be asking, 'Why would the Raiders, who are a rebuilding team, trade for a 30-year-old guard on an expiring contract?' It's certainly a fair question, but as mentioned earlier, this move wouldn't be just about this season. Las Vegas is trying to set the foundation for the future .
It would be an interesting situation for the Raiders' front office to navigate, as Linderbaum is already the highest-paid center in the league. Meanwhile, Nelson's current contract is valued at $20 million annually, and he would likely want more money than Peter Skoronski and Tyler Smith, who are each earning at least $24 million per year. So again, it may be perplexing to think why Las Vegas would invest that much money in the interior of the offensive line. Quite simple: it’s feasible.
The Raiders aren't paying substantial money to several of their top, future pieces. Ashton Jeanty and Brock Bowers are still on their rookie contracts. Meanwhile, Mendoza won't be making significant money for the foreseeable future. This is the time to overspend a little and ensure the future franchise quarterback has as many resources as possible to succeed.
Throughout the offseason, the Raiders' ownership, Spytek, and head coach Klint Kubiak have preached the plan to build and develop this team patiently. But if an opportunity presents itself to acquire high-end players who can help the team now and in the future at a relatively affordable price, those situations should always be considered.
Logan Lazarczyk is a graduate of the University of Missouri-Kansas City, where he earned a Bachelor of Arts in Communication Studies with an emphasis in Journalism. Logan joined our team with extensive experience, having previously written and worked for media entities such as USA Today and Union Broadcasting.

title: Hondo’s Mailbag: Raiders Fans Demand Answers on Struggling OL
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev.—The Las Vegas Raiders (3-4) head to Gotham this weekend to take on the New York Jets (2-5) on Sunday.
The Silver and Black are headed back East for another 10 AM PT kickoff, and they will face their starting QB from last season, Geno Smith.
But before they get on the airplane and head out, they have a tough week of practice and some tough issues that must be addressed.
Kirk Cousins currently leads the NFL in touchdown passes with 16, and nearly 1,900 passing yards is good for third.  Still, the Raiders don’t have a running game, and their offensive line is, at best, suspect.
The fan base understands exactly what is going on with this Raiders rebuild that is currently underway, and because of the 3-0 hot start, they want more.
The NFL trade deadline is looming, and a win will certainly impact the Raiders' moves.  Additionally, a loss would, as well as some around the league feel, mean GM John Spytek has a lot to consider if the Raiders lose the next two games before the deadline.
I asked you all on my social media X account to tell me what you are looking to see most besides the win, and you didn’t disappoint.
Be able to run the ball. Our interior O-line has been ass all year...
The guard's play over the last three weeks hasn't been good, and last week was terrible.  I asked Klint Kubiak on Monday about G Bryve Cabeldue and rookie OL Trey Zuhn III getting the chance to earn reps on Sunday, and his answer was direct and clear, Yes.”
That is good news.  This is a rebuilding year, but the Raiders need to foster competition as best they can to create an even bigger point of emphasis and competition.
I have lost zero faith in C Tyler Linderbaum, who has had only truly bad games, but has had nearly zero help on his right and left.
The Kubiak system is rooted in, and finds it foundational, strength in running the ball; you can’t and won’t with guard play as bad as it has been this year.
Someone to tackle, someone not named Maxx to put pressure from the D line, the destruction of this vanilla wafer offense, and letting Washington Jr. carry the damn ball.
I am a little surprised that there isn’t more consternation about the defense.  The entire time I have covered the Silver and Black, the entirety of their time in Las Vegas, it has been stop Maxx Crosby and stop the Raiders' defense.
The Raiders have spent countless millions on high-priced free agents and even rookies, and no one has been able to do it except Malcolm Koonce for half a season in 2023.
The Raiders' defensive coaches have to do better, and many players have been pathetic in the tackle box.
These men are professionals, and sloppy technique reflects on them; the CBA limits practice, and even the physicality of practice, and that had a tremendous impact on the game.
There are many reasons things have gone wrong this year, and many are legitimate. Still, the poor tackling should embarrass all of them as highly paid professionals who have done it consistently, and they've done it several times.
For Gino to have 2 int. If it could be on the first pass of the game, like against Chargers last year, that would be awesome. Not too much right?
I understand Raider Nation’s bitterness towards Geno Smith because last year was a disaster.  I can also tell you that Geno wasn’t the number one reason for the failure in 2025, and isn’t even close to the top of the list.
While I think he is a good QB, he is not elite, and no one knows this defense better than how to bait him into mistakes; they saw it every day in practice last year.
While I think he will be highly motivated to punish the Raiders, every player left from last year’s team knows that the Raiders didn’t lose solely because of Geno.
That said, if the Raiders win, I would expect Geno to have a hand in it; that is the track record of his losses in this league. I like Geno, have never hidden it, and while I think his behavior toward the Raiders fans was unacceptable and warranted punishment from the team, it doesn’t change the fact that two news teams are facing off on Sunday.
Some fight in all three phases. Two of the last three games there was practically no fight. Dominated in those games.
Good call, Doc.  I can tell you I have been impressed by this team's lack of quit, but I've also been shocked by its lack of fight.
Some of these guys' play has been terrible on national TV.  I know these men; while they certainly don’t play for free, they're not men who don’t care.
At some time, you have to come back punching and fight back.  I want to see some gut fighters in these guys.  The raw emotion that fuels this game.

title: Raiders GM John Spytek Surprises With Bold Roster Move
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev.—Say whatever you like about the Las Vegas Raiders (3-4) GM John Spytek, but you can’t avoid using the word bold.
Despite taking the high road and taking all the blame for the team’s collapse in 2025 , for the record, absolutely none of the responsibility for the collapse had to do with him; ever since his voice grew louder and he took the wheel late last season, he has been superb.
There have been some questions, prematurely in some cases, in this reporter’s opinion, about the 2025 NFL Draft class, but he has been bold and aggressive.
I first learned of him when he interned with the Detroit Lions in 2004, when Lions executives gave him the nickname “The Whiz Kid” because of his analytical nature.
Spytek bristled at my use of analytical, but the reality is that he leaves no stone unturned, like his head coach, Klint Kubiak, and owner, Tom Brady. We talked about that earlier this year when he selected Klint Kubiak as head coach.
“I would not say that I am analytical, just thorough and a lot of depth. You’re always looking for an edge. Your ability to process, maintain, and use a lot of information is huge at my job, or quarterback, or a head coach. It was cool to see the depths that Klint would go, just like Tom (Brady) would go to as a player."
"Like what is required, and how much you can process and maintain, and use. We could throw a book at a player or coach, if they can’t. It’s really about what they can use and kind of value in that process, kind of value in that process to help bring it to life.”
Spytek announced today that he was activating WR Dont’e Thornton, Jr. (DTJ) from injured reserve back to the 53-man roster.
Spytek selected DTJ in the fourth round of the 2025 NFL Draft, 108th overall. The 6’5” wideout weighs 205 pounds and runs a blazing 4.3 forty-yard dash.
Physically and athletically, he looks like a prototypical elite NFL WR. Looks can be deceiving.
He came to the Raiders during the mini-camp and OTA portion of the 2025 offseason looking like the steal of the NFL Draft. He made enormous plays and shone.
On August 14, 2025, everything changed. DTJ literally disappeared once the San Francisco 49ers arrived in Henderson. The great plays and the constant showing up, day after day, just stopped.
Teammates wondered what happened, and early in the season, even some on the staff did, too. The once-promising rookie couldn’t seem to, in the words of one coach no longer with the team, “Get any traction.”
In this reporter’s opinion, and in the view of others around the organization, nothing has changed.
A wonderful young man, I have stated many times, no one was rooting against him, just the opposite, but nothing was popping.
Just last Friday, on a team desperate for WR help, Kubiak was asked about DTJ, and his answer was interesting. “He’s making big progress. He’s done a lot of good things in practice. Still working back into getting his football legs back after missing a lot of time. But I’ve been really pleased with his effort, with his detail. He’s close.”
In deciding to elevate DTJ to the 53-man roster, Spytek let Las Vegas native DT Jonah Laulu go. Laulu was inactive against the Chiefs and the Rams, and with his former defensive line coach now the defensive coordinator, that is telling.
DTJ played in 15 games last year, caught 10 passes, and scored no touchdowns.
Laulu has started 22 games for the Raiders, including seven during his rookie year in 2024 and 15 last year. His production this year has been, at best, suspect.
Many, including me, thought DTJ might not make the initial 53-man roster, which he did, and I certainly thought that, with Jack Bech presumably coming back this week, DTJ’s days were either numbered or he was heading to the IR for the remainder of the season.
The reality is that if you trust Spytek (and he has earned it) or Kubiak (and he has earned it), they believe in DTJ at least for now, and the sophomore WR needs to seize the moment of public endorsement and turn things around.
In the NFL, a player's third year is called the money year. In that belief, DTJ is far too young to give up on, and Spytek and Kubiak are again making the statement we told you before the season.
This is a youth-movement Raiders rebuild, and keeping DTJ in the fold once again shows that while Laulu was in the money year and they clearly didn’t like what he offered comparatively, they value DTJ more.
The analytical-excuse me, “thorough” John Spytek yet again made a bold move. You can’t fault him for that, and in a year when this team isn’t going to a Super Bowl, trusting WR coach Zach Azzanni and Kubiak to develop DTJ and finding out whether he can turn it around is the correct move.
If the Raiders move on from DTJ at some point, that won’t be the story. The story will be that Spytek continues to do what he has since last December: methodically lead the franchise in a disciplined way, trust the process, and not cut corners.
No one would have complained or been shocked if Spytek cut DTJ or at least relegated him to the IR for the rest of the season. Unless he signed with the Chiefs and the young man with all of the intangibles became great.
The story isn’t whether or not DTJ turns out to be great; it is that in the early stages of a rebuild, a franchise that was once known as the team with a lack of patience who constantly let players go to thrive elsewhere, showed discipline and a commitment to the plan.
Or as they say in these parts, “Committed to Excellence.”
Who knows if DTJ will be excellent, but discipline and commitment to a proven plan clearly exemplify “Commitment to Excellence.”

title: What to Know About the Dolphins' New Guard
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins' continuing search for hidden gems landed them a former third-round pick who won a Super Bowl ring last season.
The Dolphins were awarded guard Christian Haynes off waivers from the Seattle Seahawks, making room for him on the 53-man roster by waiving rookie sixth-round pick DJ Campbell.
Haynes appeared in all seven games for Seattle this season and made five starts, but he was waived after the Seahawks acquired eight-time Pro Bowl guard Quenton Nelson this week in a trade with the Indianapolis Colts. He appeared in 24 games as a backup in his first two NFL seasons.
The Baltimore Ravens had announced earlier Wednesday that they picked up Haynes on waivers, but the Dolphins had a higher waiver priority spot because of their worse record — after the third week of the regular season, the overall league standings are used in case more than one team claims a player.
Haynes was a third-round pick out of UConn in the 2024 NFL draft who was the 81st overall selection.
This was his NFL.com draft scouting report in 2024: "Four-year starter and team captain who is sturdy at the point of attack. Haynes plays with football intelligence and sees every snap as a mandate to move opponents and finish blocks. His draft slotting could be affected by a lack of length and being limited to one position, but his determined playing style counters those factors. He’s not overly rangy but wipes out targets on pulling blocks and is capable in space, and in pass protection. The hand usage can get sloppy, allowing opponents to slip away from him, and he has a tendency to do too much grabbing. All things considered, he might outplay his draft slotting and become a solid NFL starter."
Haynes joins a group of Dolphins backup offensive linemen that consists of center Andrew Meyer, guard Jarrett Kingston, guard/tackle Caedan Wallace and tackle Chukwuebuka Godrick.
Where Haynes fit into the 10-man group obviously will come down to what he shows the coaches in practice and how quickly he can learn the offense.
Campbell becomes the second of the Dolphins' 13 draft selections to be cut from the 53-man roster after seventh-round selection Max Llewellyn.
As happened with Llewellyn, it's entirely possible the Dolphins will bring him back to the practice squad if he clears waivers, though now they're OK with taking that chance.
Campbell joined Godrick, claimed off waivers from the Kansas City Chiefs, on the inactive list every game so far this season as the clear ninth and 10th offensive linemen on the roster.

title: Breaking Down a New Willis Issue and the Two Concussions on the Dolphins' Lengthy Injury Report
full_text:
If the Miami Dolphins are going to make it two in a row after getting their first victory of the season, they might have to overcome some injury issues.
Only two players on the active roster missed the first practice ahead of the team's Week 8 game against the New England Patriots, but both rookie guard Kadyn Proctor and cornerback JuJu Brents were out because they're in the concussion protocol.
Because of the fickle nature of concussions, it's impossible to predict whether either or both will be able to play against the Patriots, and Brents was spotted on the outside practice fields at the Baptist Health Training Complex doing conditioning work, which clearly is a good sign.
The first injury report of the week for the Dolphins was a long one with 13 names on it, and a new issue for quarterback Malik Willis.
After earlier this season being listed with a toe issue and then with a thumb injury, this time Willis is dealing with a groin injury, although he was a full participant in practice Wednesday.
Another full participant was edge defender Rob Beal Jr., who has missed the past four games because of a hamstring injury.
The injury report, though, featured eight players listed as limited participants.
On the list was cornerback Reese Taylor, who missed the past three games with a quad injury, and long-snapper Tucker Addington and tight end Will Kacmarek both were on the injury report last week before playing in the 28-25 victory against the New York Jets.
The other five players listed as limited were TE Greg Dulcich (ankle), S Michael Taaffe (neck/foot), S Dante Trader Jr. (shoulder), WR Malik Washington (knee) and WR Jared Wayne (knee). Only Trader had an injury reported in the press box Sunday, so it's possible than any of the other four were injured in practice.
Head coach Jeff Hafley revealed the concussions before practice before taking questions from the assembled media.
Hafley also indicated that backup Jarrett Kingston would be taking Proctor's reps at left guard during practice. Kingston was the one who replaced Jonah Savaiinaea at right guard after the 2025 second-round pick was injured in the first half of the Week 5 loss at Hard Rock Stadium.
Kingston, who obviously is the No. 3 guard on the roster, was claimed off waivers from the Houston Texans after the cuts to 53.
If Brents can't play against New England, then Jason Marshall Jr. would take his place in a normal (four-DB) defensive alignment and Jaylin Simpson likely would be the choice to line up outside with Marshall if/when the Dolphins want to slide rookie Chris Johnson in the slot in the nickel.
New England's injury report wasn't much smaller than that of the Dolphins with 12 names, but the Patriots didn't have anybody miss practice.
The most prominent players among those who were limited were wide receiver A.J. Brown (ankle) and starting right tackle Morgan Moses (foot).
Quarterback Drake Maye was listed with a right shoulder injury, but he was a full participant.

title: Should the Dolphins Make a Trade Pitch for Former First-Round Pick? And What Should They Offer?
full_text:
We've reached the part of the NFL season when general managers are working the phones, looking to bring a shiny new toy to their city.
In some cases, it's about acquiring the final piece or two to fuel a playoff run. For teams like the Miami Dolphins , it's about gradually building a foundation that could eventually deliver a return on the investment.
The name of the day is Jacksonville Jaguars wide receiver Brian Thomas Jr., who Sports Illustrated's Conor Orr recently identified as a potential trade target for Miami ahead of the Nov. 10 deadline.
With Miami potentially selecting a quarterback early in the 2027 NFL Draft, trading for a young receiver with proven upside could give their next signal-caller a much-needed weapon.
But would Thomas be worth the investment?
After a PFWA All-Rookie campaign when he set Jacksonville franchise rookie records with 87 receptions, 1,282 receiving yards and 10 touchdowns, Thomas' role has gradually diminished to the point where he's now the team's fourth-leading wide receiver in receiving yards.
Thomas has just nine receptions for 105 yards and one touchdown through six games this season, which would rank fifth even in Miami's limited passing offense.
The regression is tangible, perhaps most evident in the fact that Thomas has failed to catch any of the last five passes thrown in his direction.
A look at his film reveals an athletic specimen who still struggles with the intricacies of route running while regularly failing to adjust to passes that require extra body control.
The trajectory that once seemed destined to make him one of the league's premier X receivers has been altered. But it's not like he's had his abilities stolen like Michael Jordan did in Space Jam .
In attempting to develop Thomas into a reliable top receiver, Jacksonville has seemingly moved away from some of the quick-hitting concepts that once allowed him to showcase his natural athleticism.
According to Pro Football Focus charting, Thomas has run just one slant route and no screens this season, limiting opportunities to get the ball into his hands quickly and capitalize on the 4.33-second speed that once had scouts enamored at the NFL combine.
There is still an explosive player somewhere in there. The question is whether Miami would be capable of bringing him back out.
The most recent comparison is Marvin Harrison Jr., who the Houston Texans acquired from the Arizona Cardinals earlier this month.
Houston gave up a 2027 second-round pick and a seventh-round selection in exchange for Harrison and a sixth-rounder, which gives an interesting benchmark for what Jacksonville might seek in return for Thomas.
For Miami, surrendering a pick in the second round should be off the table.
Productive complementary receivers can be found in the second and third rounds with proper scouting, without requiring Miami to gamble on reviving another organization's former first-round pick.
But a fourth- or fifth-round selection?
That's an entirely different conversation.
At that price, Thomas could inject some much-needed speed and life into an offense that has struggled to consistently generate explosive plays through the air.
Tyler M. Carmona is a Miami native whose work has appeared in the Miami Herald and Associated Press. He previously worked as a local television news reporter. He recently graduated from Columbia University’s Graduate School of Journalism and played college football at Savannah State University and the University of St. Francis

title: Dolphins Week 8 Power Rankings Roundup: How Big of a Move Up After First Win?
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins no longer are being viewed as the worst team in the NFL — by anybody.
At least, that's the verdict in our latest weekly survey of NFL power rankings from 10 national outlets — Yahoo Sports, Sports Illustrated, ESPN, The Athletic, NFL.com, USA Today, Pro Football Talk, FOX Sports, The Sporting News, CBS Sports — with the Dolphins posting an average ranking of 29th.
But no one has them 32nd, the worst ranking coming from Conor Orr of Sports Illustrated at 31. The Dolphins were ranked as high as 26th by NFL.com's Nick Shook in the aftermath of their 28-25 victory against the New York Jets at MetLife Stadium, a game where the Dolphins never trailed.
This obviously is a move in the right direction after the Dolphins were ranked either 31st or 32nd by all 10 outlets last week.
The Dolphins' next opponents, the New England Patriots, have an average ranking of 10.4, with a high of eighth from USA Today and a low of 11th from six outlets.
At 1-5, the Dolphins now have the third-worst record in the NFL behind the Los Angeles Chargers' 0-6 and the Tennessee Titans' 1-5. The Washington Commanders are the other team with fewer than two victories as they stand at 1-4-1 coming off their bye.
As a reminder, strength of schedule is the tiebreaker for draft position between teams that finish with the same record, with the higher the SOS, the lower the pick. The Dolphins' current combined opponent winning percentage mark of .589 is the highest in the NFL, meaning they would pick lower in any tiebreaker scenario.
That's for down the line, though, because the Dolphins are hoping to win more games after getting on the board against the Jets.
The Sporting News ( Vinnie Iyer)
Analysis: The Dolphins put on their first winning costume of the season with an offense pulling out all kinds of treats with youngster Ollie Gordon II and Caleb Douglas. They were overdue for that much-needed first win under Jeff Hafley. Watch them to play spoiler a few more times vs. better teams.
Analysis: They won! That's a great sign coming out of the bye. They aren't in the cellar of these rankings anymore as the young players continue to improve.
Analysis: “Thinking of me as a little kid in the parking lot as we (came to the Meadowlands), I was one of the those guys flipping off the buses, and now here I am," said New Jersey native and first-year Fins coach Jeff Hafley after his team upset the Jets to finally break into the win column. Way to also flip off all of those observers who thought your team might become the 0-17 bookend to the 17-0 1972 Dolphins, Coach.
FOX Sports (Ralph Vacchiano)
Analysis: Admit it. You knew the Dolphins were going to beat the Jets on Sunday. I mean, if they were going to win one game all season long, that was always going to be it. And of course, it would be at MetLife Stadium. Every Jets fan knew it when they bought their ticket to that game. The Dolphins did it in style, too. Malik Willis threw a 63-yard touchdown pass in the fourth quarter. RB Ollie Gordon ran all over the Jets for 103 yards. And the Miami defense got the big fourth-quarter stop when they needed it. Enjoy it, because things are almost certainly going to get worse — at least until they play the Jets again in Miami on Nov. 29.
Analysis: The Dolphins won a game! Malik Willis posted a passer rating north of 130! Ollie Gordon II ran hard and Caleb Douglas scored two touchdowns! Miami even survived a perfect meltdown scenario and managed to stay intact and ice a victory! Can you tell I’m excited?? Sometimes, it feels good to watch undermanned, rebuilding teams play well enough to emerge victorious. Those types of seasons are already long enough.
The Athletic (Chad Graff and Josh Kendall)
Analysis: Sure, we could focus on the Dolphins’ woeful defensive stats, but let’s focus on their no-doubter of a win. Although the final score made it appear close, they never trailed and were up 21-7 at the half and 28-17 with four minutes left. It was an impressive first victory for coach Jeff Hafley.
Analysis (on the best offseason addition, LB Jacob Rodriguez): The Dolphins were so impressed by their second-round pick this summer that they waived Tyrel Dodson, last season's starter. And the rookie has repaid their faith. Rodriguez set the tone with 14 tackles in Week 1 and eventually set a franchise rookie record with 18 tackles in Week 4. He is second in the NFL in tackles per game (10.2) and 15th in run stop wins (49). General manager Jon-Eric Sullivan said on draft night that Rodriguez would call the Dolphins' defense at some point -- and he was ready to do so in Week 1. -- Marcel Louis-Jacques
Pro Football Talk (Mike Florio)
Analysis: Only five weeks until the next Jets game.
Sports Illustrated (Conor Orr)
Analysis: I think people ripping the Dolphins for celebrating Jeff Hafley’s first win simply don’t get it. The fact that there is this much juice and energy for one of the worst teams in the NFL shows exactly where this team is headed.
Yahoo Sports (Frank Schwab)
Analysis: The Dolphins can relax. There was always the hope that the team with the NFL's thinnest roster could beat the Jets in one of their two meetings, and that happened. Everyone focuses on the winless teams in the NFL but nobody remembers the one-loss teams, so the Dolphins are spared a lot of grief that would have come had their winless season continued through November. They're still probably not the 29th best team in the NFL but they deserved a bump up after outplaying the Jets.

title: What to Know About the Latest Wave of Dolphins Tryout Players
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins' 53-man roster remains a work in progress, as GM Jon-Eric Sullivan has indicated on multiple occasions since the spring, so it was only natural to have more player tryouts Tuesday.
Especially since the team has an opening on the roster.
The Dolphins brought in eight players for tryouts Tuesday, with a heavy emphasis on the tight end position. Four of the players brought played that position, along with two defensive tackles, one quarterback and one defensive end.
As has been the case for most of the tryouts this year for Miami, the list was comprised of young players with little or no NFL game experience.
The list: QB Derek Robertson, Monmouth TE Jaheim Bell, Florida State TE Devin Culp, Washington TE Rivaldo Fairweather, Auburn TE Joshua Simon, South Carolina DE Anthony Goodlow, Oklahoma State DT Cole Brevard, Texas DT Jay Toia, UCLA
Of those eight players, Bell, Culp, Goodlow and Toia are the only ones with NFL game experience, those it ranges from five to 18 games for Culp.
Bell, Culp and Toia entered the NFL as seventh-round draft picks, while the other five were undrafted rookie free agents, including Brevard and Robertson this year. Robertson's only NFL exposure came when he attended the Jacksonville Jaguars rookie minicamp as a tryout player.
This tryout, like all the ones before, shouldn't be viewed as a precursor to a signing, though it has happened this year, most recently with Zane Gonzalez beating out three other kickers to land a spot on the practice squad after the team released incumbent Riley Patterson.
The Dolphins didn't replace Patterson the 53, which is why they have an opening, but Gonzalez can only be elevated for a game two more times before the Dolphins have to put him on the 53-man roster or find another kicker.
The likelihood is this latest tryout was about gathering intel on potential future signings. If we're looking at tight ends, the Dolphins already have three rookies at the position with third-round pick Will Kacmarek, fifth-round pick Seydou Traore and waiver wire pick-up Justin Joly, himself a fifth-round pick of the Denver Broncos.
In a full-circle moment, outside linebacker/edge defender Andre Jones Jr. rejoined the Buffalo Bills practice squad, which is where the Dolphins got him for their 53-man roster before eventually waiving him after three games.
Jones played 45 games on special teams for Miami in those three games.
Elsewhere: -- Former Dolphins punter Matt Haack had a tryout with the Tennessee Titans. -- Tackle Charlie Heck, who failed to make Miami's 53-man roster after signing as an unrestricted free agent in the offseason, had a tryout with the New York Jets. -- Tight end Ben Sims, who was waived/injured after also signing as a UFA in the offseason, had a tryout with the Seattle Seahawks.

title: Examining the Impact of the Nelson Trade on the Dolphins
full_text:
The NFL trade deadline is now two weeks away, but there was a significant trade Tuesday.
The immediate impact for the Miami Dolphins of the Indianapolis Colts beginning their expected fire sale by sending perennial Pro Bowl Quenton Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks is that their Week 10 game at Lucas Oil Stadium might become a lot more winnable than it once was.
There are potentially other implications beyond that game on November 15, though.
The reported return for Nelson, who will become a free agent after the season and no doubt will get a massive free agent deal, was a third-round pick in the 2027 NFL draft along with a fifth-round selection in 2028.
The trade compensation is important to note as a comparison point for all the teams looking or willing to deal players before the trade deadline November 10.
While they're coming off a victory, the Dolphins remain — or at least should remain — focused on the big picture and treat their personnel with the future in mind, meaning they should listen to offers for any players and maybe seek deals for those they don't see as part of the team beyond this season.
Tackle Austin Jackson has long been assumed on the way out because he's a pretty expensive player in the final year of his contract, he's not having a great year and the Dolphins have their future right tackle on the roster with Kadyn Proctor if they decide to switch him there instead of keeping him at left guard where he's showing great promise as a rookie.
While the Nelson trade compensation doesn't really apply when it comes to Jackson — as it doesn't to a whole lot of offensive linemen around the NFL — maybe it becomes a better barometer for someone like defensive tackle Zach Sieler.
The question, of course, is whether the Dolphins even want to trade Sieler, who's not only a good player in the middle of the defensive line but a leader on a team with an abundance of young players.
While Sieler isn't an All-Pro like Nelson, he is under contract through the next three years after this one, though with no guaranteed salary, giving an acquiring team flexiblity in terms of how to proceed forward with him.
If Nelson fetched a third and a fifth in a trade, what could the Dolphins get for Sieler? The obvious answer is whatever a team — say, the New York Giants — needing help at defensive tackle is willing to give up,
Realistically, it's always felt as though maybe the best the Dolphins could do was get a third-round pick and that likely would entail them giving up a late-round pick in addition to Sieler.
Jackson, because his contract expires, he has a long injury history and has had issues in pass protection, probably wouldn't fetch more than a late-round pick.
That game against the Colts will come five days after the trade deadline, and it's entirely possible that Nelson won't be the only star player gone from Indy by then.
After GM Chris Ballard was fired following the Colts' loss against the Tennessee Titans, it looks like the team is headed for a full rebuild and players like Jonathan Taylor and DeForrest Buckner also could be moved.
One thing for sure, that Colts team isn't going to look the same as the one the Dolphins saw in the 2025 opener when they left Indianapolis with a 33-8 loss.
