title: What the Week 7 Film Told Us About the Miami Dolphins
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins tallied their first win of 2026 against the New York Jets, and the All-22 film shows both triumph and room for improvement. Here’s a look at the key developments from this game along with breakdowns of some of the biggest plays.
The Dolphins’ passing game was operating as cleanly as we’ve seen it in 2026. Their 0.41 EPA per pass ranked third in the league in Week 7, and their passing yards per play was fifth at 8.9.
For the first time all season, the route concepts consistently fit the players on the field. They sent more of their eligibles on routes, found ways to space out zone coverages, and were on the same page in blitz situations.
Miami set the tone early, as Malik Willis’ first three pass attempts looked relatively similar: four or more players out on routes, no play-action, and opportunities for Willis to get to the back side of his progression.
pic.twitter.com/Q9YTDETNUW
He did so beautifully on each of the three, casually sliding from one read to the next, and capping off a 3-for-3 opening drive with a touchdown strike to the returning Caleb Douglas.
Through the first five games of the season, Bobby Slowik’s passing offense looked clunky and congested. As I’ve chronicled in the previous film breakdowns, far too many of Miami’s dropbacks involved simple two-man route concepts and shot plays. They were sprinkled into this game as well, but looked more like a changeup to the quick-game fastball.
The quick, ball-control style of the Dolphins’ passing game dominated the Jets’ blitzes. Malik Willis finished 8-for-10 for 128 yards passing when Aaron Glenn sent extra rushers, and his 14.6 EPA was the best mark in football for any quarterback against the blitz.
pic.twitter.com/dtZ2JtusmF
The only thing better than Slowik’s timely play calling was the execution from Miami’s most important pieces. On Caleb Douglas’ second touchdown, he notices the cornerback blitz, and, knowing his route is where Willis would have to go with the ball, he stops short and throws his hands up. Willis sees him in space, takes a shot on a sidearm delivery that whips around Brandon Stephens, and Douglas takes it 63 yards thanks to a crucial block from Malik Washington.
That single play was a glimpse of what could be for the future of the Miami Dolphins. Caleb Douglas looked smooth and athletic in his return, and if Willis keeps making cerebral plays in key moments, he’ll look more and more like a franchise quarterback.
Miami’s run game was just as impressive as their passing attack. EPA per rush was seventh in the league, success rate was 11th, and Ollie Gordon logged his second 100-yard game of the season.
In De’Von Achane’s absence, Bobby Slowik has maximized this unit, largely due to the amount of gap scheme runs he’s worked in. In previous years, Mike McDaniel worked almost exclusively with outside zone and toss looks, but Miami’s power and counter runs might be their best concepts in 2026.
pic.twitter.com/RDlidmHBzc
On Miami’s final drive, they ran the same power play three times in a row, and hit a 14-yard gain on their first attempt. Will Kacmarek and Austin Jackson obliterate their down-block at the point-of-attack, Kadyn Proctor’s pull makes contact with two defenders, and Ollie Gordon hurdles into the second level.
Every aspect of this rushing game looks dangerous right now. The revamped scheme simplifies reads for Gordon, while allowing Miami’s massive guards to use their strength to their advantage. Bobby Slowik’s attention to detail, timely calls, and wrinkles with motion and alignment have all created advantages that the players have capitalized on.
The Dolphins’ defense was able to get enough stops to win, but they struggled down to down. Geno Smith went 23-of-30 passing for 308 yards, including two deep shots that targeted Miami’s youth.
pic.twitter.com/SJBMzyou0A
Smith’s first pass of the game went for 52 yards, with nobody taking Omar Cooper Jr. deep down the field. In man coverage, Chris Johnson appears to signal to Jason Marshall Jr. that he'll take the outside man, but at the snap of the ball, both players play Garrett Wilson, and neither can recover before Cooper makes the catch.
pic.twitter.com/cZ4qIxWgJW
Later in the game, Cooper made another big play. With Johnson in man coverage, the Jets’ receiver fired off the line, stayed physical with Johnson, and quickly stacked him. Dante Trader Jr., who was occupied with Garrett Wilson on the near sideline, can’t get over in time, and the ball splits the defenders for a 60-yard chunk.
Compounding mistakes, especially in man-to-man looks, result in big plays. If Johnson plays through the receiver and doesn’t slow up or Trader drops closer to the middle of the field, that second explosive likely is erased.
Miami’s defense was feast or famine, making a few momentum-swinging plays that proved sufficient in eking out a victory. When challenging opponents with one-on-one situations, though, Hafley’s young secondary has plenty to clean up.
Tyler DeSena is currently a journalism student at the University of Central Florida. Prior to joining Dolphins On SI in 2026, DeSena worked with dolphinstalk.com, and created independent social media content on X, YouTube and TikTok.

title: Dolphins Week 7 Report Card: A Big Step Forward
full_text:
Whether you wanted them to or not, the Miami Dolphins have finally put one in the win column, beating the New York Jets 28-25 at MetLife Stadium on Sunday.
For a team supposedly setting football back a few decades, they’ve kept knocking on the door. Competitive losses against Minnesota and Cincinnati showed signs of progress, but costly mistakes kept Miami winless heading into its bye.
This time, the Dolphins gave themselves a chance and actually did something with it. Malik Willis delivered his best performance of the season, the running game showed it’s here to stay, and the defense made enough timely stops to survive New York’s late push.
Here’s how each position group graded out in Miami’s first win of the season.
Willis completed 14 of 21 passes for 208 yards and two touchdowns without an interception, adding 37 yards and another score on eight carries. He finished with a 130.7 passer rating.
The numbers reflect Willis’ growing comfort processing the defense. He’s moving through his progressions more naturally and showing he can create openings as well as recognize them.
On his 32-yard completion to Greg Dulcich up the seam, Willis did more than work through his reads. He turned his feet and shoulders to the right, where Caleb Douglas and Seydou Traore were running quick outs. That movement drew the safety toward the sideline, opening a window up the seam for Dulcich.
Similarly, on Douglas’ first touchdown, Willis resisted the urge to scramble or throw the ball away when his first two reads weren’t available. He stayed with the play, allowing the routes to develop and clear space before finding Douglas late in his progression on an in-breaking route.
Offensive coordinator Bobby Slowik favors 12 personnel (one back, two tight ends), but Willis’ mobility also makes a case for spreading the field. Empty sets and formations with three or four receivers can widen the defense and open running lanes through the middle, giving Willis another way to punish the coverage with his legs.
At this point, we’re out of fluke territory. We’ve all heard the legends of Ollie Gordon II’s Doak Walker year at Oklahoma State and the mysterious drought that followed, but it appears the Dolphins have unlocked that version of him again.
Gordon finished with 103 yards and a touchdown on 25 carries, giving him his second 100-yard game in his last three starts.
The 4.1 yards per carry doesn’t jump off the page, but New York knew Miami wanted to run late. Gordon still ripped off gains of 14 and seven yards on consecutive carries during the final drive.
Jaylen Wright, meanwhile, continued struggling to find running room, finishing with 8 yards on six carries before leaving with a quad injury.
Welcome back, Caleb Douglas.
After quickly winning over Dolphins fans, the rookie had barely gotten involved in Week 2 before an ankle injury sidelined him. His return gave Miami the length and athleticism it had been missing on the outside.
He caught just two passes, but both went for touchdowns, totaling 70 yards.
On his goal-line touchdown, Douglas drove vertically at full speed to get on Azareye’h Thomas’ toes, then used a hard jab step with his right foot to get the corner leaning before breaking inside.
Malik Washington remained a reliable target, catching all three of his targets for 27 yards, while Chris Bell added three catches for 25.
Miami also used Bell on shallow crossing routes out of mesh concepts, giving him opportunities to use his strength and speed against man coverage. It was a familiar look for Bell, who turned a similar drag route into a touchdown for Louisville against Miami.
After going without a target in Miami’s loss to Cincinnati, Greg Dulcich has now drawn five in back-to-back games as the Dolphins steadily work him into the passing attack.
He caught all five for 86 yards, all in the first half.
Dulcich had a 32-yard catch on Miami’s opening touchdown drive, converted a third-and-7 on the next possession and later added gains of 15 and 16 yards during the 91-yard touchdown drive before halftime.
Rookie Will Kacmarek continued to handle his blocking assignments well, but Dulcich finally delivered the receiving production Miami has been waiting for from the position.
The offensive line has had their fair share of ugly moments this season, but this wasn’t one of them.
Miami ran for 156 yards, held the ball for more than 34 minutes and, most importantly, was able to run the ball when even the people using the bathroom at MetLife stadium knew it was coming
That final possession was probably the best example. Miami lined up and ran it over and over again with a three-point lead, and the Jets never got the ball back.
Austin Jackson still had his moment, let’s not be unrealistic here, giving up a sack late in the third quarter that killed a possession, but overall this was one of the unit’s better games.
If you want one sequence to describe this unit, just watch the goal-line stand.
New York was sitting on Miami’s doorstep on first-and-goal when the Dolphins responded with a Zach Sieler tackle for loss, another stop by Josh Uche and then a Chop Robinson sack on third down.
Robinson continues to create pressure even when the sacks aren’t piling up, generating four pressures.
Malik Herring also sacked Geno Smith with 11:36 in the 3rd quarter.
That said, the run defense was less than ideal, as Braelon Allen finished with 104 yards on just 17 carries.
Jordyn Brooks did what Jordyn Brooks usually does, finishing with nine tackles and two tackles for loss.
Jacob Rodriguez, meanwhile, had his quietest game of the season with four tackles.
Here’s my weekly Pro Football Focus disclaimer: they charged Rodriguez with allowing a completion to Jets running back Isaiah Davis, but Rodriguez appeared to communicate that Jason Marshall needed to pick up the crossing route, which makes it difficult to pin the breakdown solely on Rodriguez
Mason Taylor caught two touchdowns, but both came with defensive backs in coverage, Jason Marshall and Michael Taaffe.
Miami’s rookie defensive backs continue to ride the NFL roller coaster.
Michael Taaffe read Geno Smith the entire way on his second-quarter interception, jumping Mason Taylor’s route to end a Jets scoring threat. Taylor got him back in the fourth quarter, beating him for a 12-yard touchdown.
Chris Johnson also intercepted Smith, but his own defensive holding penalty wiped out the takeaway. He later surrendered a 60-yard completion to Omar Cooper Jr. on a deep crossing route with safety Dante Trader Jr. also in the coverage area.
Smith completed 23 of 30 passes for 287 yards and three touchdowns, while Cooper finished with 115 yards on five catches.
Jason Marshall Jr. had his struggles, too. On Taylor’s first touchdown, Marshall was draped over the tight end near the pylon but couldn’t break up the pass and never looked back for the ball.
For once, there wasn’t much to complain about.
Wright averaged 26.2 yards on five kickoff returns and had a 39-yarder that helped set up Miami’s second touchdown drive.
Bradley Pinion also did his job, averaging 44.2 yards per punt with a 42.5 net.
The wind was briefly knocked out of everybody’s stomach when Wright muffed the final kickoff before recovering it, because apparently Miami can’t go an entire game without making a kickoff stressful, but this was a major improvement from the first month of the season.
For the first time this season, Miami actually made the plays necessary to win a close game.
Taaffe got the interception, the defense made the goal-line stand, and Douglas and Gordon  supplied the offensive punch the Dolphins had been thirsting for.
After spending six weeks finding increasingly creative ways to lose, the Dolphins finally figured out how to finish one.
Tyler M. Carmona is a Miami native whose work has appeared in the Miami Herald and Associated Press. He previously worked as a local television news reporter. He recently graduated from Columbia University’s Graduate School of…

title: Poup's Perspective: Why This First Dolphins Win Indeed Was a Very Big Deal
full_text:
No, the Miami Dolphins are not suddenly going to make a playoff push because they got off the schneid and got their first victory of the 2026 season Sunday.
Or let's just say it's extraordinarily unlikely because we never want to say never.
And, yes, that elusive victory did come against the New York Jets, an organization about as dysfunctional as any in the NFL, as evidenced by the fact it's got the longest playoff drought (appearance, not win because that one belongs to the Dolphins).
But, make no mistake, it was cause for celebration, not just for the players and coaches who have been working hard under difficult circumstances to become at a minimum competitive and it most definitely was cause for celebration for anybody who cares about the Miami Dolphins.
Belief. Step inside the locker room after our Week 7 win 🔊 pic.twitter.com/i20aJA405x
The video of the Dolphins' locker room celebration was something, capturing the kind of excitement you normally see when a team clinches a playoff berth or even more.
But it actually was similar for the Dolphins and not just because it was Jeff Hafley's first win as an NFL head coach.
It was the first tangible reward for the vision that Jon-Eric Sullivan and Hafley have implemented, with strong performances by quarterback Malik Willis and members of a 2026 draft class that has looked promising from the start, with Kadyn Proctor, Chris Johnson, Jacob Rodriguez, Caleb Douglas, Will Kacmarek, Chris Bell and Michael Taaffe all contributing to one degree or another to that 28-25 win against the New York Jets.
In that Dolphins video, we saw Hafley talk about asking his offensive linemen about going for it on that late fourth-down to clinch the victory and making the call to proceed after getting the response he wanted.
Truth is, it was the only acceptable response from the big guys up front because the second an offensive lineman suggests at that time it would be more prudent to punt and let the defense hold the lead, that's the time to replace the head coach, that offensive lineman or both.
We still like the idea of Hafley there showing he was going to trust his players to deliver after they accept a challenge, and that's a big part of what this season is for the Dolphins.
Jets or not, the Dolphins played their best game of the season Sunday and just like that any talk of an 0-17 season disappeared.
That it was there in the first place only was evidence of just how massive a rebuilding project the Dolphins undertook by dumping so many high-end players and taking on so much dead cap space in one year.
But the Dolphins, with Sullivan in charge, sure look like they've done a pretty good job of restocking the roster, to the extent that they could do it in the first year with their cap restrictions.
As we've said before, this 2026 season for the Dolphins isn't about wins and losses, it's about progress and developments and being able to identify a nice group of young players with whom the team can move forward as part of the nucleus.
At this point, it sure looks as thought the Dolphins have a decent number of those core pieces to keep watching and the hope is we'll see more performances like we saw against the Jets.
That absolutely includes Willis, who accomplished more against the Jets by actually trying to do less — if that makes sense. It probably wasn't an accident that he was more efficient than in any other previous while not going downfield nearly as much.
Look at Willis' stat line against the Jets and you'll notice an uncanny resemblance to that of his second start with the Green Bay Packers in 2024.
Against the Jets on Sunday: 14-for-21, 208 yards, 2 TD, 0 INT, 130.7 passer rating, 37 rushing yards, 1 TD
Against the Titans in 2024: 13-for-19, 202 yards, 1 TD, 0 INT, 120.9 passer rating, 73 rushing yards, 1 TD
That was just one game, of course, and the key will be for Willis to do it again and then again after that.
And if there are more games like from Willis, there will be more wins.
And then the first 2027 draft pick will get lower and lower, and the same goes for more performances like we saw from Douglas or Taaffe or Ollie Gordon II or Greg Dulcich.
And that should be the goal for the Dolphins and the hope for Dolphins fans.
If the Dolphins can go, say, 5-12 and have to settle for eighth or ninth overall pick, it would be more favorable for the future health of the franchise than going 2-15 or 1-16 and having the second or even first pick.
The difference between two picks within the top 10 isn't nearly as significant as having found a group of key pieces with whom to move forward.
The win against the Jets was big. And the hope should be there are more to come, even if they're not that frequent.
The focus needs to stay on the 2026 season, not the 2027 draft. And that's how it should have been all along.
Alain Poupart is the publisher/editor of Miami Dolphins On SI, host of the All Dolphins Podcast, and co-host of the Dolphins Collective. Alain has covered the Miami Dolphins on a full-time basis since 1989 for various publications and media outlets, including Dolphin Digest, The Associated Press and the Dolphins team website. In addition to being a credentialed member of the Miami Dolphins press corps, Alain has covered three Super Bowls (for NFL.com, Football News and the Montreal Gazette), the annual NFL draft, the Senior Bowl, and the NFL Scouting Combine. During his almost 40 years in journalism, which began at the now-defunct Miami News, Alain has covered practically every sport at one time or another, from tennis to golf, baseball, basketball and everything in between. The career also included time as a copy editor, including work on several books, such as "Still Perfect," an inside look at the Miami Dolphins' 1972 perfect season. A native of Montreal, Canada, whose first language is French, Alain grew up a huge hockey fan but soon developed a love for all sports, including NFL football. He has lived in South Florida since the 1980s.

title: Four Winners And Four Losers From Miami's First Win Of 2026
full_text:
Rejoice if you'd like, as the Miami Dolphins are no longer winless, taking down the New York Jets in a 28-25 thriller. If you're on the side of the room that thinks going winless would be better for "draft capital," please chill out.
No team deserves to go an entire season without winning a game. The way things are shaping up, the Dolphins are still in contention for a top pick regardless, with the only winless team remaining being the Los Angeles Chargers.
So how did Miami pull it off? The best performance of the season by their offense from the jump, alongside doing just enough on the defense to slow the Jets down. It wasn't easy, but the idea of Jeff Hafley not getting drenched in Gatorade this season has been officially put to rest.
This has to feel great for Willis, coming off a shoddy performance against Cincinnati. Instead, he shushed a lot of the doubters with a strong performance - 208 yards and two touchdowns through the air, and 37 yards and a score on the ground. Make fun of the Jets all you want, but their secondary was generally considered a tough unit.
Nothing Willis did physically stands out from what we know about his skill set. Instead, the bigger difference is what he did mentally - he was much smarter with his decision-making in this game. Whether he had to pin the ball in the right spot or escape the pocket, he made the right call more often than not.
It's a very positive sign for the Dolphins. Their quarterback looks like he has confidence again, and the big question is whether he can keep it up against tougher competition, with New England and Detroit coming to town. If he can, the idea of Miami going for a quarterback in the 2027 draft gets a bit muddled.
The offensive line played fine, but not thanks to Jackson. One mistake stands out - a missed block on third down at midfield, which led to defensive end Nate Lynn's first career sack with less than a minute to go in the third quarter. Miami looked poised to get to field goal range, but instead were forced to punt. The Jets responded with a lengthy drive, going all the way to the 1-yard line.
That was the only major negative play Jackson caused, but every play matters more when the game comes down to the wire. It's no secret that he's been a liability more often than not for the Dolphins - Pro Football Focus certainly thinks so, as he's earned a 43.7 grade. Out of all 71 eligible tackles, that's the lowest of the group.
It really seems like the future of the offensive line is bright with the consistent performances that Aaron Brewer, Jonah Savaiinaea, Patrick Paul and Kadyn Proctor have orchestrated this season. But Jackson hasn't proven himself worthy of being mentioned in that group, and that missed block might be bulletin-board material for the Dolphins to consider going somewhere else at right tackle.
Douglas walked into the land of questionable turf and proved he was the most explosive player on the field. He wasn't targeted much - only three times - but made the most of his opportunities with two touchdowns on two receptions.
The first score was great, creating separation from Azareye'h Thomas in the back of the end zone to give the Dolphins their first lead of the season. However, his second touchdown was stellar - a 63-yard sprint down the left side of the field, narrowly getting by Nahshon Wright while staying in bounds for the score, giving Miami the 11-point cushion they needed in the end.
Believing that the outlook of this game changed the moment it was announced that Douglas would play was justified. He's a natural difference-maker even as a rookie, and a red zone weapon that Willis and the Dolphins could rely on for years to come.
Unfortunately, it's almost obligatory at this point to include Wright in these lists, as he's just not reliable for the Dolphins. Once again, he failed to get past New York's defensive line, settling for 8 yards on six carries. Wide receiver Malik Washington somehow managed the same amount of yards in just TWO carries.
At this point, what's the excuse for not giving another running back on the roster a shot to back up Ollie Gordon II? Whether it's Kaytron Allen, who the Dolphins claimed off waivers back on October 9,  or Carlos Washington Jr., currently on their practice squad, how can it be any worse?
It feels bad to hammer Wright this much, especially because there was a small chance he wasn't able to play in this game due to a nagging foot injury. But the production at running back falls off so much when he's on the field that it's almost become a guarantee. Having two reliable running backs instead of one would do wonders for this offense.
It might not look like Taaffe had a major game just by the box score - three tackles and a pass deflection is just OK. But the major highlight on defense for Miami came at the hands of Taaffe - a clutch interception, considering the Jets were knocking on Miami's red zone in the second quarter.
Despite the achievement, it was a pretty standard play. Geno Smith targeted Mason Taylor right off the play action, never looking away, even when shuffling to the right before throwing the ball. Taaffe read it the whole way, jumping the route and denying the Jets another score for the rest of the half.
Taffee is in elite company, being one of three rookies with multiple picks this season (Hezekiah Masses and Genesis Smith). He's the first member of the Dolphins to do so in the first six games of his career, since Patrick Surtain in 1998. You can't ask for much more from the 158th overall pick.
Overall, this was a successful day for the Dolphins in terms of getting to the quarterback, especially when compared to their earlier struggles to do so this season. Geno Smith took a beating, with two sacks and six confirmed QB hits. However, these came at the hands of guys like Chop Robinson, Malik Herring, Chris Johnson, and Zach Sieler.
Phillips, in comparison, had a very quiet performance - just one solo tackle, stopping Omar Cooper Jr. in his tracks after a 3-yard gain in the fourth quarter. Of all the playmakers in the trenches, he was the most pedestrian. He didn't hurt the Dolphins in the long run, partially because of Sieler's contributions, but it was disappointing to see nonetheless.
We debuted the first coach on one of these lists in Week 5, with STC Chris Tabor being named a loser. It's only fair to flip the script this week, and Hafley gets the honor for having his team ready to play from the start all the way to the finish.
It was a near-complete game on offense, defense, and special teams. Even with a 0-5 record, Hafley made sure his team gave everything they had against a division rival, and they did just enough to get the job done. It wasn't always perfect - the Dolphins committed five penalties but had no turnovers at the same time.
His signature moment was the decision to go for it on fourth down on the Dolphins' final drive to ice the game as opposed to punting the ball, which would have been the safer choice. Hafley noted postgame that he asked the offensive line if they wanted to do it, and trusted them when they said yes. It turned out to be the right decision as it was the prior two times they went for it on fourth down in this game.
This was overall a mediocre performance by Marshall. He was the victim of a ridiculous snag by Mason Taylor (son of Dolphins legend Jason Taylor) in the end zone for New York's sole touchdown in the first half.
The coverage on the play by Marshall wasn't bad, though he made the mistake of never looking back for the ball. Taylor simply went up and made a remarkable catch on National Tight Ends Day, no less. It was a quiet performance by Marshall all around, which isn't necessarily a bad thing, but he'll definitely want to have that one play back.
Jake Gibson is a writer for the Miami Dolphins on SI. He began his sports journalism career with PantherNOW, the student newspaper at his alma mater, Florida International University, where he began as a sportswriter…

title: 3 RB Trade Targets Vikings Should Pivot to With Jonathan Taylor's Price Reportedly Steep
full_text:
The Minnesota Vikings should be in the market to trade for a running back this season. With the team undefeated through seven weeks, it is time for the team to focus on continuing their winning ways for what should be a deep playoff run.
Of course, the flashiest name on the market is Indianapolis Colts superstar running back Jonathan Taylor. However, the 27-year-old rushing juggernaut is likely to command a first-round draft pick as compensation.
While Taylor would be an amazing asset for Minnesota, the cost might be a little high for Vikings general manager Nolan Teasley to justify. Thankfully, other players at the position could help and cost significantly less to acquire.
The Tennessee Titans are an absolute mess this year. Despite only having one win this season, running back Tony Pollard has been one of the few bright spots on the team. Through seven games, he has carried the ball 112 times for 478 yards and four touchdowns.
Pollard's 4.3 yards per carry is better than Aaron Jones or Jordan Mason , and his 23 rushing first downs would help a Minnesota offense that struggles to move the chains.
Considering the Titans' situation this year and the need to make significant changes to improve the team, dealing a 29-year-old rusher for a mid-round draft pick makes sense. The Vikings can get a running back to finally give Jones a break and take pressure off Mason.
The running back situation with the New York Giants is complicated. Cam Skattebo is their number one rusher, but fumbling issues have led to him being sidelined this season. They still released Najee Harris despite Skattebo's struggles. Tyrone Tracy is on IR, and Greg Desrosiers Jr. is an unknown.
The Giants should be buyers at the running back position this year, much like Minnesota. If they do acquire one of the top options, Devin Singletary could become expendable in their offense and possibly be on the trade block.
Singletary is averaging 4.4 yards per carry this season but only has 18 rushing attempts this season. When New York eventually adds a running back, the 29-year-old running back will become a player the Vikings should look to acquire.
Isaiah Davis may not have the name recognition of a player like Taylor, Pollard, or Singletary, but he is in his third season with the Jets and isn't getting much work. This season, he has only 10 rushing attempts for 29 yards, but he has previously been a much more effective running back.
At 24 years old, Davis has a bright future ahead of him, but he is behind Breece Hall and Braelon Allen on the depth chart. He wouldn't be a starter for Minnesota, but he would be a player who could rotate into a game and contribute if needed.

title: Ranking the Most Likely Positions the Vikings Could Target at Trade Deadline
full_text:
At 6-0, the Vikings are a team that could be serious buyers at the trade deadline and may address more than one position.
A struggling offense and a defense lacking veteran depth could lead the Vikings to make a deal for several players. So, which positions are the most likely targets for a team looking to make a deep postseason run? Let's take a look, starting with a potential blockbuster trade.
This should come as no surprise despite the Vikings already boasting two well-respected runners. Both Aaron Jones Sr. and Jordan Mason have been decent in 2026, each averaging a respectable 4.2 yards per carry, but Minnesota also knows they're leaving a lot on the bone here too.
Neither is particularly explosive, and quarterback Kyler Murray owns the Vikings' longest rush of the season at 35 yards. Combine those restrictions with Jones' nagging knee issue, and you get a pair of rushers who don't exactly strike fear into many defenses.
For this offense to open up, the Vikings need a back who can be a game-breaker and make defenses think twice about leaving two high safeties--something opposing defenses are currently doing over 50% of the time against the Minnesota offense. Clearly, the lackluster run game isn't making things any easier on Murray and the receivers.
Jonathan Taylor or Saquon Barkley are the obvious splash candidates . But a complementary back with some home-run ability could be a more palatable solution to bring some juice to this backfield.
The Vikings reportedly had some interest in the Colts' All-Pro guard Quenton Nelson before he was sent to the Seattle Seahawks, so there's certainly reason to assume Minnesota could be in on a few other options up front as well.
After losing Donovan Jackson for the season, the Vikings have attempted to navigate the season with undrafted free agent Joe Huber at left guard and an underwhelming Will Fries on the right side. All options should theoretically be on the table: either a short-term rental or a potential future right guard if the Vikings decide to move on from Fries.
With Nelson slipping away for the relatively modest price of a third-rounder in 2027 and a fifth in 2028, it seems the Vikings aren't willing to break the bank for a guard upgrade. Still, it wouldn't be too difficult to find an upgrade at a reasonable cost. The Las Vegas Raiders' Jackson Powers-Johnson could be a potential name to watch.
Jalen Redmond picked right back up where he left off in 2025 and is graded as a top-10 defensive tackle by Pro Football Focus through seven weeks. Levi Drake Rodriguez has also enjoyed a nice year as a first-time starter, but the clear lack of depth behind them may lead Minnesota to bring in a veteran.
Rookies Caleb Banks and Domonique Orange have shown brief flashes in 2026 , but have also looked very much like first-year players. The duo was blasted out of the stratosphere on Jonathan Taylor's 38-yard touchdown run last week, and the Vikings may be looking for a bit more reliability until their youngsters develop.
However, barring injury, this position isn't a dire need, and the Vikings won't shake things up too much here outside of a possible depth addition. The Colts already dealt DeForest Buckner, but Grover Stewart is a name to watch, as he adds veteran presence and much-needed pass rush from the inside.

title: Vikings Report Card: Grading Kyler Murray Three Games After J.J. McCarthy Trade
full_text:
The Minnesota Vikings traded former first-round pick J.J. McCarthy to the New York Giants for a fifth-round pick after Jaxson Dart's season ended with a knee injury. That left Kyler Murray, Carson Wentz, and Max Brosmer as the three passers on the Purple and Gold roster.
McCarthy was traded on Sept. 28, 2026. That means the Vikings have played three games since trading away the player they selected with the No. 10 overall pick in the 2024 NFL Draft. Looking at the recent play of these quarterbacks can help fans to get a good feeling about the trade.
Since joining the Giants, McCarthy has played three games. He played only five offensive snaps in Week 5, but played 31 snaps in Week 6 and played 61 offensive snaps in the Week 7 overtime win over the Houston Texans. He is completing 63.3 percent of his passes and averaging 10.1 yards per pass attempt.
McCarthy seems to be energizing the Giants, while Murray struggles to get Minnesota's offense going. The Vikings have won every game since the trade, but Murray's play has left much to be desired.
Statistically, there are some things that Murray has done well over the last three games. He completed 65 of his 91 pass attempts (71.4 percent) and threw two touchdowns to zero interceptions. He has also run for 106 yards on 21 attempts, including a beautiful 35-yard run against the Colts .
On the other hand, over the last three games, Murray has averaged 209 passing yards per game and 6.9 yards per pass attempt. He was also sacked nine times for a loss of 63 yards. There is plenty of room for improvement.
Minnesota's 6-0 record this season is a great reason not to regret trading McCarthy, but Murray needs to be more dynamic through the air. With weapons like Justin Jefferson, Jordan Addison, and T.J. Hockenson, he should be thriving in Minnesota.
For now, Murray is still winning games with the Vikings. His passes might not stretch the field, but he isn't turning the ball over and is starting to make things happen with his feet. Once he gets more passing yards and touchdowns into the equation, he will become a much bigger asset for Minnesota.

title: Pros & Cons of a Blake Cashman Contract Extension for Vikings
full_text:
The Minnesota Vikings have a difficult decision to make regarding interior linebacker Blake Cashman. His three-year, $22.5 million contract expires after the 2026 season, and general manager Nolan Teasley needs to decide whether an extension should be offered .
Cashman is having an amazing season this year. He has a Pro Football Focus grade of 86.2. He ranks second among qualifying linebackers. He leads the Vikings with 54 tackles and is tied with Kyle Van Noy for most tackles for a loss on the team (7.5).
The 30-year-old defender is in his eighth season in the NFL and his third season in Minnesota. He's had at least100 tackles and two sacks in each of his last three seasons, making him one of the most consistent individuals in defensive coordinator Brian Flores' unit.
An all-around defender like Cashman can be hard to find. He is great at everything he is asked to do, whether it is rushing the quarterback, dropping back in coverage, or playing run support.
Cashman has played in 33 games since signing with Minnesota, starting each of those games. Because of his versatility, there aren't situations where he needs to come off the field. That has led to him playing 95 percent of possible snaps for the team.
Although he is 30 years old, Cashman is at the top of his game. Although he has only played six games for the Purple and Gold, he is already tied for a career high with 4.5 sacks and is on pace for 153 tackles if he plays all 17 games.
Vikings fans might be seeing the best version of Cashman this season. Letting a player go when they are at the top of their game is usually a mistake in the NFL, especially if they are allowed to leave the team as a free agent.
It has been nice having Cashman around for the last three seasons. What made it even better is that he is averaging only $7.5 million per season under his current contract, but that number would likely skyrocket with an extension.
The highest-paid interior linebacker in the league is Pittsburgh Steelers defender Nick Herbig, who averages $25 million per season. While Cashman likely won't demand that kind of money, it will take more than $7.5 million per year to keep him around.
The Vikings selected former Cincinnati linebacker Jake Golday with the No. 51 pick in the 2026 NFL Draft. Because of the play of Cashman and his teammate Eric Wilson, the rookie has been sidelined for much of the season, playing only 16 defensive snaps this year.
At some point, the Vikings need to hope that Golday will be a long-term answer in the middle of the defense. That might mean letting Cashman leave while he is still contributing, to allow more time for their young player to develop.
Although he's 30 years old and his price tag will go up, Cashman has been a valuable part of the Vikings' defense and should continue to be a contributor in 2027. Without more to go on, Minnesota can't feel confident handing a starting role to Golday.
It would be a mistake to allow Cashman to hit the open market. If he does, he will demand a premium price since it will be run up by teams drooling over the idea of adding him to their defense. The best possible solution is to offer an extension worth over $10 million per year to not only keep him around, but reward him for his play in Minnesota.

title: Quenton Nelson Trade Should Light a Fire That Sparks Vikings' Next Move
full_text:
Trades have started happening in the NFL, and the Minnesota Vikings need to get involved. They have a 6-0 record through the first seven weeks of the season, and a smart trade would help to keep the team competitive.
The Vikings should look to improve their offensive line . Through six games, Minnesota has surrendered 18 sacks, and the linemen have been flagged for 18 penalties, including seven false starts and eight holding penalties.
Minnesota missed out on acquiring All-Pro guard Quenton Nelson. He was traded from the Indianapolis Colts to the Seattle Seahawks, but there will be other opportunities for the Purple and Gold to reinforce the offensive line.
A torn meniscus caused starting left guard Donovan Jackson to be placed on injured reserve, ending his season. Joe Huber has been filling in for him, but has been average at best, with a 59.5 Pro Football Focus grade . Huber has also been called for two false-start penalties in 201 offensive snaps played.
Starting right guard Will Fries has a run-blocking PFF grade of 64.3, but his pass-blocking grade of 48.7 leaves much to be desired. He has also been called for two holding penalties this year, adding to his pass-blocking struggles.
Minnesota needs to watch the trade block in case an interior offensive lineman becomes available who can help protect starting quarterback Kyler Murray. Here are a few guards who could be available before the trade deadline on Tuesday, Nov. 10:
There aren't many guards who have the potential to be shopped for a trade, so the Vikings may need to make some calls to see who is available. The best bet is to call franchises that might be looking to rebuild or acquire future assets since they are struggling to win games this season.
Nelson fetched a premium price for the Colts. The Seahawks gave Indianapolis a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick for the 30-year-old blocker. However, it isn't very often that a player who is an eight-time Pro Bowler, three-time first-team All-Pro and three-time second-team All-Pro becomes available.
The Vikings have a difficult schedule ahead of them. Minnesota's next four games are all against teams with winning records this season. The Purple and Gold should do whatever they can to give the team the best opportunity to continue winning games this season, and that includes trading for a starting guard.

title: Vikings Verdict: Judging J.J. McCarthy, RB Trade Targets & Other Overreactions Ahead of Week 8
full_text:
The Vikings are 6-0, but it hasn't stopped fans from casting doom up and down the roster . Despite the unblemished record, the play itself has often been lacking, and the team may need to make some dramatic changes sooner rather than later .
Is a blockbuster trade in the cards? Do the Vikings have a Justin Jefferson problem? Let's dive into those and more overreactions ahead of Week 8.
At 6-0, the Vikings could, and maybe should, be buyers at the upcoming trade deadline. And one position that makes a ton of sense is adding at running back. Jordan Mason and Aaron Jones Sr. are fine enough, but therein lies the issue.
Fine gets you some solid numbers, decent pass protection, and good reliability. What fine won't get you is a scared defense, explosive, game-changing plays, and someone to take over the game when and if Kyler Murray stumbles.
Trading for a top talent like Jonathan Taylor or Saquon Barkley, just to name a few, wouldn't come cheap, and the Vikings would have to dig deep into the stash of 2027 draft picks to acquire them. On the one hand, a second- or even first-round pick is a lot to give up for a veteran at a position that almost requires youth.
But on the other hand, when else will your team be 6-0 with a generational defense?
As the 32nd ranked team in offensive success rate, the Vikings offense is clearly still missing something. Getting better at running back won't solve everything, but there aren't many other feasible ways to improve this ailing offense by December.
After just two games, McCarthy really already has the media talking about how the Giants could be moving on from Jaxson Dart in favor of their newest signal caller. Truly. He's thrown for nearly 500 yards in just five quarters over the last two weeks for New York, and is either in some sort of brief flow state or the Vikings just let another franchise quarterback out the door.
It's truthfully way too early to have an opinion on McCarthy's future.
After all, his first career start against the Bears in 2025 saw him win Offensive Player of the Week, just to follow it up with two interceptions in a 22-6 beatdown against Atlanta the following week. His career sample size is still just too small. Still, at 23 and with obvious arm talent, the question of why the Vikings moved on so early and for so little in return is certainly an annoyance, at the very least.
McCarthy may not end up being the answer in New York either, but it's clear his ceiling is years away from being reached, and the Vikings bailing on their youngster so early is surely disappointing. It's hard to know what went on behind the scenes, but he probably should've gotten another stab at the starting job with Minnesota in 2027.
Jefferson is, and has been, known as one of the best receivers in the game, but the Vikings seem to be the last to know.
Despite all his talents, Jefferson is averaging just 6.2 targets per game, a far cry from the 11.1 or 11.5 numbers that other top players like Jaxson Smith-Njigba or Ceedee Lamb are seeing, respectively. Jefferson also has yet to eclipse 100 yards in a game this season, and even his 1,000-yard streak could very much be in danger if he misses another game or two.
Sure, the Vikings aren't airing the ball out 40 times per game, instead focusing on safe, smart, small-ball, but it's hard to forgive not targeting your best player. Clearly, other teams have figured out ways to scheme and then eventually throw to their top option. So what's the deal here?
It's possible that Murray and Jefferson are still working out chemistry issues, or that Jefferson still isn't 100% after spraining his ankle against Tampa Bay. Those are potentially valid, but for the most part, there's really no reason the Vikings shouldn't be looking Jefferson's way on nearly every dropback.
As great as it is to never turn the ball over by only throwing four-yard flat passes to tight ends and running backs, eventually the training wheels have to come off for a grown-up offense.

title: Rewarding Kyle Van Noy Should Be Among Vikings' Priorities After Week 7
full_text:
The Minnesota Vikings signed edge rusher Kyle Van Noy this offseason to take pressure off Andrew Van Ginkel and Dallas Turner. However, he has more than exceeded expectations in Brian Flores' defense and deserves to be rewarded for his play.
Despite being 35 years old and in his 13th year as a pro, Van Noy is tied for the most tackles for loss among all Vikings defenders. He is tied with inside linebacker Blake Cashman at 7.5 and is showing no signs of slowing down.
As soon as general manager Nolan Teasley is able, Minnesota should lock him down for one more season by signing him to an extension. Keeping him with the Purple and Gold ensures the Vikings' strong edge-rush presence at a low cost.
Van Noy is averaging 19.2 defensive snaps per game, which is approximately 32 percent of the Vikings' total defensive snaps this year. In that limited role, he has still recorded 12 tackles, two quarterback hits, and 1.5 sacks.
What makes the Van Noy signing this offseason even more impressive is that Minnesota brought the two-time Super Bowl champion and former Pro Bowl edge rusher in on a one-year, $2.75 million deal to play for the 2026 NFL season.
Getting the type of production that Van Noy is experiencing this season at that cost is a huge bargain. His excellent play hasn't gone unnoticed by Pro Football Focus , which have him rated as the ninth-best edge rusher in the league out of 112 qualifying players with a grade of 85.1.
Although he can get after opposing quarterbacks at a solid rate, his real strength this year has been defending against the run. He has a PFF run defense grade of 86.3, which is the fourth-best of any edge rusher this season.
There's no reason not to lock Van Noy down for another season. He, Van Ginkel, and Turner have formed a dangerous trio of edge rushers who should return for the 2027 season. Plus, rewarding Van Noy for his play this season with a pay increase or bonuses would go a long way toward showing the veteran defender how much his contributions to Minnesota's defense are appreciated.
If Van Noy wants to play next season, it should be with the Vikings. And the team needs to make bringing him back a priority.

title: Myles Price's Injury Could Open Door for One Vikings Letdown to Save His Roster Spot
full_text:
Against the Indianapolis Colts in Week 7, Minnesota Vikings wide receiver and return specialist Myles Price left the game and did not return. He took a big hit after catching a punt and was evaluated for a concussion.
Price has been an asset for the Vikings as a return specialist this season. In six games, he returned 18 kickoffs for 552 yards, and he leads the league with 250 punt return yards and a touchdown on 13 opportunities.
Price could be forced to miss time this season while going through concussion protocol in Minnesota. If that happens, the door could be open for a disappointing rookie to finally make an impact on the team this season.
Although wide receiver Tai Felton is listed as the backup return specialist on the Vikings' official website, that doesn't mean that dynamic rookie running back Demond Claiborne won't get an opportunity to showcase his return skills.
At Wake Forest, Claiborne returned 22 kickoffs for 579 yards and two touchdowns. His speed and elusiveness would make him a dangerous weapon on special teams to help win the field-position battle.
Claiborne doesn't have the same kind of experience on punt returns. In college, he fielded two punts, but did not record any return yardage. The only other player to return a punt for the Vikings in the last two years is Jeshaun Jones, who had only two returns for five yards in the 2025 season finale against the Green Bay Packers.
For Claiborne, something has to happen. The rookie running back was inactive in Week 7 against the Indianapolis Colts, while the team cut DeeJay Dallas, signed him to the practice squad, elevated him and played him for 20 total snaps between offense and special teams.
It feels like the Vikings are only keeping Claiborne on the 53-man roster out of fear of another team signing him if he is released to be signed to the practice squad. That roster spot seems to be held hostage at the moment, but finding a role for him as a kickoff return specialist would give him some value to the roster.
When one player goes down with an injury, others have to step up. In the case of Price's concussion, this is an opportunity for Claiborne to prove that the sixth-round draft pick in the 2026 NFL Draft can give the Vikings some production on the field.

title: Vikings Must Act Quickly If They Want to Trade for Colts' Jonathan Taylor
full_text:
As the Vikings continue to debate potential trade deadline plans , one potential partner has already put up their 'For Sale' sign.
The storefront is officially open in Indianapolis as the Colts' fire sale has begun . Indy made its first major trade Tuesday, sending star left guard Quenton Nelson to Seattle for a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick  (h/t: ESPN ’s Adam Schefter).
Compensation update; The Seahawks are sending a 2027 third-round pick and 2028 fifth-round round pick to the Colts in exchange for Quenton Nelson. https://t.co/17B0bR47yV
The move signals a shift in priorities for a 2-5 Colts team coming off a defeat in Minnesota. With no first-round selection after last year’s Sauce Gardner trade, Indianapolis seems desperate to acquire whatever draft capital it can, and contenders will likely be circling for the chance to add any available talent.
One man who needs to be in the mix? Vikings general manager Nolan Teasley.
His target? Three-time Pro Bowl running back Jonathan Taylor.
With the Colts opening up their phone lines, the time to act is now.
The Vikings’ offense desperately needs a boost as they enter the most challenging stretch of their schedule.
While the defense and special teams are performing at an elite level, the offense is becoming a serious concern (h/t: Warren Sharp). Short of a midseason change at quarterback , the best way to get the offense on track is an explosive RB, and no rumored target fits that bill quite like Taylor.
the Minnesota Vikings are only undefeated team left on early downs this season, their offense: #32 with 29% success rate #32 with 18% of plays gain a 1st down #32 with 24.0% of plays gain 7+ yards 62% of its series reach 3rd down #1 most in the NFL
According to Spotrac , Taylor is under contract for two more years, with cap hits of $21.02 million and $22.98 million in 2027 and 2028 , respectively.
Rumors have circulated about Taylor’s potential availability in recent weeks, and the Vikings have consistently been linked to a possible deal. Speculation only increased after Nelson was traded to Seattle, but one NFL insider seemed to pump the brakes .
NFL insider Adam Schefter joined "The Pat McAfee Show" Tuesday afternoon, stating, “My understanding is that the owner (Carlie Irsay-Gordon) doesn’t want to trade Jonathan Taylor.”
"My understanding is that the Colts don't wanna trade Jonathan Taylor.. If I had to guess today I don't think that they will trade Jonathan Taylor" ~ @AdamSchefter #PMSLive pic.twitter.com/LJ7WY63hAa
Personally, I interpret this to mean one thing: up those offers.
The Colts are clearly heading toward a rebuild, so why hold on to a 27-year-old back who likely won't be at his peak by the time they finally build a semi-competitive roster? To me, it’s a call to action to GMs everywhere to get aggressive. It’s time for Teasley and the Vikings to play ball.
The Vikings may be the last undefeated team in the NFL, but that won’t last much longer if their offense doesn't get on track. With a November schedule consisting of games against the Lions, Bills, Packers, 49ers and a feisty Falcons team, the Vikings need help, and they need it now.
Explosive plays have been nearly nonexistent in the Vikings’ running game over the last two seasons, and a trade for Taylor would immediately fix that. He's recorded runs of 20-plus yards in five of seven appearances so far, including a season-high 38-yard score against the Vikings.
Why are the Vikings interested in running backs at the deadline? Lack of explosive runs. Here are the longest runs of each season since Kevin O’Connell took over as coach in 2022: - 2022: Dalvin Cook, 81 yards - 2023: Ty Chandler, 31 yards - 2024: Cam Akers, 58 yards - 2025:…
Even with two weeks left until the NFL trade deadline, acting soon on a Taylor trade is the right move. It may come at a premium, but Teasley and the Vikings cannot afford to risk another NFC contender picking up the star back.

title: Potential Vikings Defensive Concern May Have Emerged Ahead of Week 8 vs. Lions
full_text:
It isn't a secret that the Vikings' defense has been stellar this year. Heading into Week 8's NFC North clash with the rival Lions, the Purple and Gold are allowing the second-fewest yards (252.8), second-fewest passing yards (155.0) and fewest points allowed per game (12.3).
That said, even the best units face obstacles.
Week 7's win over the Colts might have highlighted a potential concern for the Vikings' defense in the coming weeks. Superstar running back Jonathan Taylor had 18 rushing attempts for 95 yards and a touchdown in Week 7, an average of 5.3 yards per attempt. It was the second most rushing yards they've allowed to a running back this season, as well as the second time in the last three games an opposing RB has gone for 90-plus yards.
The list of running backs Minnesota will face in the next few weeks is intimidating and will test the Vikings' defense as they attempt to continue their winning ways this season. This gauntlet starts on Sunday in Detroit.
Given the upcoming schedule, the last thing that the Vikings need is to find out that star RBs are their defense's kryptonite.
Here is a list of the running backs the Vikings will face in the coming weeks:
That list of running backs is full of star players who can change the course of a game at a moment's notice. Even with McCaffrey dealing with a thigh issue, he is a player who needs to be accounted for every time he touches the ball. That's without mentioning that he leads the NFL in rushing touchdowns, while Robinson is the yardage leader on the ground.
The run defense has been the most questionable part of defensive coordinator Brian Flores's unit this season, but the Vikings still allow the tenth fewest rushing yards per game this season (97.8) and are bound to see that average increase after the next five weeks of opponents.
Minnesota is getting fantastic play from its defensive line this year. Jalen Redmond in particular has a Pro Football Focus grade of 81.7 , ranking him fourth among 126 qualifying defensive linemen. Another defender in the trenches who is playing well is Levi Drake Rodriguez, with a PFF grade of 62.2.
To this point, Taylor is the best running back the Vikings have faced this season, and he nearly broke 100 yards while finding the end zone on a 38-yard run. Minnesota will need to contain the opposing rushers over the next five weeks to prove its defense can compensate for an anemic offense against some of the top offenses in the league.
Their first test comes in the form of Gibbs and the Lions this weekend. The otherworldly RB has had success against the Vikings, converting 92 carries into 431 rushing yards and 18 catches into 121 receiving yards while scoring nine total TDs in six all-time matchups—including two 100-yard performances.
The Purple and Gold can't allow big runs against them if they hope to win the field-position battle against the explosive offenses coming up on the schedule. Stopping those superstar running backs needs to be the top priority if the Vikings hope to stay on top of the NFC North.
Otherwise, the Purple and Gold might have another need to address before the NFL trade deadline on Tuesday, Nov. 10.

title: 3 Areas the Patriots Need to Improve In Ahead of Week 8 vs. Dolphins
full_text:
FOXBORO — Sitting at 4-3 and second in the AFC East, the New England Patriots enter their Week 8 matchup against the 1-6 Miami Dolphins as seven-point favorites. However, this matchup presents more challenges than the initial eye test may suggest . Miami is fresh off its first win of the season, and despite their struggles, the Dolphins have a roster with plenty of young talent capable of making life difficult for New England. Running back Ollie Gordon is coming off his most productive outing as a pro, toting the rock 25 times for a career-high 103 yards and a touchdown. Quarterback Malik Willis also provides his own set of challenges. Drafted by the Mike Vrabel-led Tennessee Titans in 2022, Willis is a dual-threat QB who can hurt a defense with his legs.
Malik on the move! 🏃‍♂️ 📺 @NFLonCBS pic.twitter.com/fChyf2Ob5L
"They play extremely hard," Vrabel told the media at his Wednesday press conference. "I think that they've continued to improve, and I know that they're probably – and they should be – excited to play at home in front of their crowd. We'll have to go on the road inside the division here and continue to improve." While New England may be favorites on paper, they'll need to clean up several areas to ensure that when they head back to Foxboro, they do so with another tally in the "win" column.
The Patriots are coming off a Week 7 outing against the Chicago Bears in which they rushed 14 times for 70 yards, both season lows. Their 122 rushing yards per game ranks 11th in the NFL. However, a lack of consistency has led to stretches in which the Patriots struggle to establish the run, limiting their offensive potential.
Of course, New England's injury streak has significantly affected its offensive line. Guards Alijah Vera-Tucker, Mike Onwenu and Greg Van Roten have all been placed on injured reserve. The Patriots are now relying on Walter Rouse, Matt Pryor and Ben Brown, who is recovering from a knee injury sustained against the New York Jets. That's not to mention fullback Reggie Gilliam and wide receiver Mack Hollins, both of whom made noticeable contributions as run blockers before landing on IR. Hollins' absence has been particularly noticeable , as the Patriots' wide receiver corps has struggled to block downfield. That includes A.J. Brown, who drew criticism from fans after missing several blocks in the Week 7 loss to Chicago. “I won’t make any excuses,” Brown said when asked if his ankle had affected his ability in the run game. “I missed a couple of blocks. I’ll leave it at that.” If New England can get its ground game back on track, including finding ways to get the struggling TreVeyon Henderson going, it could provide a much-needed boost to the offense.
The Patriots, up to this point in the season, have failed to create big plays on returns, an area where they had success last year. That starts with Marcus Jones, who is coming off an All-Pro season in which he averaged 14.3 yards per punt return and scored two touchdowns. Through seven games in 2026, Jones is averaging 11.3 yards per return and has yet to record a return longer than 19 yards.
The kick return unit has also struggled to make an impact. According to FOX Sports, New England's kick returners are averaging 24.9 yards per return, ranking 25th in the NFL. Their longest return of the season is just 37 yards, good for 27th in the league. With the Patriots struggling to generate explosive plays on special teams, a change at kick returner may  be worth considering. Kyle Williams and Corey Kiner have primarily handled those duties, but Henderson could be an intriguing alternative. When asked about the possibility of giving Henderson opportunities as a kick returner, Vrabel didn't rule it out of the picture. "I think that that's probably something that we'll always consider and weigh the options," Vrabel said. "We'll focus here on Miami and what we feel like we need to do to be able to create some positive momentum in the return game, whether that's with Corey or Kyle, and then certainly take a look at anybody else."
In his rookie season, Henderson returned nine kickoffs for 209 yards, averaging 23.2 yards per return. And while preseason production doesn't always translate to regular-season success, Henderson returned a kick 100 yards for a touchdown in his first preseason game against the Washington Commanders in 2025.
THE FIRST TIME HE TOUCHED THE BALL IN THE NFL!!!! @TreVeyonH4 | @NFL 📺: WBZ pic.twitter.com/NcT2a635nx
If the Patriots want a change, Henderson could be an enticing option given his home run-hitting ability.
Missed tackles have been an issue for New England at times this season, and the problem peaked against the Bears. The Patriots missed 17 tackles against Chicago , a season high and a mark that is hard to overcome against any opponent. "The tackling wasn't good enough, not against this team," Vrabel said after the game. "I would say that we need to turn the ball over and tackle better, and those are fundamental skills."
Jones (six), Charles Woods (three) and Robert Spillane (two) were the Patriots' biggest offenders. Against a Miami offense coming off their most productive performance of the season, New England can't afford to give the Dolphins extra yards through poor tackling. The Patriots luckily don't need to overhaul their defensive approach, but they do need to execute the fundamentals more consistently.

title: Patriots Week 8 Injury Report: Great News Across the Board
full_text:
The New England Patriots returned to practice on Wednesday after a day off to continue game preparation for Week 8's match against the Miami Dolphins (1-5).
As the result of extended time from last Thursday's loss to Chicago, positive light has been shined on an injury riddled Patriots team — which is RotoWire's eighth-highest ranked team when it comes to injury impacts. On the first injury report of Week 8, the Patriots have their least amount of limited or non-participants since Week 1's opening practice.
Here's the report from Wednesday's practice:
Participation Level/Injury Designation
Participation Level/Injury Desgination
Three immediate pieces that standout on the injury report is the return of cornerbacks Carlton Davis, Channing Canada, and Karon Prunty. The three have each missed four games this season, leaving the cornerback room to rely on star Christian Gonzalez — who's also faced injury troubles this season — Marcus Jones, and Charles Woods.
With a fully healthy cornerback room, the Patriots secondary can begin to prohibit opponents' passing attacks (such as that of Luther Burden III and Omar Cooper Jr. in the past two games). Last year's Patriots' secondary, consisting of similar personnel to this year, was elite when fully healthy.
"I'm happy to be back out here and be a full go," said Davis ahead of Wednesday's practice.
The Patriots offensive line drills had Matt Pryor and Walter Rouse starting. The fifth and sixth options at guard made their debuts in the starting five last Thursday against the Bears. With Alijah Vera-Tucker on injured reserve and Ben Brown listed as questionable, at the moment, it seems the two will keep their position as the starting inside offensive linemen.
On the outside, Morgan Moses is listed as limited with a foot injury for the second week in a row. After sustaining the injury against the Jets, Moses activation against Chicago came as somewhat of a surprise, as the 35-year-old was able to play the entire game. Still listed as limited six days later, his status will be one to watch in the coming days.
The offensive line going through drills. Looks like the interior will have Walter Rouse (LG) and Matt Pryor (RG) again this week. pic.twitter.com/SdKdm4S47D
Another thing to note is Marcus Bryant's full participation on Wednesday. He's been out since the start of the season and is still on the injured reserve, though his IR activiation period is coming to a close soon — meaning the Patriots will have to decide whether they use one of their five remaining injured reserve activations for the season on Bryant.
Brown is listed with an ankle injury and was a limited participant in Wednesday's practice. His ankle injury is the same one he suffered in Week 1 against Seattle that landed him on injured reserve.
In the seven practice appearances since Brown's return to play, he's only been a full participant once (the Wednesday before the Bears' game where the Patriots held a walk-through).
While the Pats have been mindful of Brown's ankle, there could be more explanation to his limited status. Not only does it leave uncertainty for Miami's defense which is preparing for a dwindled receiver room that is likely to rely on Brown, but a lighter Wednesday practice leaves room for Brown to participate in most drills in a limited capacity.

title: Patriots Secondary Not Taking Dolphins WRs Lightly Ahead of Divisional Matchup
full_text:
FOXBORO — The New England Patriots are 4-3. The Miami Dolphins are 1-5. On paper (and on the football field), the Patriots should easily beat their division rivals in Week 8 on Sunday.
But this is not a Dolphins team that the Patriots are taking lightly. It's a team that's trending in the right direction, winning its first game of the season a week ago and has a quarterback in Malik Willis who can extend plays with his legs.
For Christian Gonzalez, he knows that while this offense might be powered by the running attack, the Dolphins have a crop of talened wideouts that they'll need to deal with.
"I think the receivers, they're young, but they're talented on the outside," Gonzalez said Wednesday. "They've shown a lot that they can go up, make plays, go downfield, make plays, catch the ball, make plays.
"So they got talent over there, and I mean, it's a division game, so we know what those mean. So it'll be (a) fun little matchup."
Through seven weeks, the Dolphins' wideouts aren't among the league leaders in many statistical categories. Malik Washington, who caught a touchdown in the matchup these teams had back in January, leads the team in receptions (26) and receiving yards (289). That group also has rookies Caleb Douglas and Chris Bell that get a good chunk of snaps.
Interestingly enough, to show you have little production this unit has put up, 26-year-old Ryan Miller is Miami's fifth-leading receiver with 92 yards. Right now, he's on the Patriots practice squad.
That's not a unit that most people would feel worried about. That doesn't mean Gonzalez — one of the NFL's best at his position — is taking them any differently than he would another group of pass catchers.
"They've shown they can make plays," he said. "I mean, Bell and Douglas, they look like they're good receivers. I mean, they're out there, they're in the NFL starting for their team. So, they have talent and it's a good challenge, especially when you haven't played them, you haven't seen them. So, I mean, we're looking forward to it as a secondary."
The Patriots should use this trip to Miami as a get-right game, a chance to rebound from their primetime loss to the Chicago Bears . While a secondary that's now getting Carlton Davis (neck) back into the fold will key in on the passing game, the defense will still be prepared to stop Willis and his scrambling ability.
"Looking at the stats, he's basically second on the team in rushing," Kindle Vildor told Patriots On SI. "That's a big part of their offense, so we got to make sure that everybody (is) following their keys."
This will be the first time that Mike Vrabel and these Patriots go up against this new-look Miami team, led by first-time head coach Jeff Hafley. The record might not reflect it, but the Patriots are not overlooking what could be a quick-hitting offense on Sunday.
"They create X plays, they're tough to tackle," Vrabel said. "They're doing a really good job of continuing to improve."

title: Patriots Should Pounce on Now-Available Colts WR (and Drake Maye's Former Teammate)
full_text:
As it stands right now, the New England Patriots have four healthy wide receivers on their active roster. Should they add another one ahead of the Nov. 10 trade deadline?
Well, according to a recent report from ESPN's Jeremy Fowler , one popular name should become available — and it's one that could be a perfect match for Drake Maye and the Patriots.
Fowler reported Wednesday that Indianapolis Colts wide receiver Josh Downs has requested a trade. Downs, who was drafted by the Colts in the third round back in 2023, spent two seasons with Maye at North Carolina in college.
The Colts' firesale — in which they've already traded away Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner — could end up seeing Downs get moved. The Patriots do have some wideouts on IR that may end up returning to the field ( Mack Hollins - calf , Romeo Doubs - shoulder), but adding a familiar face for Maye to the offense could help add another layer of big-play ability.
"I'm open to whatever," Downs told ESPN's Stephen Holder. "Whatever comes my way, comes my way and we go from there."
This season, Downs has 26 receptions for 307 yards and no touchdowns in a Colts offense that hasn't looked like it's clicked at all. Since his rookie season, the 25-year-old has 198 catches for 2,140 yards and 11 touchdowns.
The one year that Downs and Maye overlapped with the Tar Heels (2022), they connected for 94 catches, 1,029 yards and 11 touchdowns.
That connection could work for this offense. Right now, A.J. Brown (who hasn't looked like himself three games into his tenure), DeMario Douglas, Kyle Williams and Efton Chism III are on the 53-man roster. Kyle Dixon, Cameron Dorner, Cameron Brayboy and Ryan Miller are on the practice squad.
If Brown was to flip a switch and look like his usual self on the field , the Patriots might not feel pressured to swing a trade with the Colts. But if Brown's slow stretch continues (he did miss four games with a high-ankle sprain suffered in Week 1), they might feel inclined to get some new blood in the building.
Seven games in, the Patriots are sitting at 4-3 and have an offense that could compete for a Super Bowl title. Maye is — expectedly — carrying the load, even with some of his offensive weapons not being featured each and every week. Sometimes it's Douglas catching two touchdowns in a game, or maybe it's Chism grabbing a game-winner.
Downs might give the Patriots some more consistency at the position, especially when you factor in his multiple seasons of 700+ receiving yards.
With the Colts wilting away in the AFC standings and Downs' clear desire to be shipped off now public, the Patriots might not have to give up a lot for him. But the Patriots appear like they should somewhat buy and this could be a god first step.

title: Analyzing How Patriots' Trade Acquisitions Have Fared in 2026
full_text:
The NFL's trade deadline is two weeks away , and while the New England Patriots could end up making a move, I don't see them doing anything major. Maybe a depth piece here or there could help, but if you're expecting a big name — I wouldn't expect it.
Plus, the Patriots have already worked the trade phones quite a bit this season. Since the start of the 2026 calendar year, the Patriots have made six trades (not counting the ones they made during the draft) and brought in four players who have suited up this season.
We're seven games into the season, and the Patriots have gotten various results from their trade acquisitions. Here's a look at how they've done with the playing time they've gotten.
Brown was the biggest get for New England this offseason and it was one that felt like was obviously happening for a while. The Patriots sent a 2027 fifth round pick and a 2028 first round pick to the Philadelphia Eagles for Brown, who would instantly rise to the top of their wideout depth chart.
But it hasn't been that simple. After three receptions in the season opener, Brown suffered a high-ankle sprain and would be placed on IR. Since returning to the field in Week 6, he's caught just six passes for 75 yards and hasn't found the end zone yet.
His time will come and his lack of statistics hasn't been from a lack of talent. Brown will certainly break out of this funk and show why the Patriots paid a heavy price to get him.
The Patriots traded away fan favorite wide receiver Kayshon Boutte during the summer months, shipping him off to the Houston Texans. In return, the Texans sent second-year safety Jaylen Reed and a 2028 seventh round pick.
Through seven weeks, it doesn't feel like either side has come out on top so far. Reed has been more of a rotational player, racking up just nine tackles and one pass breakup on 116 defensive snaps. He's been mainly a special teamer on several units.
For the Texans, they haven't gotten a lot of production out of Boutte either. He's been stashed on the depth chart, and has caught just 15 passes. He's caught three passes in three separate games to this point in the year.
As the Patriots were trimming their roster to 53, they went out to bring in some external players. One of those was Kiner, a running back who was about to be released by the Arizona Cardinals . Instead of letting him hit waivers, the Patriots sent a 2028 seventh rounder for the second-year player.
Kiner has been the Patriots' third back this season, carrying the ball 35 times for 151 yards. Against the Raiders in Week 5, he had a fumble on his rush of the game. One week later, he followed that up with eight-straight carries to help milk a 26-19 win over the Jets .
Another player who came via a late August trade, Rouse was traded from the Minnesota Vikings for a 2028 seventh round selection. After being a healthy scratch for the first few games, Rouse switched from tackle to guard to help plug up some holes on a very injured offensive line.
Rouse came in because of injury in Weeks 3 and 6, and then made his first start of the season in Week 7 against the Bears at left guard. According to Pro Football Focus, he's allowed five pressures on 65 pass blocking snaps.

title: Patriots Host Feel-Good Halloween Costume Party for Pediatric Cancer Patients
full_text:
FOXBORO — For New England Patriots linebacker Benton Whitley, his Tuesday evening meant a little bit more. An off day from his time on the practice field, the 27-year-old — who grew up in Springfield and played his college ball at Holy Cross — traded in his pads for a Bullseye onesie.
He was one of 13 Patriots players who dressed up as Pixar characters for the team’s annual Halloween party for local pediatric cancer patients.
Nearly 40 children from Boston Children’s Hospital, Dana Farber Cancer Institute, Hasbro Children’s Hospital, Mass General Hospital and UMass Memorial Hospital made the trip for games, food and activities. A couple members of the MLS’s New England Revolution also came in costumes.
Whitley’s mother passed away in 2017 of cancer, so this event was extra important to him.
“This kind of hits close to home,” Whitley told Patriots On SI inside the Sports Illustrated Pavilion.
“I’m glad to do anything I can. … I feel like it just allows us to get out and meet some of the people who are supporting us in the stands, making our connection with the stadium and the community that much stronger.”
The Patriots entered the building set to cheers and a smoke machine. Some of them embraced the characters that they were dressed as. Linebacker Erick Hunter raised his fist proudly as Buzz Lightyear. Tight end Hunter Henry sped down the stairs like Lightning McQueen. Offensive tackle Walter Rouse, dressed as Russell from “Up,” had his own set of balloons.
Linebacker Robert Spillane , a father of two, came in his own Sully onesie and spoke about why he feels passionate about giving back.
“Young children who go through hardship, they deserve smiles,” Spillane told Patriots On SI. “They deserve opportunities to feel like kids. To go out there and just be a kid. And this is one of those nights where everyone’s dressed up, just having fun, enjoying the moment.”
The highlight of the day was when rookie tight end Tanner Arkin — dressed as Mr. Potato Head — faced off against a kid in Jenga. The game lasted for quite a while, drawing a massive crowd and cheers for both sides. Hunter grabbed the microphone to announce every move, and Rouse chimed in with some color commentary here and there.
Hunter might see himself with a future in broadcasting now.
“That wouldn’t be bad, I wouldn’t mind it,” Hunter told Patriots On SI. “I feel like I could do it. That was a good introduction right there.”
Whitley had some of his own tough battles, losing a game of cornhole.
“These kids are actually putting up a fight in the competition,” he laughed. “This is actually pretty cool.”
“This town ain't big enough for the two of us.” — Julian Ashby, probably pic.twitter.com/XMjdhpvrwr
Other players, like Julian Ashby , played checkers. Kids were also treated to decorating cookies, and designing tote bags and pumpkins. Players were happy to be stopped every which way for a picture or an autograph.
Between the white lines, the Patriots are sitting at 4-3 heading into a road Week 8 battle with the Miami Dolphins. But for one night a few days ahead of Halloween, the players were happy to make a difference off of the field.
“Seeing these kids come up to us with big smiles, realizing that we’re in costume, but we’re football players,” Spillane said. “That means something to them. Just seeing them smile today is what it’s all about.”
“New England is a special place,” Hunter said. “You can see why the way the organization is run is beautiful. It’s a beautiful place here.”
