title: The Path to Production for Young Patriots WR Kyle Williams
full_text:
FOXBORO - Kyle Williams has seen increased playing time as injuries pile up in the New England Patriots' wide receiver room. However, that uptick hasn't translated into consistent on-field production, as Williams has recorded just six catches for 147 yards and a score through seven weeks.
Williams, the 69th pick in the 2025 NFL draft, entered 2026 with high expectations after a rookie season that showcased his game-breaking speed and deep-ball ability.
His development was a major storyline during summer training camp, even with a crowded WR room, as Williams reached the end zone in all three preseason matchups.
Tommy DeVito threw a dime and Kyle Williams never broke stride 😤 PHIvsNE on @nflnetwork Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/hkdcirz8nJ
Now, with Romeo Doubs (shoulder) and Mack Hollins (calf) sidelined on injured reserve , the Patriots need production from their remaining receivers more than ever, which raises an important question: How can New England get Williams more involved?
Williams' ability to stretch the field is well established. With his 4.40-second speed, he has the tools to threaten defenses over the top and create explosive downfield plays. It's what has made him such an enticing target on the boundary.
And while Williams has struggled on comeback routes (0/2 with one interception when targeted on routes returning to the line of scrimmage), the next step in his development could be finding ways to utilize that speed over the middle of the field.
Incorporating more crossing routes in the short and intermediate passing game could give Williams more opportunities to use his speed in open space. Instead of consistently asking him to beat defensive backs downfield, the Patriots could create easier opportunities for him to get the ball in his hands and make plays after the catch.
According to Pro Football Focus, Williams has caught all three of his targets between the numbers for 67 yards, an encouraging return that suggests there could be room to expand his role in that area of the field.
Increasing his opportunities in the middle of the field would also play into Williams' offseason training, as the wideout emphasized improving his lower-body strength to handle physical coverage, get off the line of scrimmage, and become more comfortable working across the middle.
“Play strength was definitely something that I wanted to emphasize,” Williams told the media. “I knew that I needed to get my lower half stronger and bulk up a little bit, coming across the middle, getting off press and all that type of stuff. So that was one of my biggest emphasis, mobility and just putting on a little weight.”
The Patriots invested a third-round pick in Williams for a reason. As opportunities open up in the receiving corps, finding creative ways to use his skill set could be the key to turning his increased playing time into reliable, consistent production.

title: True or False: Debunking Narratives Surrounding the 4-3 Patriots
full_text:
With three on the season, the New England Patriots have already accumulated the same amount of losses through seven weeks than they had in 17 weeks last year.
This New England team has far more holes this year than they had last year, which has created headlines across local and national media outlets. Here are some common threads with an analysis on the truth to each narrative:
One of the biggest struggles for the Patriots this season has been navigating a carousel of wide receiver injuries. New England has struggled to keep their new-look receiver room on the field. The Patriots have only been fully healthy at receiver for three quarters of play in 2026 — which came in Week 1 against Seattle.
They've placed A.J. Brown, Mack Hollins, and Romeo Doubs on the injured reserve, which is not only half of the rostered receivers, but their top-three receivers. With Brown's return in Week 6, the Patriots are limited to four wide receivers.
However, they've been able to manage an efficient passing game with just four active receivers. Josh McDaniels has intentionally created plays to utilize other weapons on the field. In last week's loss to Chicago, running back Rhamondre Stevenson was the Patriots' leading receiver. Hunter Henry and Eli Raridon have hauled in three touchdowns combined over the past three weeks.
With Hollins able to be activated as soon as Week 9 vs. the Packers, and Doubs able to return one week after that, stability will hopefully find the Patriots' receiving room soon.
Last Thursday, the Patriots rolled out their fifth and sixth-string guards to protect Drake Maye against the Bears defense. With guard being certainly their most injured position, many have taken the Patriots as buyers for another guard at the trade deadline.
With Quenton Nelson heading from Indianapolis to Seattle, the guard market is shaken up. While the Patriots will most likely show interest, acquiring a guard isn't a neccessity for this team.
The first reason in opposition of a trade is the likelihood that Ben Brown and Alijah Vera-Tucker return to play soon. Brown is still on the active roster after dealing with a knee injury, and Vera-Tucker can be activated in Week 12.
A larger reason to have faith in the offensive line is the dominance of both tackle positions. Will Campbell and Morgan Moses have provided elite protection for Maye. Additionally, Maye's strength in navigating the pocket comes from pressure up the middle. So long as the outside of the line is secure, pressure applied on Maye won't be an issue.
Second year running back TreVeyon Henderson has not started his sophomore season as excitingly he did his rookie year. Last year's leading rusher for New England has nearly a third less carries than Stevenson on the year, and saw half the amount of touches than his counterpart against Chicago.
In life, I struggle, I suffer, I’m tempted, I’m tested, sometimes I feel so weak. But when I am weak, I am strong. Because Christ, He is my hope, He is my strength, He is a firm foundation that never fails. Jesus is worthy of it all. May He be glorified always, not just on the… pic.twitter.com/uVWp8f8I6a
While Henderson has been the recepient of much criticism online, there are some caviats that factor into his on-field production. The Ohio State alum entered this season with an ankle injury suffered in training camp. In Week 6 against the Jets, Henderson sustained a new injury to the same ankle . The high ankle sprain that would usually land players on the injured reserve, didn't cause Henderson to miss anytime.
Considering his ability to play through the injury, his perfomance has certainly been impacted by it. Henderson is also the product of an offense that needs extra pass protection (see previous point) and Stevenson is better equipped to fill that need. The Patriots are still confident in their second-round pick from a year ago, and his 3.9 yards per carry, which are more than Stevenson, suggest that he'll remain an essential part of this offense.
New England's injury troubles have identified this team as one to utilize the trade deadline. They've had delve deep into their depth chart and practice squad to field a team in some weeks.
If the Colts are having a fire sale, Grover Stewart is the player I’m most interested in.
The trade deadline provides an opportunity for the Patriots to not be so reliant on their depth, and have temporary solutions to their holes. More specifically, New England could look at acquiring a linemen, cornerback, or linebacker.
However, if Mike Vrabel and Eliot Wolf choose to make a move, it will be for a temporary solution that addresses the teams depth. This means, fans shouldn't expect a big deal to be done with top trade deadline targets (such as RB Jonathan Taylor - IND, WR Quentin Johnston - LAC, or LB Nolan Smith - PHI).
The Patriots are a team that is still building their core. Draft picks are still a very essential resource for this young squad (especially considering the value they gave up for A.J. Brown). Unlike other high expectation teams like the Los Angeles Rams, the Patriots aren't in win-now mode, and don't have to overreact to three losses.
This current roster, while depleted, has shown that it compete with the best teams in the NFL.
Right now, the Patriots sit in second place in the AFC East, two wins behind the Buffalo Bills (5-1). In their Week 4 meeting, the Patriots got a leg up on the Bills, beating them in Buffalo, but Week 7's setback loss could put winning the division in jeopardy.
We certainly can't assume that Week 7 is the last loss the Patriots will take all season, but looking at Buffalo's remaining schedule, there are a lot of games that could go unfavorably for the Bills. Buffalo will travel to Minnesota (6-0), Denver (5-2), and Green Bay (4-3) and have to host Baltimore (4-3), Chicago (5-2) and Kansas City (5-1).
Noting that the Patriots and Bills are common opponents with each of these teams except for Baltimore, these six games could determine the AFC East. But none will be more influential than Week 13's game in Foxboro.
With New England having an easier strength of schedule remaining than the Bills , contention for a second straight AFC East title is more than possible.

title: Patriots Trade Deadline Tracker: Every Rumor for New England with 2 Weeks to Go
full_text:
The NFL's trade deadline was pushed back a week this year, so the New England Patriots and 31 other teams will have until Nov. 10 to try and get deals done this season.
The Patriots , currently sitting at 4-3 and in second place in the AFC East, could end up being active on the market. Injuries across the board and potential depth issues at other places could led Eliot Wolf and Mike Vrabel to try and improve the team somehow, someway.
Aleady in this calendar year, the Patriots have made a few trades. Back in March, they shipped away Garrett Bradbury and Marte Mapu before acquiring A.J. Brown in a block buster deal with the Philadelphia Eagles three months later. During the summer, Kayshon Boutte was dealth to the Houston Texans and during roster cuts, the Patriots also sent draft picks for Corey Kiner and Walter Rouse.
So could they end up making a deal mid-season? Here's all the rumors, quotes and storylines that are surrounding the Patriots as the trade deadline looms.
Could the Patriots — the team with Mack Hollins and Romeo Doubs on injured reserve — end up adding a wideout? ESPN reported that Indianapolis Colts wideout Josh Downs requested a trade after a pair of his teammates were shipped away on Tuesday.
Downs spent two seasons with Drake Maye at North Carolina, scoring a career-high 11 touchdowns during the 2022 season. The Patriots only have four healthy wide receivers on the active roster right now, but adding Downs for what could be a cheap deal might help elevate the passing attack.
Seven games in, Downs has 26 receptions for 307 yards.
A few days after the Patriots' 30-24 loss to the Chicago Bears , Vrabel spoke with reporters about how the team is stacking up prior to their Week 8 game with the Miami Dolphins. One of the questions posed was about if the Patriots will be active on the phones.
His answer left the door open for a deal being made, but the head coach also didn't officially dig a potential move into the sand. Like most coach-speak, Vrabel discussed how the Patriots would make moves to try and improve the overall roster in totality, and not try to single out a certain spot that needs upgrading.
"We're going to try to do everything we can to help the team," Vrabel said. "I don't know if we will or we won't. I would imagine that we'll try to do everything that we can to help us, within reason, and makes sense for us. I don't know how you want to interpret that, but I'm sure we'll listen and talk, just like everybody else does."
Some positions that the Patriots could end up attacking are running back, offensive guard (with a myriad of injuries hitting that group), interior defensive line and some backup cornerbacks.

title: Veteran OG Eligible to Return Off IR — Do Patriots Activate Him This Week?
full_text:
FOXBORO — Could the New England Patriots end up getting some help back this week against the Miami Dolphins? It's not out of the realm of possibilities.
Offensive guard Greg Van Roten , who has been on injured reserve for the last four game with a thigh injury, is eligible to return to the active roster this week. Speaking to reporters Monday afternoon, Mike Vrabel shared that the team has considered making that transaction this week.
"Probably won't see him today, but maybe this week, we'll see where that goes" the head coach said prior to practice. "I think him and (safety) Dell (Pettus) are eligible potentially to try and get back out there and kind of see where that goes, but we'll have to make a decision."
Van Roten is one of several offensive linemen who's gotten banged up this season. After Mike Onwenu broke his ankle in Week 2 against the Pittsburgh Steelers, Van Roten stepped in to help fill that hole at right guard. He would practice as the starter all week in practice and start against the Jacksonville Jaguars the following game.
But Van Roten would get hurt in that game and be ruled out. He'd be replaced by converted tackle Walter Rouse, and was placed on IR two days later.
The Patriots have also seen Alijah Vera-Tucker (hamstring) and Ben Brown (knee) get hurt in subsequent weeks. Last week against the Chicago Bears, the Patriots rolled with Rouse and Matt Pryor as their starting guards.
"I think the protection, I mean, I’m sure it could have been better. We just had some critical penalties," Vrabel said postgame. "Being able to handle the environment, third-and-short, whatever it may have been, and those are certainly unfortunate. That’s just beating ourselves. But I think I mean, I’m sure they played okay. I’m sure they played hard. Just without seeing it though it’s hard to say. But I know they competed."
Pryor has experience all over the offensive line and could earn a larger role if Van Roten doesn't return.
"Matt's done a nice job," Vrabel saaid. "Matt's come in, he's protected well. I think that he's still getting comfortable, but he's ... tough to get around. He's got heavy hands and he gives us a chance most of the time."
The Patriots could end up getting Brown back this week, as he suited up for practice as reporters were in the locker room. Should Van Roten return, he'll have three weeks to be activated to the 53-man roster or his season is over.
The Patriots will be back on the practice field in two days, which will be another opportunity for them to make a decision on the veteran guard. They also have one more week to make a decision on tackle Marcus Bryant, who's been designated to return off of IR with an ankle injury .

title: The Good, Bad and Ugly From Saints' 16-10 Loss to Steelers in Paris
full_text:
Hoping to build momentum ahead of their upcoming bye week after a major victory last week, the New Orleans Saints instead fell 16-10 to the Pittsburgh Steelers on Sunday in Paris, exposing several recurring issues under coach Kellen Moore .
New Orleans' offensive struggles continued as missed scoring opportunities proved costly as the Saints fell to 2-5.
From an emerging young playmaker to a disastrous rushing performance, here is a look at the good, the bad and the ugly from the Saints' disappointing loss to Pittsburgh .
One of the few bright spots in New Orleans' disappointing loss was rookie wide receiver Barion Brown's emergence.
The sixth-round pick got a chance to show his explosiveness, finishing with three receptions for 57 yards and adding another 97 yards on four kickoff returns.
His biggest offensive play came in the first half when he caught a 49-yard pass from Tyler Shough , setting up Daniel Carlson 's 38-yard field goal.
Brown also returned a kickoff 42 yards in the second quarter, setting up a possession that ended with Shough's 1-yard touchdown pass to Devaughn Vele .
Despite those contributions, Brown received just three targets.
That limited involvement raises questions about whether coach Kellen Moore is maximizing one of the offense's most explosive young playmakers.
With rookie Jordyn Tyson still sidelined by a hamstring injury, Brown has a chance to become a more consistent contributor alongside Chris Olave and Vele.
New Orleans gets a vital jolt on offense from Brown's explosive speed and big-play dynamism.
Following a sluggish 281-yard performance against Pittsburgh, integrating him must become a top priority for the Saints. To fully leverage the rookie's skill set, Moore ought to scheme designed touches, vertical routes and run-after-catch opportunities for him. Given how much he has delivered on minimal opportunities, Brown has earned a larger role.
In a narrow 16-10 loss to Pittsburgh, kicker Daniel Carlson missed a crucial 52-yard field goal in the fourth quarter — his fourth failure in 11 attempts this season. This ongoing volatility in special teams poses a critical problem for the 2-5 Saints.
The fourth-quarter miss was particularly damaging because New Orleans had already wasted a promising red-zone opportunity earlier in the second half. Rather than positioning themselves to tie or take the lead with a field goal late in the game, the Saints remained trapped in a six-point deficit.
Carlson's 63.6% conversion rate stands in sharp contrast to Steelers kicker Chris Boswell , who accounted for nine points by flawlessly making all three of his field goals (from 28, 47 and 39 yards).
With three one-score defeats recorded this year, New Orleans simply lacks the margin for error to withstand repeated scoring blunders in tight contests. Carlson's continuous field goal woes add to head coach Kellen Moore's list of bye-week priorities, as unreliable special teams only exacerbate the team's offensive stalls, defensive breakdowns and turnovers.
While much of the focus has centered on Tyler Shough's growth, an inept rushing attack still severely limits the Saints' offensive ceiling.
Sunday's outing represented a new low point for the ground game.
New Orleans generated a paltry 18 rushing yards across 17 carries, resulting in an abysmal 1.1 yards per carry.
The stat line is even more damning because Shough — a quarterback whose primary role isn't to lead the run game — was the team's top rusher with just 7 yards on three carries.
It is downright appalling that primary backs Alvin Kamara (six carries, five yards) and Kendre Miller (eight carries, six yards) both logged more rush attempts than total yards gained.
This embarrassing output highlights a backfield without a true lead option, further compounded by an offensive line that failed to establish leverage up front.
Such complete non-production is intolerable at any level of football—especially when relying on a developing quarterback to sustain drive after drive.
By stifling the run, Pittsburgh's defense put the burden entirely on Shough's shoulders.
Even with Shough connecting on nearly 79% of his passes, New Orleans repeatedly stalled because it lacked offensive balance.
Unfortunately, this isn't merely a single bad afternoon.
The Saints' season-long inability to establish the run has made the offense predictable and easy for physical front sevens to counter.

title: 3 Takeaways From Saints' Loss to Steelers: Same Problems, Different Country
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints traveled across the Atlantic Ocean hoping to build momentum heading into their bye week and salvage their season. Instead, they returned home with its fourth loss in five games and it just seems like another repeating nightmare for Who Dat Nation.
New Orleans fell 16-10 to the Pittsburgh Steelers on Sunday at Stade de France in Paris, dropping to 2-5 through seven games under second-year coach Kellen Moore . It was the NFL's first regular-season game in France.
Despite another efficient passing performance from quarterback Tyler Shough , the Saints struggled to establish their rushing attack, failed to capitalize on scoring opportunities and couldn't get off the field defensively when it mattered most.
The loss marked New Orleans' third one-possession defeat this season, reinforcing concerns about the team's ability to execute in critical situations.
Here are three takeaways from another disappointing performance from the Saints performance.
For all the attention surrounding Shough's development, New Orleans' inability to run the football continues to undermine its offense.
Sunday's performance might have been its most concerning yet.
The Saints finished with just 18 rushing yards on 17 attempts, averaging a dismal 1.1 yards per carry.
Even more alarming, Shough led the team with 7 rushing yards on three attempts. However, he is a quarterback and that is not his job.
But for Alvin Kamara (six carries for five yards) and Kendre Miller (eight carries for six yards) to have more carries than rushing yards is disgusting.
It shows the lack of life in a running back room without a primary option, compounded by an offensive line struggling to create leverage.
That level of production is unacceptable for any offense regardless of the level of play, especially one relying on a young quarterback to consistently move the ball.
Pittsburgh's defense shut down the run, forcing Shough to carry nearly the entire offensive load.
Although Shough completed nearly 79% of his passes, New Orleans could not consistently finish drives because it lacked balance.
The problems extend beyond one disappointing performance.
New Orleans has struggled to generate consistent production on the ground throughout the season, making the offense increasingly predictable against physical defensive fronts.
Because of the rushing problems, the Saints had to rely on Shough again.
Shough did everything you could ask of him, completing 30 of 38 passes for 278 yards and a touchdown. However, one costly mistake ultimately changed the game's complexion.
Trailing 13-10 at the start of the second half, New Orleans put together a 13-play drive that moved the offense inside Pittsburgh's 10-yard line as the Saints appeared positioned to take their first lead of the afternoon.
Instead, Shough threw a pass intended for Chris Olave , which Steelers linebacker Payton Wilson intercepted at the Pittsburgh 11-yard line.
The turnover erased a scoring opportunity and let Pittsburgh respond with a field goal, extending its lead to 16-10.
The interception proved costly, but it also highlighted the impossible position Shough has found himself in because of New Orleans' offensive struggles.
Despite completing nearly 79% of his passes, the quarterback could not afford even one mistake because the Saints had virtually no rushing attack to complement him.
That is an unrealistic expectation for any quarterback, much less one still developing at the NFL level.
Shough showed he could move the football against a Pittsburgh defense, distributing the ball effectively and keeping New Orleans competitive despite a one-dimensional offensive approach.
However, his play reinforced a troubling reality: when Shough plays well, the Saints can win; when he makes one mistake, the operation unravels.
Until Moore builds a credible run game and finishes drives, Shough bears an unreasonable load and New Orleans must create an offense where its quarterback does not need to be perfect to win.
Unless the Saints give Shough a credible rushing attack and adequate protection, they risk repeating a familiar chapter in franchise history: asking a talented young quarterback to overcome problems far beyond his control, much like Archie Manning decades ago.
Daniel Carlson 's fourth missed field goal in 11 attempts this season — a 52-yarder in the fourth quarter — kept New Orleans trailing in a 16-10 loss to Pittsburgh, highlighting a critical special teams weakness for the 2-5 Saints.
The missed 52-yard attempt came while the Saints trailed 16-10 in the fourth quarter, keeping Pittsburgh's lead at six points. Carlson's 63.6% success rate contrasts with Steelers kicker Chris Boswell , who converted all three attempts (28, 47 and 39 yards) for nine points.
The fourth-quarter miss was especially costly as New Orleans had already squandered a promising red-zone drive earlier in the second half. Instead of entering the final minutes needing only a field goal to tie or lead, the Saints remained six points behind.
Carlson's kicking struggles add to head coach Kellen Moore's bye-week concerns. For a team hampered by offensive inefficiency, defensive lapses and turnovers, unreliable special teams further shrink a narrow margin for error.
With three one-score losses this season, New Orleans cannot afford missed points. Sunday's loss highlights that the Saints lack the margin for error to overcome recurring scoring mistakes in tight games.

title: Saints Fans Should Know These 3 Things About the Steelers Before Sunday
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints (2-4) enter Sunday's historic matchup against the Pittsburgh Steelers (4-2) at Stade de France, looking to build momentum after their 34-27 win over the New York Giants .
However, Pittsburgh presents a considerably different challenge.
Under first-year coach Mike McCarthy , the Steelers have established themselves as a competitive AFC North contender, winning four of their first six games despite an offense that has struggled to consistently produce explosive plays.
Pittsburgh enters Sunday's contest averaging 22.8 points and 320.5 yards per game, ranking 18th and 21st in the NFL, respectively. However, its defense has been considerably more effective, allowing 307.5 yards per game, the ninth-fewest in the league.
For Saints coach Kellen Moore , Sunday's matchup offers a chance to secure consecutive wins for the first time this season before the team's Week 8 bye.
Here are three things Saints fans should know about the Steelers.
While 42-year-old Aaron Rodgers continues to anchor Pittsburgh's offense with his elite ability to read defenses and capitalize on errors, the Steelers' aerial game has produced fairly modest results.
Across six games, Rodgers has completed 61.4% of his pass attempts for 1,487 yards, throwing 12 touchdowns against five interceptions.
Despite these respectable individual metrics, Pittsburgh ranks just 18th in the league through the air, averaging 221.3 passing yards per contest.
Physical wide receiver DK Metcalf gives Rodgers a dependable downfield threat capable of winning contested balls and creating opportunities on intermediate routes.
However, Rodgers' statistical split against specific zone schemes presents a critical storyline for this matchup.
NFL Next Gen Stats reveals that Rodgers has struggled against Cover 3, registering a 32.9% success rate—the third-lowest figure among qualified quarterbacks—compared to a 52.9% success rate against all other zone schemes.
This dynamic is especially relevant given that New Orleans deploys Cover 3 on 55.9% of defensive dropbacks, leading the entire NFL.
Consequently, defensive coordinator Brandon Staley must balance disciplined zone coverage with an effective pass rush to contain Pittsburgh's passing attack.
While Rodgers draws significant focus, the Steelers' ground attack could pose a greater threat to New Orleans.
Running back Jaylen Warren has rushed for 460 yards on 84 carries, averaging 5.5 yards per attempt.
His ability to gain yards after contact, identify lanes and contribute in the passing game gives Pittsburgh multiple offensive options.
That creates a difficult matchup for New Orleans.
The Saints allow 138 rushing yards per game, ranking 30th in the NFL, while Pittsburgh averages 99.2 rushing yards per game, ranking 20th.
Despite Pittsburgh's modest team average, Warren's efficiency indicates the Steelers can exploit the Saints' run defense.
While returning veteran linebacker Kaden Elliss should bolster the Saints' run defense, containing Warren remains a critical priority. Allowing Pittsburgh to establish its ground game early will open up play-action opportunities for Rodgers.
While Pittsburgh's offense has experienced inconsistencies, its defense remains the team's most reliable strength.
The Steelers enter Sunday's matchup allowing 21.3 points and 307.5 yards per game, ranking 12th and ninth in the NFL, respectively.
A key part of its defense has been its ability to defend the pass as the Steelers have surrendered just 204.3 yards per game, the eighth-fewest in the league.
Pittsburgh has also recorded 16 sacks and six interceptions through six games, contributing to a plus-three turnover differential.
Outside linebacker T.J. Watt , who has a team-high 4.5 sacks, remains one of the league's most disruptive defensive players.
Alex Highsmith provides another formidable presence on the edge, while veteran defensive tackle Cameron Heyward anchors the interior.
The Steelers also one of the league’s top cornerbacks, eight-time Pro Bowler Jalen Ramsey , giving their secondary an experienced playmaker who can create turnovers.
For Saints quarterback Tyler Shough , protecting the football will be especially important.
Shough has thrown for 1,443 yards, 12 touchdowns and five interceptions this season, but his performance against zone coverage presents a potential concern.
According to Next Gen Stats , Shough has thrown five interceptions against zone coverage this season, tied for the second-most among qualified quarterbacks.
Pittsburgh has utilized zone coverage on 82.8% of opposing dropbacks, with five of its six interceptions occurring against zone concepts.
This creates a compelling schematic test between Moore's offense and Pittsburgh's defense.
If Pittsburgh generates pressure without compromising coverage, Shough may struggle against an opportunistic unit. To build on last week's win, New Orleans will need to establish the run, avoid clear passing downs, and minimize turnovers.

title: Saints vs. Steelers: Injury Concerns Mount Ahead of Historic Paris Showdown
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints face several injury concerns as they prepare for Sunday's historic international matchup against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Stade de France in Paris.
Running back Alvin Kamara and starting offensive guard Cesar Ruiz headline New Orleans' injury report, while Pittsburgh is monitoring several key defensive players, including T.J. Watt, Alex Highsmith and Jalen Ramsey.
According to the Saints' official Thursday injury report , 11 New Orleans players were listed Thursday, with three missing practice and three participating on a limited basis.
The Saints (2-4) are looking to build momentum following Sunday's 34-27 victory over the New York Giants, which snapped a three-game losing streak. Meanwhile, Pittsburgh (4-2) enters the matchup seeking its second consecutive victory.
Both teams have several injury situations worth monitoring before Friday's final practice report.
The Saints' biggest offensive concerns involve Kamara and Ruiz, who have been dealing with back and knee injuries, respectively.
Kamara was limited for the second consecutive practice Thursday, leaving his availability worth monitoring heading into Sunday's game.
The veteran running back remains an important part of Kellen Moore's offense, particularly as New Orleans attempts to establish a more consistent rushing attack.
Ruiz's situation is potentially more concerning. The veteran offensive lineman missed practice Wednesday and Thursday because of a knee injury, raising questions about his availability against Pittsburgh's defensive front.
However, Jeremiah Wright played well in his absence during New Orleans’ win over the Giants last week.
Meanwhile, linebacker Kaden Elliss (calf) and edge rusher Anfernee Jennings (knee) were limited for the second consecutive day. During today's player roundtable , Elliss was asked if he would be available to play Sunday, and he said, "Yes."
There was some encouraging news for New Orleans.
Shough, who appeared on the report with a left-hand injury, participated fully in both practices. Cornerback Kool-Aid McKinstry (head) and defensive lineman Nathan Shepherd (illness) also practiced without limitations.
Running back CJ Donaldson (shoulder) improved from limited participation Wednesday to a full practice Thursday.
Kicker Daniel Carlson missed his second consecutive practice because of a personal matter unrelated to injury (he and his wife are having a baby), while defensive lineman Davon Godchaux received a rest day Thursday.
Backup quarterback Spencer Rattler was added to Thursday's report with a knee injury but participated fully.
Pittsburgh is also dealing with significant injury concerns, particularly on defense.
The most notable development Thursday was star edge rusher T.J. Watt, who was limited with a calf injury after sitting out Wednesday's practice for rest.
Watt's status matters, given the Saints' offensive line concerns. The former NFL Defensive Player of the Year has 4.5 sacks through six games.
Fellow pass rusher Alex Highsmith remained limited with a groin injury, while veteran defensive tackle Cameron Heyward missed his second straight practice for rest.
The Steelers also received encouraging news about star cornerback Jalen Ramsey, who returned to practice on Thursday, albeit in a limited capacity. He missed Wednesday's session with a wrist injury.

title: Saints Stock Up: 3 Heroes From New Orleans' Win Over Giants
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints earned a much-needed victory over the New York Giants as they broke a three-game losing streak.
Now, the Saints are in Paris as they turn their attention to the Pittsburgh Steelers to win consecutive games for the first time this season. However, it will be a tough task: Pittsburgh still has a solid quarterback in Aaron Rodgers at 42, and the offense has plenty of weapons; on defense, they have a solid pass rush.
After fully reviewing the Saints’ win over New York and looking at which players have been trending upward, here are three players whose stock is rising.
The Saints historically produce standout special teams performers, including Morten Andersen , Michael Lewis , and Steve Gleason .
Linebacker Isaiah Stalbird has continued that tradition this year, keying special teams unit success and executing the decisive sequence of the game.
Down 10-3 late in the second quarter, New Orleans seemed poised for a halftime deficit before Stalbird made a game-altering play on coverage.
The second-year backer stripped the ball from Charlie Jones on a kickoff return, which tight end Oscar Delp recovered to set up New Orleans inside the red zone.
Shough converted the takeaway into points, finding rookie Bryce Lance for a game-tying touchdown right before the break.
That turnover shifted game momentum entirely and helped spark a 31-point unanswered run that gave New Orleans a 34-10 lead before the Giants mounted a furious fourth-quarter comeback.
Cornerback Martin Emerson Jr. posted his top outing of the year in the 34-27 victory, accumulating seven tackles, two interceptions, and four pass breakups.
His effort earned an 88.4 defensive rating and a 90.2 coverage rating from Pro Football Focus, leading all team defenders in Week 6. Emerson was named NFC Defensive Player of the Week for his efforts.
Emerson held opponents to four catches on 10 targeted passes while picking off throws from Jameis Winston and J.J. McCarthy . The performance provided valuable depth after Kool-Aid McKinstry exited due to a migraine.
Rookie guard Jeremiah Wright capitalized on unexpected playing time against New York, filling in when starter Cesar Ruiz left with a knee injury in the second quarter.
If one thing is certain, the run game started to click when Wright went into the game as he added toughness to the interior line, anchoring a run game that piled up a season-best 175 yards. If you want to know how much of an impact Wright had? When the Saints ran to the right, they averaged just over 5 yards per carry. When they ran to the left? 3.1-yards a clip.
The fourth-round selection surrendered just a single QB pressure in his most extensive action of the season.

title: Five Potential Trade Targets for the New York Giants
full_text:
The New York Giants are “in it to win it.”
Through the first seven weeks of the season, Big Blue has driven its way to a 4-2-1 record and sole possession of first place in the NFC East for the first time since 2015.
Though few may have expected such a rapid turnaround, coach John Harbaugh and his staff have helped cultivate a team that is (for the most part) playing opportunistic, fundamentally sound football.
In fact, Harbaugh all but confirmed that the team plans to keep the pedal to the metal after New York’s impressive 27-21 overtime victory over the Houston Texans.
“Now, you've got to make something of it. It doesn't mean anything if you don't build on it,” Harbaugh said.
“It doesn't mean we're going to win a championship yet. But it means we have an opportunity, though. We're going to be in this thing until the end now.”
Still, the Giants know where they need to improve. They'll use the current bye week to fine-tune their on-field planning and execution, and they will also be diligent in upgrading their personnel by the Nov. 10 NFL trade deadline .
Beyond their biggest need at defensive tackle, the team is expected to fortify its depth at running back and along the offensive line.
With that in mind, here are five players the Giants may look to acquire via trade in the coming days.
Given their need for a physical interior run defender, Tomlinson would make a great deal of sense for Big Blue. The 10-year veteran originally entered the NFL as a second-round selection by the Giants in the 2017 NFL Draft. He spent four seasons in New York, starting all 64 games in which he played.
The 32-year-old signed a one-year, $7.5 million contract with the Chargers this offseason, but he has failed to work his way into the Bolts’ starting lineup. Tomlinson has compiled eight total tackles, 0.5 sacks, and one run stuff in four appearances for Los Angeles while backing up starter Jamaree Caldwell.
If moved, the veteran defender would leave the Chargers with no dead money, while costing the Giants just north of $150,000 per week.
Perhaps a second tour of duty in East Rutherford, under defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson, could spark an on-field renaissance for Tomlinson while addressing Big Blue’s need at interior defensive line.
With two-time All-Pro DeForest Buckner headed back to the San Francisco 49ers, the Colts have all but confirmed their plans to rebuild. Though Buckner may have arguably been the more intriguing option, Stewart could also help fill New York’s need.
Through seven games this season, Stewart has logged 22 tackles, 0.5 sacks, and one pass-breakup. Last season in 17 games played, the 33-year-old tackle racked up 55 tackles, 0.5 sacks, a forced fumble, an interception, and four passes defended.
Trading Stewart would give the Colts approximately $12.3 million in cap savings — a valuable windfall for a team looking to spend this offseason. For the Giants, the 6-foot-5, 295-pound nose tackle could provide a massive upgrade to a run defense which currently ranks 25th in the NFL.
Although intra-divisional trades are rare in the NFL, the Commanders may be enticed to move on from their Pro Bowl defensive tackle for the right offer.
At 1-4-1, Washington is falling fast in both the division and conference standings. With Payne in the final year of his contract, the club is reportedly listening to offers.
Payne’s $16.4 million salary may deter some teams, but New York can take on a rental who knows the NFC East well. Despite his declining pass-rush ability, the 6-foot-3, 320-pound lineman is still an effective run defender.
In six games this season, Payne has seven total tackles, five quarterback hits, two tackles for loss, two run stuffs, and one forced fumble. His divisional knowledge and on-field experience could be a valuable asset to a young team making a playoff push.
Even if their focus remains on upgrading their defensive front, the Giants may still be in the market for a veteran running back to bolster their newly resurrected run game.
Before arriving in Tennessee in 2024, Pollard spent five seasons running the ball for the Dallas Cowboys. His elusiveness in the open field, combined with his abilities as a backfield receiver, makes him a provocative target — even at age 29.
This season, the Pro Bowl back has rushed for 478 yards on 112 carries (4.3 yards per attempt) with four touchdowns. He has also caught 11 passes for 50 yards. Being in the final year of his deal, the Titans may look to move his $6.7 million base salary for the right price.
If Tyrone Tracy Jr.’s hamstring keeps him out longer than the minimum four games he’s required to spend on IR, Pollard could help strengthen New York’s running back corps, which includes Cam Skattebo, Devin Singletary, the newly acquired Greg DeRosiers, and practice squad rusher Phil Mafah.
Despite its roller-coaster journey this season, the Giants’ offensive line has performed well. Though their play hasn't been perfect, they've done their jobs well in both pass protection and run blocking. Still, the Giants may be wise to keep a close eye on available talent to fortify their interior depth.
Center John Michael Schmitz likely headed to free agency after being replaced in the starting lineup by Bryan Hudson; New York could look to the Seahawks’ center as an interior depth piece. Olu Oluwatimi is in the final year of his rookie deal and is scheduled to be an unrestricted free agent this offseason.
With Oluwatimi having lost the starting center job to Jalen Sundel, Seattle may be motivated to move the 6-foot-3, 309-pound lineman rather than risk losing him in free agency. The Giants should be interested, provided the price is right.

title: Joe Schoen Explains Why the Giants Extended Jameis Winston's Contract
full_text:
The New York Giants extended Jameis Winston’s contract by two years and $13 million before Jaxson Dart’s season-ending knee injury forced the backup quarterback to step in.
Dart went down seven snaps into the team’s Week 2 game, and Winston, the Giants’ hand-picked backup, stepped in.
The extension, which added two years to a deal that was due to expire after this season, lowered his cap hit and ensured Winston remains with the club through 2028.
Yet rather than stick with Winston, New York gave up a fifth-round draft pick to acquire J.J. McCarthy from the Minnesota Vikings, a quarterback Big Blue intends to start for the rest of the season.
Knowing Winston might not have been the ideal fit to run the Giants’ offense as designed full time, if something happened to Dart, why did the Giants bother to extend him?
The answer is that Winston was never meant to be a long-term answer, but rather a guy who could step in for a series or a game or two, which is exactly what he did.
“When you’re talking about a backup quarterback that also has leadership, that can lead not only that room, but the team,” general manager Joe Schoen said.
Winston, Schoen noted, has kept the Giants in games where they held a fourth-quarter lead or at least a tie, which is what the team wants from a backup when he's pressed into action.
But for the Giants and how their offense was designed to operate, having Winston run the offense for most of the season was something that raised questions about the sustainability of the plan.
Winston may not have been an ideal fit to go the distance in this offense, but his value to the organization remains high because he brings veteran leadership.
Despite his role as QB2, he was voted a team captain and sits on the eight-man leadership council chosen by head coach John Harbaugh.
Schoen recognized the importance of having a veteran quarterback after learning the lesson during his time in Buffalo when after the Bills drafted quarterback Josh Allen, they didn’t have a solid veteran presence in place to help the young signal caller.
Having seen how Winston has helped McCarthy and Dart in the meeting room has made the investment in keeping Winston around undoubtedly worth it for Big Blue.
Winston, to his credit, has been the picture-perfect model of professionalism despite the outside noise surrounding his play, dubbed “The Jameis Winston Experience,” and his demotion from the starting lineup.
The coaching staff hasn’t totally cast him aside in game planning. Last week, he successfully ran the Giants’ version of the “Tush Push.”
But his biggest contribution, which is what initially endeared him to the organization, lies in his willingness to lead by example.
“Serving leadership is very important in everything that we do. First, by example, out there on the field, how you go about your work, how you apply it in the film room, how you’re open and sharing things through your experience that you have encountered,” Winston said.
With McCarthy now under center, Winston’s job is to keep the quarterback room steady, a role the Giants valued enough to pay for before Dart ever got hurt.

title: What the Giants Must Fix Before Returning from Bye Week
full_text:
The New York Giants are enjoying a much-needed bye this week, sitting atop the NFC East, a position they’ll keep regardless of what happens in the division this coming weekend.
While the players are off enjoying a mini vacation of sorts, general manager Joe Schoen and head coach John Harbaugh are not resting; both want to ensure the Giants maintain their place atop the division when they resume play in Week 9 with a road game against the Philadelphia Eagles.
While Schoen, Harbaugh, and the rest of the Giants’ braintrust plot how they intend to handle the final days before the trade deadline and future roster moves, here are two things that should be at the top of their to-do list to keep them in the crow’s nest.
By far the most disappointing development of the 2026 season has been the performance of the defensive line depth behind starters Shelby Harris and D.J. Reader.
Second-year man Darius Alexander, whom the team undoubtedly hoped would continue to build on the flashes he showed at the end of last season, has been hot and cold, particularly in run defense.
C.J. Okoye has been a disappointment since the Giants acquired him in a trade with Baltimore, which received the Giants’ 2028 seventh-round draft pick.
Okoye has played 82 defensive snaps, 41 against the run, and has four tackles to show for it, two of them for loss. He was a healthy scratch for the team’s Week 6 game against the New Orleans Saints.
And rookie Bobby Jamison-Travis, who has played 38 defensive snaps (27 against the run), is still getting his feet wet after being inactive for the first five games of the season.
As a result, when Harris and Reader need a breather, the Giants have become more susceptible to big-play runs, with opposing rushers averaging 4.4 yards per carry when one or both are on the field and 5.2 yards per carry when neither is.
The Giants have added defensive lineman Dean Lowry to the mix, signing him to the practice squad this week. But if Big Blue does nothing else this week, it has to zero in on the defensive line, given what the braintrust has seen so far from the depth.
The Giants’ running game had a huge moment last week against the Texans, exploding for a season-best 188 yards (the fourth-best rushing total in the league in Week 7) on 34 carries, with 180 of those yards coming from the running backs.
But overall this season, most of the Giants’ rushing woes have come on between-the-tackles runs.
Per Next Gen Stats, only Tyrone Tracy Jr. (+1.6) and Devin Singletary (+0.3) have positive Rush EPA figures, while lead running back Cam Skattebo sits at -8.8.
Further, Skattebo’s rushing success rate between the tackles this season is 37.3%, the fourth-lowest among 15 running backs with at least 50 attempts.
While not all interior rushing struggles fall solely on the offensive line, it’s still an area Big Blue would like to improve moving forward. Some of those struggles have been on Skattebo himself for not always following his blocks.
Whatever the issue, the Giants will want to fix it when they return from the bye, especially with the Eagles (11.6% run stuff rate, 26th in the league) and Commanders (10.5% run stuff rate, 31st in the league) struggling to stop runs between the tackles.

title: Schoen: Giants “Happy Where We Are,” but Still Exploring Deadline Moves
full_text:
The New York Giants are in a rare situation, at least lately, sitting alone in first place in the NFC East with a 4-2-1 record at the halfway mark of the 2026 season, which coincides with their bye.
What makes it unusual is that the Giants, given what they’ve accomplished under head coach John Harbaugh, don’t necessarily have to be buyers or sellers with the November 10 trade deadline approaching.
But far be it from the Giants to be content with where things stand with their roster, which, despite their winning record, has lost several key players such as quarterback Jaxson Dart, outside linebacker Brian Burns, defensive lineman Chauncey Golston and returner Braxton Berrios.
General manager Joe Schoen, who, like Harbaugh, has the NFC East crown firmly in his sights, said he’s “happy where we are” and that he “really likes the team.”
But that doesn’t mean he’s about to rest on his laurels. Rather, he’s looking to keep improving the roster, and how the team goes about it matters.
“There are a lot of factors into it, in terms of where we are pick-wise. We don’t have a fourth or a fifth right now. So, you take that into account,” Schoen said on Tuesday.
“In some situations, that may rule some players out. Maybe that’s their value. Maybe a third is too rich or a sixth isn’t enough, so you start looking at future picks and contract status, and where we are depth-wise. So, a lot of factors that we’ll look at and who’s going to be available, who’s really available.”
The Giants’ biggest needs, at least for the short term, include defensive line depth, but given Harbaugh’s recent comments about longing for a Derrick Henry type of situation, running back is clearly on the team’s radar as well, even though the unit had a breakout game last week against the Houston Texans’ run defense, which was ranked third in the league at the time.
Questions remain about whether the Giants will make an offer for Colts running back Jonathan Taylor, who is rumored to be available as part of Indianapolis’ fire sale.
Schoen and his staff have also been exploring other scenarios around the league in their quest to give Harbaugh what he needs to keep the team competitive through its postseason push.
But there is also a question of what makes sense, whether that’s making a trade, signing a street free agent or plucking someone off another team’s practice squad, such as what the Giants did in signing running back Greg Desrosiers on Tuesday.
In other words, not every move has to be a big splash.
“It’s easy to say, go sign X, Y, and Z position, but if a team’s really not ready to get rid of somebody where they’re asking too much, it doesn’t match up with where you see the value, then it doesn’t make sense to do it,” Schoen said.
“So, we’re going to look at all the available options. And, certain teams have already started some trades, and we’ve been in contact with those teams and have a pretty good idea of who may or may not be available. And again, it’s got to make sense, short-term and long-term, when you make those moves.”

title: Banged Up but Winning: Giants Hold the NFC East Lead at the Bye
full_text:
Franchise quarterback. Elite pass rusher. Anchor middle linebacker. Let's start with how season-ending injuries in critical spots have created numerous obstacles for the New York Giants , who enter their bye week atop the NFC East.
Sure, they haven't always painted a pretty picture in fighting their way to a 4-2-1 record, but NFL teams don't get any extra credit for style points. The reality is that the Giants have already beaten the second-place Dallas Cowboys (3-4) and are one of five NFC teams to have two or fewer losses this season.
Piece by piece, coach John Harbaugh has called upon the depth chart built by general manager Joe Schoen to navigate significant detours along the way.
"It's just a matter of keep growing and keep building our execution and our ability to do things the right way at a high level. It takes that; it's a race," Harbaugh said this week.
"It's a marathon, but a marathon - I've been told - is a series of sprints, one after another. That's really what we're doing, a series of sprints, so we'll get a little bit of a break here, grab some Gatorade and a granola bar at the table, and then we'll be back into the race when we get back."
General managers usually say the season is the easiest part of their jobs because they're in charge of offseason roster building. It's clear Schoen and Harbaugh collaborated to improve the Giants' depth from the moment the new coach was hired, and it didn't come only through the draft with the likes of linebacker Arvel Reese and Francis Maguinoa.
The retention of middle linebacker Micah McFadden in his comeback from a broken foot, the signing of veteran cornerback Greg Newsome and the return of former Giants safety Jason Pinnock are just a few of the significant moves that have paid dividends.
Yet none may be more important than the early-season trade that sent a fifth-round draft choice to the Minnesota Vikings for quarterback J.J. McCarthy, who was sensational in his first Giants start while beating the Houston Texans on the road in overtime.
QB Jaxson Dart, LBs Brian Burns and Tremaine Edmunds, DL Chauncey Golston and Roy Robertson-Harris, WR Calvin Austin, and RET Gunner Olszewski. Each was expected to play a key role, but season-ending injuries have forced the Giants to rely on improved depth to maintain their preseason goal of challenging for the playoffs.
Schoen explained how the team expects to move forward in the second half of the season in his annual state-of-the-team address during the bye week. title: After Buckner Trade to 49ers, Two More D-Line Trade Targets for the Giants
full_text:
The New York Giants ’ biggest need ahead of the trade deadline remains their defensive line.
Despite pouring so many resources into the unit since the offseason, including the recent signing of veteran Dean Lowry to the practice squad, the depth behind starters Shelby Harris and D.J. Reader remains suspect, particularly against the run.
When either or both of Harris and Reader are on the field, opposing offenses have averaged 4.4 yards per carry. When one or both are off the field, that average has jumped to 5.2 yards per carry.
Their absences have also been felt on third down. When either or both of Harris and Reader have been on the field, opponents have converted 64.3% of their third-down attempts. When both have been off the field, that percentage has increased to 71.4%.
If the Giants are all in on making a run for the NFC East title this year, and they clearly are, it may be worth trading for a veteran defensive lineman who can provide more consistency, particularly against the run, where the defense has been erratic.
With DeForest Buckner traded from the Colts back to the San Francisco 49ers for a fourth-round draft pick , here are a couple of other options the Giants could consider to upgrade their defensive line depth.
The Dolphins are going nowhere this season as they work their way out from under the salary cap mess created in part by releasing quarterback Tua Tagovailoa.
So it’s fair to wonder whether they might embark on a fire sale to add to their nine picks in 2027.
Zach Sieler, in the first year of a three-year, $64 million deal signed with Miami this past offseason, has historically been a solid defensive lineman, according to his PFF grades . This year, that hasn’t been the case, but then again, few Dolphins players can be described as solid.
Sieler, a seventh-round pick of the Ravens under Harbaugh in 2018, has 13 quarterback pressures and 13 stops through six games. He has missed only three tackles.
If the Giants were to acquire Sieler, they would be on the hook this year for $76,470 for each week he is on their roster. Per reports, Sieler would prefer to stay with Miami .
As for compensation, Buckner, a three-time Pro Bowler and two-time All-Pro, fetched a fourth-round pick, so the Giants could ask the Dolphins for one of their two sixth-rounders in 2027, the second of which they acquired in the trade that sent offensive lineman Daniel Faalele to the Jaguars.
Or, if the Giants don’t want to keep draining their 2027 draft picks, they might offer a 2028 pick instead.
Like Sieler, Dalvin Tomlinson has a connection to Giants head coach John Harbaugh, albeit through Harbaugh’s brother, Jim, the Chargers' head coach.
Tomlinson, 6-foot-3 and 317 pounds, began his career as the Giants' second-round pick in 2017. He spent his first four seasons with Big Blue, then signed with the Vikings as an unrestricted free agent. After two seasons in Minnesota, Tomlinson spent two years with the Browns and one with the Cardinals.
He signed with the Chargers this past offseason on a one-year deal worth up to $6.5 million.
Tomlinson is another player who could potentially be worth a sixth-round pick in a trade. If the Giants acquired him, he would cost a cap-friendly $158,235 per week.
He can also earn $30,000 for each week he is active, with playtime incentives of up to $1 million based on cumulative game snaps and a $300,000 weight clause, according to Spotrac .

title: Giants Place RB Tyrone Tracy Jr. on IR; Add Former Chargers Runner to Roster
full_text:
Another week, another New York Giants player is heading to injured reserve.
Running back Tyrone Tracy Jr., who injured his hamstring in the second quarter of Sunday’s game against the Houston Texans, will be placed on IR this week, general manager Joe Schoen announced ahead of his annual bye-week press briefing.
Tracy, the team’s fifth-round draft pick in 2024, has appeared in all seven games this season without making a start.
He has 19 rushing attempts for 55 yards and two touchdowns and has caught five of seven targets for 54 yards and a touchdown. He was looking to record his third straight season with 1,000 scrimmage yards, but that goal now appears to be a long shot.
Taking Tracy’s spot on the 53-man roster is running back Greg Desrosiers, whom the Giants signed off the Chargers’ practice squad. Desrosiers, 5-foot-11 and 200 pounds, signed with the Chargers as an undrafted free agent out of Memphis after this year’s draft.
Desrosiers had a six-year college career, playing two seasons each for Louisville, Massachusetts and Memphis. He finished with 211 carries for 1,302 yards and 16 touchdowns, and 76 receptions for 612 yards and seven touchdowns as a receiver.
This past summer, Desrosiers appeared in all three preseason games for the Chargers, rushing for 166 yards on 23 carries with one touchdown and catching one of two targets for eight yards.

title: Giants Make Long Anticipated Practice Squad Signing
full_text:
The New York Giants are finally signing defensive lineman Dean Lowry to their practice squad, general manager Joe Schoen confirmed.
Lowry, who played for the Steelers until they released him after this past summer’s training camp, was first linked to the Giants in September , but the chatter died down quickly when the move didn’t materialize.
Lowry suffered a torn ACL in August 2025, so the Giants may have waited to see how his rehab progressed this past summer.
Either way, Lowry, 6-foot-6 and 300 pounds, brings veteran experience to a defensive line group that, outside of starters D.J. Reader and Shelby Harris, has been inconsistent, especially against the run.
The Packers selected Lowry in the fourth round of the 2016 draft out of Northwestern. He played for Green Bay until the 2022 season before moving on to the Vikings for one season and then to the Steelers.
Lowry, 32, has appeared in 132 regular-season games with 85 starts and has 271 career tackles, 23 tackles for loss, 16.5 sacks, one interception and five fumble recoveries.
His best season came in 2021 with Green Bay, when he recorded five sacks in 17 starts.
Lowry’s skill set likely aligns with what the Giants previously had Chauncey Golston doing on the defensive line: a rotational pass rusher at 5-technique, or at 3-technique in an odd front.
Golston is on season-ending injured reserve with a neck ailment.
The Giants released receiver Jason Brownlee fromt he practice squad to make room for Lowry.

title: What Giants’ Week 7 Win Changed About Their Trade Deadline Plans
full_text:
Maybe, just maybe, the New York Giants ’ roster needs aren’t what they thought they were.
Ahead of their Week 7 game against the Houston Texans, the Giants were thought to need a running back to boost a sagging rushing attack. The unit ranked 22nd in the league at a dismal 3.8 yards per carry, its 629 rushing yards ranked 16th, and its offensive success rate of 43.2% ranked 20th.
But after head coach John Harbaugh challenged his running backs to step up, they delivered a historic performance. For the first time since October 1950, four different runners scored a touchdown in a 27-21 overtime win over the Texans.
With the rushing game delivering 188 yards on 34 carries against what had been the league’s third-ranked run defense, New York has quelled the calls for a trade for a running back such as Colts star Jonathan Taylor, who is believed to be among those the Colts are considering moving by the November 10 trade deadline.
This isn’t to say that the Giants won’t need to add to the running back group at some point. New York is undoubtedly holding its collective breath that the hamstring injuries suffered by Cam Skattebo and Tyrone Tracy Jr. heal up over the bye.
But with the running game boosted not just by the backs themselves but also by the insertion of quarterback J.J. McCarthy, who brings back the RPO threat, the need to trade for a running back isn’t as great as it once was.
That all being said, the Giants still need to watch the future.
Running back Devin Singletary is in the final year of his contract, and there is no guarantee he’ll be back with the team after this year.
Skattebo, despite the energy he brings to the game, is still part of a rotation that has seen him primarily handle the early-down and goal-line duties, casting doubt on whether he’s a legitimate RB1 or just someone who, by virtue of the Giants’ running back room, has been thrust into that role.
And Tracy is more of a change-of-pace back than the bell cow Harbaugh seems to want in the offense.
Remember, it wasn’t that long ago when the Giants reportedly had strong interest in former Notre Dame running back Jeremiyah Love, who was taken one pick before the Giants went on the clock this past April.
It also wasn’t that long ago that Harbaugh yearned for a workhorse running back like the one he had in Baltimore with Derrick Henry. He said he “would love for us” to have “a Derrick Henry circumstance.”
But Harbaugh and the Giants must honestly answer whether they are one running back away from not only making the postseason but also staying there once they do.
If their current running backs keep delivering as they did against the Texans, they could defer adding a workhorse running back until next offseason, when they can get someone either in free agency or on a rookie contract via the draft.

title: Giants Rookie Report: Reese, Mauigoa and Fields Shine in Overtime Win Over Texans
full_text:
Earning a hard-fought road win one week after an embarrassing home performance marks a rising, maturing football team. When rookies overcome the same circumstances, then you really have something cooking. John Harbaugh is building a culture on the New York Giants .
Big Blue’s first-timers responded after a Week 6 loss to the New Orleans Saints, playing a key role in Sunday’s 27-21 overtime win over the Houston Texans.
Several rookies dazzled, but a couple of outings were underwhelming. Let’s check in on the rookies after a jubilant Week 7.
The former Ohio State star linebacker has had some lows in his first NFL season, but the highs have been far more frequent and mighty impressive.
Arvell Reese demonstrated his superb athleticism and excellent hustle on one play, pressuring Texans quarterback C.J. Stroud before running downfield to make the tackle. Only a select few can cover the field that swiftly, and they are not typically rookies.
Reese contributed to a relentless defensive attack, posting half a sack and seven total tackles. A No. 5 overall pick should have exceptional physical gifts, but there is no guarantee he will play with a high motor. Reese is fulfilling both categories so far.
Miami powerhouse Francis “Sisi” Mauigoa has occasionally looked like a weak link on the offensive line, which is understandable given his move from tackle. Still, at other times he has carried himself like a seasoned pro. His showing in Houston definitely falls under the latter.
Mauigoa recorded a 100 percent pass-block win rate, per Pro Football Focus, providing stalwart protection for J.J. McCarthy in his first Giants start and creating more opportunities for the Cam Skattebo-led backfield.
His continued development could determine just how good this O-line and offense become.
Malachi Fields officially introduced himself to fans with a breakout game at NRG Stadium. The 6-foot-4 wide receiver used his size and strength to punish Houston. He recorded a career-high four receptions for 83 yards.
With tremendous sideline awareness, Fields created space and then shook off the defense for 40 yards after the catch. He was every bit the deep threat that Joe Schoen and John Harbaugh invested in at the NFL Draft. And he is just getting started.
The Giants will not achieve meaningful success unless the defensive tackle group is solid. Bobby Jamison-Travis may be the missing link the team has been searching for over the last couple of years. He added an indisputable boost in Week 7.
The sixth-round selection was an active member of a run defense that held Woody Marks to a meager 3.5 yards per carry. He logged 24 snaps , six more than he did against the Saints, and could get even more after the bye.
Jamison-Travis does not need to be a Day 3 gem. Competent play will more than suffice.
The returning Paulson Adebo filled in for the injured Greg Newsome II, leaving no room for Colton Hood in the secondary. He did help out on special teams, however.
The No. 37 overall pick played 14 snaps and appeared to hold his own. Until he learns the nuances of being an NFL cornerback, Hood will have to make the most of his chances in the third phase of the game.
J.C. Davis added immediate value at left tackle in Week 6, when Andrew Thomas was evaluated for a concussion. With Thomas back this week, Davis did not see time on the line and instead got some work on special teams.
The unit was sharper than it was against New Orleans, and the 6-foot-4, 322-pounder did his part. If needed, Harbaugh should feel comfortable giving the AP All-Big Ten first-team selection more opportunities on the O-line.
Generally a reliable special teams contributor, sixth-rounder Jack Kelly took a slight step back in Houston. He missed a tackle , which is always a concern in coverage situations.
Still, Kelly deserves some trust given the film he has put together for New York in 2026.
The undrafted kicker is in free fall. Dominic Zvada is surely running out of chances after missing 56- and 44-yard field goals against the Texans. Those blunders could easily have been the difference in the game if the squad hadn’t excelled in most other areas.
Zvada is still in a precarious position. All the goodwill he stored by nailing his first nine field goal attempts has nearly evaporated.
Harbaugh is not ready to make a change yet, though, so the 2024 Big Ten Kicker of the Year must straighten out during the bye week.

title: Latest Jets Signing Suggest Bad News for T'Vondre Sweat Injury Concerns
full_text:
Any hope Jets fans had for head coach Aaron Glenn and the team this year hit a low point last Sunday, as Gang Green fell to the winless Dolphins, 28-25, at MetLife Stadium.
The defeat dropped New York to 2-5, and Glenn’s AFC East losing streak continues. With the loss, Glenn became the ninth coach since the 1970 NFL merger to start his career 0-8 against his own division.
Despite the humiliating loss and public outcry from fans over the past few weeks, Glenn is unlikely to be fired mid-season and should have the rest of the year to turn things around. However, he’ll have to do so without defensive tackle T’Vondre Sweat, who went down in the team’s loss to Miami.
The injury occurred in the second quarter when safety Dane Belton attempted to tackle Dolphins quarterback Malik Willis and accidentally hit Sweat’s knee. Although the 25-year-old walked off the field, New York ruled him out for the rest of the game with a knee injury.
Before listing Sweat as week-to-week on Wednesday ( h/t ESPN's Rich Cimini ), New York bolstered the defensive line depth on Tuesday by adding Amari McNeill to the practice squad. The undrafted free agent from Colorado spent the summer with the Kansas City Chiefs before being waived during final cuts.
With David Onyemata still on injured reserve, McNeil’s arrival suggests that the Jets could be without Sweat for multiple weeks.
DT T'Vondre Sweat (knee) and ED Joseph Ossai (ankle) are in the week-to-week category, per Glenn. #Jets
With New York struggling against the run last season, ranking 29th in rushing yards allowed per game (139.5), and transitioning to a new defensive scheme, the team traded edge rusher Jermaine Johnson II to the Titans for Sweat in March.
Since entering the league in 2024, the former Texas Longhorn has quickly emerged as one of the best interior linemen against the run. Sweat has earned a 75 and a 79.2 run-defense grade in his first two seasons, per Pro Football Focus, ranking among the top 10 interior defensive linemen in the category each year.
Sweat hasn’t replicated similar success with the Jets; however, his 67.8 run-defense grade still ranks highest among the team’s interior defensive linemen, per PFF . Although New York’s run defense hasn’t improved with Sweat’s addition, ranking 24th in rushing yards allowed per game (127.7), the unit will suffer in his absence.
With his massive 6-foot-4, 366-pound frame, Sweat commands double teams and clogs the running lanes. Without him, the Jets lack a similar physical presence up front.
Additionally, this isn't the first time Sweat has missed extended time. He missed five games last year with an ankle injury and missed the first three weeks of this year’s training camp with a hamstring injury he suffered in mid-June.
Although we shouldn’t expect Sweat to be sidelined as long as he was last season, the Jets’ decision to bring in McNeill suggests they’re preparing without their starting nose tackle for some time.
McNeill went undrafted after spending five years between Tennessee and Colorado. With the Buffaloes, he earned a rotational role on the defensive line, posting 77 total tackles, seven sacks, 39 pressures, and three forced fumbles in 32 games.
His best season came in 2025, when he recorded 21 total tackles, half a sack, and 11 pressures in nine games, earning an 81.5 overall grade, per PFF . McNeill’s experience and solid production at Colorado earned him an opportunity to prove himself in Kansas City.
Playing 76 defensive snaps across the team’s three preseason games, McNeill recorded one tackle and four pressures. Although he showed some promise, his lack of NFL experience makes it unlikely that we will see McNeill suit up in green and white anytime soon.
New York has relied on a four-man interior rotation, with Sweat sidelined, and will likely split his snaps among Jowon Briggs, Darrell Jackson Jr., Jack Heflin, and Harrison Phillips.
While McNeill gives the Jets additional depth, his signing doesn’t mean we’ll see him on the field. With Heflin’s elevation, New York has other options to help fill the void left by Sweat, including Jackson Jr. and Heflin, who will likely see more snaps in the rotation.
Still, the timing of McNeill’s signing raises concerns about how long the Jets expect to be without Sweat. With New York already struggling to stop the run and Glenn needing wins to save his job , losing one of their key contributors is significant.
In the meantime, Gang Green will need the rest of the unit to pick up the slack and step up quickly before the run defense becomes a bigger problem than it already is.

title: Mason Taylor's Hot Streak Is Actually a Good Thing for Kenyon Sadiq's Jets Outlook
full_text:
Coming off a humiliating loss to the previously winless Dolphins last Sunday, the Jets are in a familiar position once again as they appear to be on their way toward another lost season in Gotham.
There is no denying this was a rock-bottom performance against a Dolphins team that hadn't led in a single game coming into Week 7, before they immediately set the tone with an opening-drive touchdown. If there was a silver lining, though, second-year tight end Mason Taylor had a career performance, bringing in five catches for 62 yards and two of New York's three TDs.
As disappointing as it was that the Jets dropped a winnable game and fell to 0-8 against divisional opponents in head coach Aaron Glenn's tenure, Taylor has clearly become one of quarterback Geno Smith's top targets with an uptick in receptions in each of his last three games since returning from a thumb injury.
One assumes Taylor's hot streak is not beneficial for rookie TE Kenyon Sadiq, who has been quiet with just four combined catches in his last four games since he went off for seven catches, 105 yards, and a TD in the Week 3 loss to the Lions. However, additional attention on Taylor could open the door for more favorable matchups for Sadiq and allow him to fully take advantage of his elite athleticism.
It seems like forever ago since Sadiq arrived on the NFL scene with a vengeance. As Taylor struggled to get off to a good start and dealt with a thumb injury, Sadiq showcased his versatility with a rushing TD in the season-opening win over the Titans and made this sensational diving catch for his first career NFL TD reception (h/t NFL) two weeks later.
Kenyon Sadiq's FIRST career TD 👏 @NYJvsDET on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/Hi0wg1aL4R
Since then, he has taken a backseat to Taylor and rarely been involved in the offensive game plan. Granted, that shouldn't be a huge surprise considering the coaching malpractice from offensive coordinator Frank Reich and his inability to get the ball to WR1 Garrett Wilson.
If he can botch his top receiver's usage, there is no reason to expect anything different regarding Sadiq's touches. After all, his overall grade from Pro Football Focus (64) ranks 23rd out of 30 qualified TEs . That said, he's also credited with 102 yards after the catch and has proven to be someone who can make plays in the open field when he receives the ball.
Just because Taylor was a stud and has shown he can be versatile himself as a talented receiver who can also make a positive impact as a blocker, there is no reason Sadiq should be ignored in the passing attack and not take on a larger role with his skill set.
With the athleticism and raw receiving ability, Sadiq is easily someone who could see more snaps at WR and still make just as much of an impact, while Taylor commands the majority of the TE duties. Aside from rookie Omar Cooper Jr., who has returned from a high ankle sprain with back-to-back 100-yard receiving games and two TDs, there has not been much consistency among the wideouts.
Wilson only has a pair of 100-yard games this season and just six combined catches on nine targets in the last two games. Even Adonai Mitchell, whose return from a finger injury last week was expected to boost Wilson's performance by taking some attention away from him, had zero catches on three targets in his return.
Due to the inconsistency behind Cooper on the WR depth chart, combined with his emergence, the Jets have an opportunity to utilize Sadiq more often to provide a little more stability. Throw in the fact that Isaiah Williams has failed to take advantage of his opportunities and has not even been targeted since Week 5, and the door is definitely open for Sadiq if the coaching staff chooses to use him that way.
Not only can Taylor's success take some of the burden off Sadiq as he continues to refine his technique, but it can also allow him to utilize his hybrid pass-catching abilities, while Taylor handles the more physical and standard TE duties.
As bad as Sadiq's recent stretch has looked, especially compared to how the season began, it may not be the worst thing if Taylor primarily assumes the TE role and more favorable matchups are available for Sadiq to exploit as either a TE or WR if that is what the offense sees fit.
